channel.title: Podcast — The world is too loud. Read what matters.
channel.description: Every day, the judgements worth remembering from 201 Chinese- and English-language podcasts. Points and quotes carry timestamps — tap one and you are back at the second it was said. Quotes are checked word for word and figures back to the source; anything unverifiable is cut, not published.

item.title: New Housing Fund Rules: Take What You Can, but Don't Treat It as Savings
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-zhixing-公积金新规-能取则取-但别把它当存款/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-zhixing-公积金新规-能取则取-但别把它当存款/
item.description: The housing provident fund is not savings you can withdraw at will; fraudulent withdrawal gets you pursued and barred from any withdrawal for three years. But the new rules put renting first in the withdrawal order and scrap the rent-to-income ratio cap — money you should take, you should still take.
item.content:encoded:
The housing provident fund is not savings you can withdraw at will; fraudulent withdrawal gets you pursued and barred from any withdrawal for three years. But the new rules put renting first in the withdrawal order and scrap the rent-to-income ratio cap — money you should take, you should still take.

Three people in different situations — a self-employed worker, a young professional, a property owner — each run their own numbers, turning the 20 clause changes in the new rules into concrete decisions. The second half on flexible-employment contributions and the comparison with the system-inside track is especially informative.

13:10 Six months after auto-withdrawal, I paused it myself
After Zhou Yi activated Beijing's no-threshold monthly rent withdrawal of 2,000 yuan, she found the money slid into another card the moment it arrived, completely decoupled from the mental account for paying rent. By month's end, once her spending card was maxed out, it was automatically deducted from that card, adding friction to daily life. After confirming the fund balance earns 1.5% interest — higher than the roughly 0.95% on a one-year bank time deposit — she paused the withdrawal the next day. Yu Bai noted this contrasts with the advice three years ago to ‘take everything you're entitled to and use everything you can’; two young colleagues in the department had made the same choice. Lao Qian cautioned that this is indeed inefficient use of funds, but most people can't achieve the efficiency they imagine — people just cook their own books.

21:12 The housing fund is not savings; not being able to withdraw is the norm
Yu Bai walked through an extreme scenario: a young person loses their job and goes home with no liquid funds, a few tens of thousands in the provident fund, but the home is owner-occupied, so it qualifies neither as a home purchase nor as renting. Even if the new rules allow withdrawal for renovation or property fees, if the family has no such needs, there's nothing to be done. If you risk fraudulent withdrawal under a fabricated pretext, you'll be pursued to return the full amount and barred from any withdrawal for three years. So both approaches hold — ‘take everything you're entitled to’ and ‘treat it as forced savings at a higher rate than a demand deposit’ — the key is the individual situation.

23:43 The new rules put renting first in the withdrawal order
This revision adjusts 20 clauses in total. First, renovating an owner-occupied home and paying property fees for an owner-occupied home are included in the withdrawal scope for the first time; the fund no longer serves only loan-based home purchases. Second, renting withdrawal previously required rent to exceed a set proportion of household wage income; this version removes that restriction, and renting is placed first in the withdrawal order. Third, flexible-employment workers are formally brought into the system for the first time — self-employed individuals and part-time workers can contribute voluntarily and apply for provident fund loans. In addition, the management center must reply to withdrawal applications within three days and to loan applications within ten days, and nationwide mutual recognition of contribution records is being advanced.

30:18 The share of contributions lent out has fallen from 70% to 30%
The figure Lao Qian saw: this year, the share of provident fund contributions lent out is as low as just over 30%, while at the peak it was over 70% — a steady decline in just a few years. In other words, the theoretically most stable, lowest-rate, highest-quality lending channel is actually used by only just over 30% of people. This directly reflects how low the willingness to buy homes is. Lao Qian also points out the new rules point toward housing consumption rather than leverage: renting moved to first place, property fees and renovation can be withdrawn, thresholds greatly lowered — supporting measures as the real estate market shifts from an incremental to a stock phase, and also echoing aging: the monthly withdrawal ratio turned up in 2023, exactly corresponding to the 1960s cohort retiring.

32:20 If you want to buy a home, be careful about withdrawing
Yu Bai warns: the provident fund loan amount is tied to the account balance — in some cities you can borrow 16 times the balance, in others 20 times, varying by city. Guangzhou also has multiple caps; when applying, the smallest of several standards applies. For example, for a first or second owner-occupied home the minimum down payment is 20%, so a 1 million yuan home can't be loaned more than 800,000; and monthly repayment exceeding 50% of monthly income is also disallowed. So before withdrawing the fund as living expenses, check your city's loan rules. Yu Bai is also cautious about the buy logic of ‘rent-to-price ratio close to the provident fund rate, only a down payment short’: you also have to consider depreciation, price fluctuations, and how to withstand risk once a 600,000 down payment is locked up.

44:05 Flexible-employment contributors carry the full amount alone
For flexible-employment workers, the contribution base and rate are calculated the same as for employees, but there's no employer paying half — effectively one person bears the full 10% to 24%. The contribution base must be self-declared: below 10,000 no proof is needed; above 10,000 you must log into the individual income tax app and check your tax details as documentation, to prevent over-declaring to extract a higher loan amount. Zhou Yi did the math: 10,000 at 10% to 24% is 1,000 to 2,400 yuan, and this money isn't counted in income tax, but if you don't use it you lose out. In addition, most pilot cities require 6 to 12 consecutive months of contributions before applying for a provident fund loan, and most don't allow retroactive lump-sum payments.

47:33 Inside the system, the provident fund is an invisible benefit
Zhou Yi asked a friend with a public institution post back home, who openly showed a screenshot of her provident fund account: monthly deposits were more than double Zhou Yi's, and the balance already exceeded her savings. The friend lives at home with no rental need, so the fund just accumulates as forced savings or future loan capacity, plus an occupational annuity, with the contribution base including all bonuses and subsidies. Lao Qian adds: the provident fund is tax-free, and with the individual pension capped at 12,000 yuan a year and taxed at 3% on withdrawal, those inside the system already get an extra layer of tax advantage. On the data: in 2025 the national average annual wage for urban non-private unit employees was 129,441 yuan, for private units 71,590 yuan — while working hours run the other way.

52:44 Full provident fund contributions are a slice for judging a company
Lao Qian's judgment on ‘is a company that pays the provident fund a better choice’ hasn't changed at all: a company that pays the full provident fund shows it respects employees and respects the rules, meaning it's likely well-run in every aspect, not playing games with policy. He goes further: this points to not making profit maximization the first goal, treating people as people, and the invisible returns show up elsewhere. Zhou Yi did the math: a wage base of 100, take-home just over 70, but the boss pays over 130 — everyone in the chain feels aggrieved. Lao Qian cites Ford's Model T wage increase — letting workers afford a car and have time to use it wasn't capitalist conscience, it was a better utility function.

item.title: Stablecoins Are Not a Duopoly: Big Companies Want Their Own Coin
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-empire-稳定币不是双寡头-大公司要发自己的币/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-empire-稳定币不是双寡头-大公司要发自己的币/
item.description: The multi-stablecoin debate returns: Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins, Circle's USDC network effect is underrated, but if rates fall to 2-3% its revenue gets cut in half.
item.content:encoded:
The multi-stablecoin debate returns: Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins, Circle's USDC network effect is underrated, but if rates fall to 2-3% its revenue gets cut in half.

Regulation, stablecoins, Circle Arc, the Meta vs Instinct fight, Polymarket's talent war — high information density, and the back half is worth more than the front half.

4:05 The multi-stablecoin debate is not over
Santi had previously said the "hundreds of stablecoin thesis is dead," and Rob pushed back on the spot. Rob says he knows of multinationals issuing their own stablecoins right now: SoFi, Verve, two bank consortia, the Stripe consortium, MoneyGram, Western Union are all doing it, and Bridge already has its own stablecoin internally for treasury management. His mechanism: big companies hold a lot of cash, and if they can earn yield on it, they have an incentive to issue their own coin rather than use USDC or USDT. Santi pressed: don't these big companies have FX desks at JP Morgan and Morgan Stanley? Rob said it depends on the company's size and the complexity of its global treasury management — Western Union's remittance corridors in Africa and Latin America are something JP Morgan's correspondent banking network can't do well.

13:18 CLARITY failed, but nobody has really given up
The Senate voted down the CLARITY Act on Tuesday 49 to 50, with 60 votes needed. Three Republicans — Susan Collins, Josh Hawley, Jerry Moran — voted against, and every Democrat they had been counting on voted against too. Santi said not to over-read Tillis's turn, since Kirsten Gillibrand said that same day she is still pushing the legislation. On Polymarket the odds of passage fell as low as 4% at one point, then came back to 8%. Markets fell on the news, with Coinbase down 10% and Circle down 12%. Rob said it's worth remembering that dozens of people worked on this bill for a year, including staff on the Banking Committee and the Agriculture Committee.

16:58 The SEC gives tokenized stocks a five-year exemption
The SEC issued an order granting tokenized securities trading venues (TSVS) a five-year interim conditional exemption, letting them trade tokenized NMS stocks through permissioned AMMs and liquidity pools without registering as exchanges, and liquidity providers got a limited market-maker exemption. Two key conditions: token holders must get the same rights as the underlying stock, such as dividends and voting; and third-party tokenization requires written notice with an opportunity for the issuer to object. Santi read it out and said this clause could directly break the current onchain tokenized stock practice — if AMC can object, you can't just throw AMC onto Hyperliquid. Rob said this was almost certainly coming, because onchain tokenized stocks currently create strange dislocations after hours and pre-market, and Robinhood pairing memecoins with tokenized stocks is an example.

22:43 The winner in tokenization is the whole ecosystem
Rob said it's hard to point to a single winner. The obvious beneficiaries are issuers, existing exchanges and clearinghouses, new exchanges that want into the US market (Coinbase, Polymarket, Lighter, Hyperliquid, Backpack), global neobanks, and new transfer agents and core infrastructure providers like Alpaca. Santi said his first reaction was Superstate and Securitize, and Securitize was up 16% that day. Rob said this looks more like a rising tide lifting all boats than value concentrating in one place. He added that as more assets come onchain, everything onchain gets bigger — more liquidity, more users, better infrastructure, more stablecoin issuance.

29:06 S&P buying Open Zeppelin is buying data
S&P is a ratings agency with a roughly $120 billion market cap and about $14 billion in revenue; this week it first led Kao's Series B extension (Kao raised its B four years ago, and this time may have raised about $50 million, bringing the B to about $110 million total, with investors including RBC, DRW, Broadridge, BNP, Nasdaq), then acquired smart contract security firm Open Zeppelin. Rob said the acquisition surprised him, since Open Zeppelin doesn't seem like a company that would run a process to sell itself. His read: S&P gives ratings, and it can use Open Zeppelin for real-time risk benchmarks and data, to assess what's happening inside protocols, and then sell that to clients. Santi said he heard this is the first of many, and that traditional capital markets data and analytics players (Moody's and others) will do more deals like this. Rob said a lot of crypto companies raised a lot of money and have good products but aren't good enough as standalone businesses, and companies like S&P grow into conglomerates by repeatedly buying good niche products and then bundling them for you through a terminal.

37:40 Circle pushing memes on Arc day one was a misstep
Circle launched Arc, with more than 190 partners on day one and over $220 million in TVL pre-seeded in a Morpho vault. Rob said he doesn't understand why Circle came out on day one pushing a bunch of memes, since Arc had always been positioned as a payments-first chain, talking about agentic finance, privacy, FX liquidity, real commercial activity. He said this is the exact opposite of the story Circle has told for a long time, and it left a lot of people with a bad impression. Santi said he went to Circle's launch event yesterday, and the room and Twitter were two completely different worlds — within an hour he met people from BlackRock, DTCC, ICE, Visa, MoneyGram, and Circle's convening power is extremely strong; if they had launched purely on the original positioning, it would have landed much better. Rob said Circle may have been looking at the success of Robinhood chain, but Robinhood is a trading platform and Circle is a payments company, and having bought Taza Pay it should stay in its own lane.

42:38 Circle's revenue gets cut in half by rates
Rob said he doesn't expect 4% to 4.5% rates to last forever, and that rates will normalize to between 2% and 3%, which means that if Circle is just an interest-income business, its revenue at the current TVL gets cut in half. He also said that as a payments stablecoin, if it can't share yield with end customers, there isn't much reason to hold large amounts of it. Circle's agreement with Coinbase requires giving 50% to Coinbase, which puts it at a disadvantage competing with new stablecoins. So Circle is working to become a payments company and get a payments company multiple, and Arc and Circle Payment Network are both part of that story. Santi said not to underestimate USDC's network effect — in DeFi there is now only one thing that matters for liquidity, and that's USDC; every DeFi founder needs USDC on their platform.

46:14 Instinct's reckoning comes in month four
Rob said companies are now getting bigger faster and raising more faster, that venture capital as a market structure is broken, and that the hottest companies see valuations rise faster and faster regardless of fundamentals. He said a company's first big reckoning usually comes in year four, but Instinct's first big reckoning will come in month four — because the two biggest companies in the world are about to ship direct competitors, Grokbot and Meta's Muse. Santi said from his own use Muse is six to eight times better than Instinct; Instinct is clearly compute-constrained, and on the same question Muse is sometimes 10 to 15 minutes faster, fails less, and can route around the roadblocks Resy has set up for these products. Rob said he doesn't know how growth investors are comfortable at this valuation, and the only thing that could prove them wrong is Instinct sprinting to train its own model, but that takes a billion dollars to build data centers.

item.title: Prediction Markets Aren't Casinos, but 90% of Volume Comes From Sports
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freakonomics-预测市场不是赌场-但九成交易量来自体育/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-freakonomics-预测市场不是赌场-但九成交易量来自体育/
item.description: Kalshi traded four years of compliance for 90% market share, but its revenue structure looks more like a bookmaker's; what's truly underrated are quiet markets like FDA approvals.
item.content:encoded:
Kalshi traded four years of compliance for 90% market share, but its revenue structure looks more like a bookmaker's; what's truly underrated are quiet markets like FDA approvals.

The first half is founder narrative; the value is in the middle and back: how contracts are written, sports at 90%, regulatory risk. Worth listening for anyone who wants to understand prediction market mechanics.

8:16 Comply for four years first, then open your first market
Kalshi's two founders wrote "regulatory first" into the company's principles, spending four years getting regulatory approval before launching their first market. Mansoor says this is anti-Silicon Valley: others build the product first and patch in compliance later, while they asked the federal government up front how the thing should be regulated. The cost was nearly giving up almost every day for the first four years, held together by "the cost of regret is too high." The payoff came in 2024, when a federal appeals court ruled Kalshi could list election contracts, landing before the presidential election. Mansoor attributes the 90% market share directly to this path: institutions prefer to plug into a platform inside the system, because changing the rules from outside the system is harder.

15:36 Prediction markets force you to shut up, not to take a stance
Robin Hanson lays out three mechanisms that make prediction markets more accurate than polls or expert interviews. First, people being interviewed have an incentive to be interesting, dramatic, and to please the questioner, while the market only rewards being right. Second, the market gives you an incentive to shut up about topics you don't understand — you only bet in the few markets where you genuinely have an edge, whereas interviewees will answer confidently on things they don't know. Third, the market doesn't require you to have a direct opinion on a topic; it invites you to find mispricings and errors in others' pricing, and pays you to correct them. He closes with an old poker-table line: sit down, look for the sucker, and if you can't find one, the sucker is you — so don't play that market.

20:48 Internal prediction markets die from project owners' excuses
Eli Lilly ran an internal prediction market in the early 2000s that successfully predicted which drug compounds would pass Phase III trials; Google also ran a project called Google Profit. Both were considered effective, and neither survived. Hanson's explanation: the project owner wants to know whether they'll deliver on time, but what they want even more is a good excuse if they fail. And the best excuse is precisely "everything was going fine, and then at the last minute something nobody could have foreseen happened." A market that continuously and accurately predicts whether you'll be late invalidates that excuse in advance, so nobody wants it to exist.

22:58 Domain expertise is not the key ability for forecasting the future
Mansoor cites Philip Tetlock's Superforecasting research: put experts in a given domain (say, geopolitics) up against a group of non-experts forecasting the same set of events, and the non-experts win. His explanation is that domain experts become too doctrinaire over time, while people who can step back and look at things calmly are better calibrated and less biased. Mansoor says this is a fairly heretical statement in politics, academia, and financial analysis circles — it implies that if you want more accurate answers, you should look for a diverse group of participants who pride themselves on self-calibration, critical reading, and filtering information, not an authority in some field. He treats this as Kalshi's underlying logic.

33:28 One contract takes a month to write, for grammar and apostrophes
Nicole Kagan writes the contracts and self-certifies them with the CFTC. The most complex category is "what someone will say in a given speech," and they recently rewrote the rules because a pile of grammar questions came up: what if there's an apostrophe? If they misspeak or mispronounce it, does it still count as the same word? What if it appears inside a proper noun? What if the livestream cuts out midway and it's uploaded somewhere else later? These rules took over a month to write, seven or eight pages, extremely detailed. When Bloomberg reported on it, they guessed the rules were for automated processing and must be for AI; Kagan says that's not it at all — they were written so users could understand them, and they never considered that "something a human can understand is probably something a computer can understand too."

35:35 When you can't judge a winner, settle at the last fair price
Kalshi's contracts are usually binary: pay $1 if the event happens, $0 if it doesn't, with every position fully collateralized — if one side bets 30 cents, someone must bet 70 cents. But some situations can't be judged yes or no. Cardi B was clearly dancing in her seven-second Super Bowl halftime show cameo, but she had no mic and it couldn't be confirmed whether she was singing, so the team said "we are epistemically uncertain" and settled at the last fair price. Another case is 50-50: when multiple people win simultaneously, each settles at 50 cents. Kagan says they have the right to do this when whether an event meets the criteria is "genuinely unclear," and they've already revised the halftime show contract — the new rules require an audible lead or backing vocal, and under the new rules Cardi B counts as not having performed.

41:52 90% of volume comes from sports, and that's the most uncomfortable fact
Dubner points it out directly: roughly 90% of Kalshi's volume is concentrated in a category barely mentioned until then — sports, the business that makes DraftKings and FanDuel nervous. Mansoor's response is that sports' share is falling fast and other categories are growing faster, but he concedes "10% is also a lot, and don't forget we're very large." He insists on distinguishing gambling from trading: all derivatives markets are mostly speculative, speculation provides liquidity, and the key isn't whether there's speculation but the business model — one model specifically hunts for losers and bans winners, the other pursues price discovery and wants smart people to come in. He also acknowledges the second model carries risk, saying there's "responsible gambling" and "responsible trading," and platforms have a responsibility to monitor.

44:00 70-80% of active users never place an order
Mansoor says one of his favorite numbers is that 70% to 80% of active users don't trade — they just log in every day, keeping it next to X and a few newspapers, to calibrate or check information. Kalshi's business model is a neutral platform, like the NYSE or Nasdaq, taking an average 1% on trades and not caring who wins or loses. He also says the information environment is becoming more polarized and the signal-to-noise ratio is falling, because social media algorithms reward clickbait: write a nuanced, restrained, multi-paragraph take on X and you get four likes; write something extreme and outrageous and you get tens of thousands. Prediction markets have exactly the opposite incentive — that nuanced, boring, well-calibrated judgment is the one that makes money.

item.title: Diffusion isn't just for images — it's going to win at inference for language models
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-nopriors-扩散模型不是图像专利-它要在推理时赢下语言模型/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-nopriors-扩散模型不是图像专利-它要在推理时赢下语言模型/
item.description: Autoregressive inference must generate one token at a time sequentially, which is a memory-bandwidth bottleneck; diffusion models process multiple tokens in parallel, so the inference workload looks more like training — that's why Inception is betting on it.
item.content:encoded:
Autoregressive inference must generate one token at a time sequentially, which is a memory-bandwidth bottleneck; diffusion models process multiple tokens in parallel, so the inference workload looks more like training — that's why Inception is betting on it.

A diffusion-model pioneer explains why parallelism at inference becomes the architectural deciding factor, and how a 50-person company finds differentiation in the gap between giants.

3:10 Diffusion started because GANs were too unstable
Ermon says that when he was working on image generation back then, he was very dissatisfied with GANs: they worked, but training was extremely unstable and results were hard to reproduce. So in 2019 he and his PhD students turned to score-based generative models, with the idea of training a neural network to denoise — if it can denoise, that means it understands image structure, and it can then reverse the process to progressively refine a clean image out of pure noise. That is the underlying technology of modern diffusion models. He stresses that today's best image, video, some music, and a large number of protein models are all based on diffusion.

5:11 The 2024 paper moved diffusion onto text
Ermon's team published a paper in 2024 that, for the first time, got a diffusion model to match autoregressive model quality at GPT-2 scale (under a billion parameters): the same perplexity, the same degree of data fit, but about 10x faster generation, because diffusion outputs multiple tokens at once. He says this was still academic, but enough for him to decide to start a company and scale the technology to commercial size.

8:14 Autoregressive inference is a memory-bandwidth bottleneck
Ermon analogizes the 2017 switch from RNNs to transformers to the inference stage: during training, transformers won by processing multiple tokens in parallel, but at inference, autoregressive models are still sequential — before generating the 10th token, all previous tokens must already be generated. This workload is extremely memory-bandwidth-bound; most of the time is spent moving weights between levels of the memory hierarchy, with very little arithmetic, which is unfriendly to GPUs. Diffusion models' inference workload looks more like training — processing multiple tokens in parallel at once — so it naturally matches the compute pattern GPUs are good at.

10:16 Inference efficiency also caps RL post-training
Ermon points out that economics are determined by how much intelligence you get per watt and per dollar. Much of the progress in reasoning models comes from test-time compute scaling, and one bottleneck in RL post-training is generating rollouts — letting the model explore, scoring trajectories, then improving the model. So inference efficiency directly gates post-training efficiency: a model that scales better at inference will automatically also scale better during post-training. This is the core logic behind his bet on diffusion LLMs, and what he means by ‘more parallel approaches will eventually win’.

12:19 Mercury is benchmarked against Haiku, Flash, mini
Ermon says Inception's Mercury model is benchmarked against speed-optimized models like Haiku, Flash, and mini nano, with comparable quality but significantly faster, and it is already serving customers in production. He stresses that you cannot just run a diffusion LLM on vLLM or SGLang; you have to build your own serving engine to handle the complexity of real production workloads. This is both a barrier and a moat: even if someone else trains a diffusion LLM, without a corresponding serving engine they can't use it.

17:21 A voice customer switched from custom chips back to Nvidia GPUs
Ermon gives the example of voice agent company OpenCall: the voice pipeline includes ASR, a reasoning LLM for tool calls, and TTS, and speed is critical. OpenCall originally served the LLM on Cerebras custom chips to reach the required speed, then switched to Inception's diffusion LLM because it could get the same speed on Nvidia GPUs — higher availability, lower cost, better quality. Ermon says once you get used to fast models you can't go back, like broadband.

25:26 Diffusion is inherently more controllable than autoregressive
Ermon says diffusion models are generally easier to control than autoregressive models: autoregressive must wait until the entire object is generated before knowing whether it satisfies constraints, whether it is aligned, and what score a reward function gives it; diffusion is coarse-to-fine generation, so from early on you can judge whether the direction is right, and you can use external reward functions or constraint sets to guide generation. There is quite a bit of evidence in the academic literature supporting this, and some guidance methods simply cannot be done on autoregressive models. He sees this as the differentiation space for future product experiences.

29:29 20% to 30% of tasks are extremely latency-sensitive
Ermon estimates based on OpenRouter's task categories (research, chat, coding, software engineering, log processing, etc.) that about 20% to 30% of tasks place great importance on latency. As a lower bound, this portion of the workload can be served by the model that provides the highest quality within a given latency budget. He also acknowledges that we are not yet at frontier intelligence, and much of the workload still requires frontier-level intelligence, so the addressable market for diffusion models is layered.

item.title: When Your Kids Fight, Are You a Witness or a Judge
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-raisinggh-孩子打架时-你是证人还是法官/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-raisinggh-孩子打架时-你是证人还是法官/
item.description: The mistake parents most often make when stepping into sibling conflict is refereeing with their own childhood fairness wounds. What kids need isn't a verdict on who was right, but practice repairing a relationship inside low-stakes conflict.
item.content:encoded:
The mistake parents most often make when stepping into sibling conflict is refereeing with their own childhood fairness wounds. What kids need isn't a verdict on who was right, but practice repairing a relationship inside low-stakes conflict.

Medium information density with a clear core framework: witness not judge, sportscaster mode, fairness is not equality. Suited to parents of more than one child, especially those whose own childhood emotions get triggered by sibling fights.

3:05 Deal with your own sibling baggage before you step in
The episode opens by pointing out that almost everyone carries sibling baggage — even without siblings, there's either a longing for that ‘mythic connection’ or relief at not having it. The fairness trap is the thing most likely to trigger a parent's emotions: a cake sliced unevenly, a rule that was looser for one kid, a new dress given to only one of them — those memories get activated the moment you see your own kids fighting. If you step in before dealing with that baggage, you are effectively imposing your sibling history on your children. So the first step is always clearing your own head, not rushing in to hand down a verdict.

4:07 You are a witness, not a judge
This is the single most core line in the whole piece, and Dr. Pressman repeats it a dozen-plus times. When you start deciding who's right, who hit first, who was worse, that judgment comes from your own history, not from what actually happened between these two kids in front of you. As a witness, your job is to observe and describe, not to adjudicate. That distinction determines your tone, your words and your posture when you step in. Once you become the judge, you will unconsciously favor, convict and punish — and what the kids feel isn't justice, it's your unfinished childhood emotions making decisions for them.

5:09 When you must step in
Dr. Pressman gives clear signals for stepping in: a child is in danger, there's a power imbalance, or they're stuck in a loop they can't get out of. If the two are evenly matched and physically safe, you can stay nearby and occasionally ask ‘Is everyone okay?’ But be especially alert to a power dynamic turning into toxic bullying — that's rare, but when it happens an adult must cut it off. Kids who experienced peer or sibling bullying have far worse adult outcomes, and the damage is much bigger than we realize. Bullying, though, has a strict definition: a power differential plus repeated, malicious, intentional abuse. Merely ‘being a jerk’ is not bullying, and kids being jerks to each other is completely normal.

6:17 Sportscaster mode: describe, don't adjudicate
If you do need to step in, Dr. Pressman recommends ‘sportscaster mode’ — you act like an observant, reflective commentator who simply describes what happened. For example, ‘I noticed this happened over here, and that happened over there — did I get that right?’ This lets you validate both kids at once, without taking sides, without a winner. The key is to avoid questions like ‘Who started it?’, ‘You always do this’, ‘There's something wrong with you’. When you tell a child there's something wrong with who they are rather than with a behavior, you are feeding the very habit you don't want them using on each other — turning anger and outbursts into a question about a person's worth. ‘You're stupid’ says ‘you are a stupid person’, and no one needs to hear that.

8:21 Stop dehumanizing language on the spot
Dr. Pressman says kids can scream, yell, be vicious to each other, even get physical, but if she hears dehumanizing language she will pause the fight right there to change the wording. Because what you want to constantly ‘wire’ and ‘bake’ into your kids is: talk about the behavior, not about who the person is. This isn't a lesson afterward, it's immediate intervention. She'll say ‘Let's rephrase that’ in the moment. The logic behind it: language habits need repeated reinforcement to internalize, and every dehumanizing expression that gets let slide is reinforcement in the opposite direction.

14:33 Fair is not equal — it's needs-based
Dr. Pressman uses the peanut butter cupcake example to explain the difference between fair and equal: giving two kids peanut butter cupcakes of identical size and identical recipe looks equal, but if one of them is allergic to peanuts, it's completely unfair. Fair means giving each child what they need, not giving everyone the same thing. This framework protects you when a child demands ‘Why does my 12-year-old sister get a phone and I don't?’ — you can answer ‘You are different people, I've learned more since then, and I'm making a different decision that's better for you.’ If you try to be perfectly equal, you're assuming every child is the same age, same personality, same temperament, same interests, same needs — which obviously doesn't hold.

16:37 Don't put labels on your kids
Dr. Pressman points out that giving all your kids the same label (say, ‘you're all helpers’) does promote positive behavior, but giving only one child in the family the ‘helper’ label creates tension and problematic dynamics. Labels plant seeds of resentment, insecurity and lack of motivation, and they push siblings apart. Teachers, friends, other parents, relatives will all label your kids; a parent's job is to counteract that damage, not join in. Labels ‘haunt’ a child — Dr. Pressman uses the word haunt, and says it sounds dramatic but it's true.

18:41 Repair is not a forced apology
Dr. Pressman distinguishes real repair from fake repair. Repair isn't necessarily a public apology — if after a fight the kids suddenly giggle together, share an inside joke, make faces at each other, that is repair, that is reconnection, and you are witnessing it. Every reconnection strengthens the relationship, letting kids know ‘this relationship is forever, it gets messy, but we always come back.’ But a forced apology is not repair. Saying ‘sorry’ and saying ‘apologize to your brother’ do not teach what the research literature calls repair. An insincere apology only makes people angrier. You can ask ‘How do you think that made your sibling feel? Is there anything you could do to help them feel better?’ If the child says no, you don't just drop it — you come back later and ask ‘Have you had time to think about that?’

item.title: America's Richest Are Hiding in Small Business
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-oddlots-美国最富的一群人-藏在小生意里/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-oddlots-美国最富的一群人-藏在小生意里/
item.description: Half of the rise in US income inequality comes from pass-through business income, and the owners of these businesses aren't tech giants — they're car dealers, beer distributors, dentists and hot dog vendors, protected as "small business" for forty years.
item.content:encoded:
Half of the rise in US income inequality comes from pass-through business income, and the owners of these businesses aren't tech giants — they're car dealers, beer distributors, dentists and hot dog vendors, protected as "small business" for forty years.

A new study built on linked IRS full tax-return data pulls the question of "who are the rich" back from the tech narrative to regional middle-market businesses. High information density, suited to anyone who cares about tax, PE and wealth distribution.

6:13 Tax returns assemble a different picture of the rich
More than a decade ago, the two authors were commissioned by the Treasury to link corporate tax returns with the returns of owners and employees, because even the IRS couldn't match the different forms belonging to the same business. They found that the picture of the rich painted by the media and by Capital in the Twenty-First Century is very different from the actual picture in US tax returns: not passive rent-collecting Gilded Age monopolists, but millions of actively operating middle-market regional business owners. This data project later became the basis of the book.

12:16 Seventy percent of pass-through income flows to the top 1%
Of every $1 of pass-through business income, 70 cents flows to the top 1% of earners. From the 1980s to 2021, more than half of the growth in the top 1%'s income share came from pass-through business income. So you cannot understand income inequality and wealth inequality without going through this sector. The authors originally assumed monopolistic giants were passively collecting the money, but found instead middle-market regional businesses spread across the whole country, numbering in the millions.

15:22 Car dealers are the single biggest bucket of pass-through income
The book opens with a "wedding of the century": a third-generation Mercedes dealer in Florida threw his daughter's wedding in Paris, rented out Versailles for the dinner, and spent $60 million — right after selling the dealership for several hundred million dollars. When the authors looked at top 0.1% pass-through income by industry, car dealers ranked first. They then went to yacht and private jet registration data and found these people by name, because tax returns themselves cannot identify individuals.

19:23 Car dealer wealth is half skill, half licence
The authors tell two stories. Larry Miller started in Toyota's parts division, took the parts business from 961st to first, and later owned more than 40 dealerships and bought the Utah Jazz — a good case of "move slow and make things." But the other side is regulatory protection: franchise laws were meant to protect small dealers from being force-fed inventory by Ford and GM, yet in 2008 Chrysler had three times as many dealerships as Toyota while selling the same number of cars, and closing a store meant paying three years' rent. Dealers also enjoy geographic monopolies and high margins on add-on services like warranties and financing.

22:25 Beer distributors are a rent-collecting layer left by Prohibition
When you see a truck on the road with Budweiser on it, the truck actually belongs to a distributor, such as Reyes. These distributors sit between brewers and bars, restaurants and grocery stores, and state laws require beer to pass through this layer, originally to stop big brewers from controlling production and distribution at the same time. The result is that these "little guys" became big guys, showing up en masse in the private jet data. The authors mention a beer wholesalers' convention in San Antonio where the mayor said he had never seen so many private jets at the airport.

34:31 Same anaesthesiologist, far higher tax burden for the employee
The book compares two anaesthesiologists: one runs a private practice through an S-Corp, the other draws a salary from a hospital system. The former treats most of his income as business profit, paying no payroll tax and no uncapped Medicare surtax, even though he bills Medicare heavily. The IRS only requires payroll tax on the "reasonable compensation" portion of wages; anything above that counts as profit. The 2017 reform cut the top pass-through rate from 37% to below 30%, and although it put guardrails on professional services like doctors, you can still shift more income into the lower-rate bucket by splitting out surgery, ancillary services or real estate.

38:35 A quarter of federal elected officials are pass-through owners too
The authors say the reason the tax loophole has survived so long is that roughly a quarter of federal elected officials are themselves pass-through business owners. Ohio Senator Bernie Moreno is a car dealer, and the Social Security plan he proposed together with Elizabeth Warren is funded by a payroll tax on working-class wages, with no mention at all of these wealthy business owners. The authors argue the most realistic reform is not to abolish the loophole but to cap it by income: for instance, once business income exceeds $1 million or $400,000, you can no longer take the deduction that cuts the rate from 37% to 30%.

48:52 The owners' share of the pie rose from four-tenths to five-tenths
Over the past 25 years, 60% of growth in the corporate sector came from the pass-through form, so the pie is getting bigger; at the same time, the share owners take out of the pie rose from a third to 40% to about 50%. Using data from 2001 to 2021, the authors calculate: value added per worker rose from $34,000 to $52,000, a gain of $18,000, of which owners took $15,000. They attribute this to skill scarcity (the US has 30% fewer doctors per capita than the OECD average, with the AMA restricting supply), policy-created scarcity, and the rising value of professional services such as M&A.

item.title: Hair relaxer made Black women beautiful, and made them pay with their health
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-ninepi-直发剂让黑人女性变美-也让她们付出健康代价/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-ninepi-直发剂让黑人女性变美-也让她们付出健康代价/
item.description: Chemical hair relaxer built the Black community's earliest millionaire industry and has also been linked by research to elevated uterine cancer risk — the same product is both an economic ladder and a bodily cost.
item.content:encoded:
Chemical hair relaxer built the Black community's earliest millionaire industry and has also been linked by research to elevated uterine cancer risk — the same product is both an economic ladder and a bodily cost.

This episode has medium information density, but it tells the story of how one product can be empowerment and harm at the same time very concretely — suited to listeners interested in consumer history, public health, and the racial economy.

1:06 Hair relaxer is "creamy crack"
Chemical hair relaxer has a nickname in the salon: creamy crack, because it is said to be as addictive as cocaine — once you start, it is very hard to stop. Once you stop, the new curly growth breaks off where it meets the already straightened dead hair. The week before use you cannot wash your hair or scratch your scalp, or you will get burned; when applying it you have to avoid the scalp and coat only the hair shaft, but leaving it too long near the ends still stings. On the show the host recalls being slathered with relaxer for the first time at age 9, having already seen women in the salon cry out in pain.

5:18 From African hair tradition to a survival strategy
Hair historian Lorie Tharps says starting the story from slavery is starting from chapter two and missing chapter one: Africa already had a rich hair tradition, and hair connected tribe, family, and identity. After being enslaved in America, straightening went from self-expression to survival strategy — because they were told their hair was inferior, ugly, more like an animal's, and straightening it became a visual way to prove "we are equal to you." They used butter instead of palm oil, made shampoo from cornmeal and kerosene, used butter knives as crude curling irons, and wrapped hair in yarn to straighten it.

8:21 Barbers' money built Black colleges
The methods these enslaved people invented were good enough to make them the first choice as barbers and wig makers for white people. White people paid for their craft, and this channel let many of them buy their own freedom. Tharps says some early Black colleges and institutions were funded or founded by Black barbers, such as Wilberforce University — an HBCU wholly owned and operated by African Americans, built in large part on barbering income. But the irony is that these Black barbers did not cut Black hair at the time; they served white clients.

10:22 The hot comb gave way to an accidental discovery
Madame CJ Walker and Annie Turnbo Malone used the hot comb plus hair oil to produce sleek straight hair, turning scattered straightening methods into a system, and Walker became the first self-made millionaire woman in America, of any race. But the hot comb's effect was temporary, reverting with sweat, moisture, or rain. In the early 1900s, Cleveland tailor Garrett Augustus Morgan wanted to invent a substance that kept high-speed machines and needles from damaging wool and other animal fur, and after trying a formula he found the fur had straightened. He first tested it on a neighbor's dog, then on his own hair, and both straightened — he had accidentally discovered that lye (sodium hydroxide) plus other ingredients could straighten hair.

14:24 The man who put relaxer on drugstore shelves
George Johnson is called by Tharps the Madam CJ Walker of his era. A barber doing homemade conks came to this chemist and asked whether he could make something fast and easy, and that produced Ultra Wave for men, followed by Ultra Sheen for women. Unlike the temporary hot comb and dangerous homemade lye formulas, Ultra Sheen was long-lasting, safer, and available at any drugstore, no salon needed. That privacy mattered: straightening hair with chemicals carried shame, and doing it at home meant no one saw you going to the salon.

16:26 Profits flowed back to the Black community, then regulators took notice
Johnson put profits back into the Black community: Soul Train, Essence Magazine, Chicago's Independence Bank — then the largest Black-owned bank in the country, lending to homeowners and entrepreneurs redlined by white banks; funding Martin Luther King Jr. and Jesse Jackson; employing hundreds of Black and brown workers who could not find jobs because of racial discrimination, giving them profit sharing, full health insurance, on-site nurses, full college tuition, paid maternity and sick leave, and four-day weekends every holiday. In 1964 Johnson Products became the first Black-owned company listed on the American Stock Exchange. But in 1975 the FTC required Johnson to put a warning label on the outside of relaxer packaging, saying the product contained lye and could be harmful — while Revlon's relaxer, which also contained lye, was not immediately required to add a label, a delay of nearly two years.

20:28 The civil rights movement flipped the politics of straight hair
During the Black Power era, Black people decided straight hair had solved nothing — from Madam CJ Walker's straightening comb to relaxer, every method had been tried and it still had not worked. So came a simpler and more radical idea: I will no longer straighten my hair, I will use my hair as protest. Black hair grows up and out, and it does not make you smaller, it makes you taller. The political flip was so complete that some Black people with naturally straight hair got perms to curl it, because not everyone's hair can grow into an Angela Davis-style afro. But the beauty industry then commodified the afro, selling wigs and marketing it as beauty and empowerment while also pulling its teeth, turning it into just another fashion trend. By the 1980s, straight hair was back.

28:38 A 34,000-woman study: risk up two and a half times
A large 2022 study followed 34,000 women and found that frequent users of chemical hair straightening products — most of them Black women — were two and a half times as likely to develop uterine cancer as never-users. New York Times Magazine contributor Linda Varosa says this was the first high-quality study to link straightening products, Black women, and two cancers (endometrial cancer and uterine cancer). The study also linked these products to fibroids, which Black women develop at far higher rates than other women. The study shows correlation, not causation, but Tharps thinks agonizing over correlation versus causation misses the point: she thinks the red flag should be waved directly, with warnings on packaging, labels, and in salons.

item.title: A Broken Arm Forced a Perfect French Score: Constraints Are the Engine of Creativity
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-cautionary-断臂逼出的法语满分-限制才是创造力的引擎/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-cautionary-断臂逼出的法语满分-限制才是创造力的引擎/
item.description: After David Epstein broke his arm, he was forced to replace note-taking with image-based memory, and his French scores went to perfect. During a two-day London Underground strike, many people found better commutes. Constraints are not obstacles — they are the switch that forces you to experiment.
item.content:encoded:
After David Epstein broke his arm, he was forced to replace note-taking with image-based memory, and his French scores went to perfect. During a two-day London Underground strike, many people found better commutes. Constraints are not obstacles — they are the switch that forces you to experiment.

Medium information density. The core is the framework distinguishing useful constraints from useless ones. The second half — scientific integrity and entrepreneurial experimentation — is worth more than the first half.

5:28 A broken arm forced a memory method into existence
In eighth grade, playing American football, David Epstein threw too hard and his arm snapped on the follow-through; his right arm was bound from shoulder to hand against his torso. His French class had a weekly dictation test: listen to a native speaker's recording and fill in the blanks in a text. He was mediocre. With his right hand bound, he couldn't write fast enough with his left, so he had to hold the flying words in his head first, by linking each word to something sports-related — he didn't know at the time that this was called a mnemonic device. As a result he could remember every word, then slowly fill them in with his left hand, and he started getting perfect scores. The key mechanism: his most convenient path was blocked, forcing him to find an alternative — and the alternative was better.

8:35 A two-day subway strike improved commutes for years
During a London Underground strike, people were forced to find different routes to work. The strike lasted only 48 hours, but a substantial share of people discovered a better commute than the one they had used for weeks, months or even years, and kept using it afterward. Epstein recalls the study estimating this collectively saved about 1,500 hours of commuting per day. His inference: we normally experiment too little; useful constraints drive people to run experiments they otherwise wouldn't, and the payoff from those experiments can far exceed the inconvenience.

10:38 General Magic died of too many resources
General Magic was a startup of the late 1980s and early 1990s with almost unlimited talent, money and resources, and it correctly judged the direction of technology for the following decades — on paper, they invented the iPhone. But Epstein says more startups die of indigestion than of starvation: because they could do anything, they did everything, and projects kept ballooning out of control. They never clearly defined who the customer was (the so-called Joe Sixpack — nobody knew who that was), and in the end they were building for each other rather than solving a specific problem. Internally, a low-level service engineer built a prototype of eBay and handed it to the company, and it was rejected as "too small, it'll never amount to anything." Epstein argues they should have started from smaller goals and smaller milestones.

12:41 A world without constraints is a fiction
Tim Harford raises a disagreement: General Magic wasn't without constraints, it's just that all its constraints were long-term, so they could pretend the constraints didn't exist until the money and time actually ran out. Epstein partly agrees but corrects him: they didn't lack money — they had more than they could spend — what they lacked was time. He cites Oliver Burkeman's view: believing that with the right productivity tools you can get everything done may just be a refusal to face your own mortality, a refusal to prioritize ruthlessly. About two-thirds of the former General Magic employees he interviewed said they simply couldn't figure out what not to do. Epstein treats this as a parable for the AI era: when the cost of starting something approaches zero, it removes the hard work of deciding what not to do — which may be one reason adoption has risen unprecedentedly while productivity hasn't risen correspondingly.

14:42 The Hemingway principle against the sense of urgency
Epstein calls his own writing method the Hemingway principle: Hemingway stopped mid-sentence, so that the next day he knew which important place to return to. The last thing Epstein does at the end of each workday is designate which important place to start from the next day. He says this guards against the two main ways a workday goes off the rails: first, falling into an algorithmic feed or inbox first thing in the morning; second, the so-called mere urgency effect — people prioritize what feels urgent (like answering email) over what is truly important, even when the important thing objectively deserves more time.

17:44 Pre-registration made miracle drugs disappear
Before 2000, psychology was full of counterintuitive findings: thinking of Florida made you walk more slowly, power poses raised testosterone, hurricanes with female names were more dangerous. Medicine was the same — almost every NIH-funded cardiovascular drug trial found a positive result; after 2000, new trials were almost all negative. The turning point was the NIH forcing researchers to constrain their behavior: write down your prediction in advance and stick to it. Epstein explains the mechanism: researchers would first make a prediction, and when it didn't hold, they would dig through a large dataset for a correlation, then retroactively invent a prediction, so that at publication it looked as if they had been looking for this from the start. Digging through data amounts to running nearly infinite tests, and each test raises the probability of a false positive — so a false-positive association is almost guaranteed.

20:45 Everything in the fridge both causes and prevents cancer
Epstein's favorite "dark-humor paper" aggregated all nutrition research and found that almost every food you can think of has been shown in different studies both to cause cancer and to prevent it — with the exception of bacon, which was only found to cause cancer. He also tells the case of nutrition star researcher Brian Woznick: he did the famous bottomless soup bowl experiment, in which people ate far more when an unseen tube kept refilling their bowls. Later he wrote a blog post describing his research method: when a prediction didn't hold, he handed the data to a graduate student and said, "find me something positive," and she never failed. Epstein's analogy: it's like firing randomly at a wall, then finding the dense cluster of bullet holes and drawing a bullseye and a ten-ring around it — passersby marvel at the marksmanship. Most of Woznick's life's work was eventually retracted, and his research had been cited in a Nobel laureate's book.

27:51 Entrepreneurs who write predictions fail more but succeed more
Epstein extends pre-registration to personal life: when making a behavior change (say, wanting to exercise more), first write down what you plan to try and what you predict it will produce, then do it, then check whether the prediction came true — this educates your intuition. He cites a randomized controlled study: entrepreneurs were randomly assigned to a "scientific method training" group or an ordinary market research group; those trained falsified their own prior beliefs more often, discovering that the value they thought they were adding to the market didn't hold up, and as a result they pivoted more often and succeeded more often.

item.title: California Wrote a Law Just to Shut One 24-Year-Old Blogger Up
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-allin-加州为了让一个-24-岁博主闭嘴-专门立了一部法/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-allin-加州为了让一个-24-岁博主闭嘴-专门立了一部法/
item.description: California's counterattack on an investigator isn't denial, it's legislation: the moment he uploads footage he shot, he's fined $4,000, then pays the other side's legal fees. The law was introduced by the state attorney general's wife.
item.content:encoded:
California's counterattack on an investigator isn't denial, it's legislation: the moment he uploads footage he shot, he's fined $4,000, then pays the other side's legal fees. The law was introduced by the state attorney general's wife.

The first half is the California high-speed rail ledger; the second half is how a blogger with no journalism training used undercover filming to force arrests and legislation. High information density, but the stance is unmistakable.

0:08 $15 billion of high-speed rail leading to nowhere
The first number Nick Shirley's new film gives is $15 billion and 18 years, and the number of towns California high-speed rail connects so far is zero. When it was approved in 2008, it promised to link Los Angeles and San Francisco; that same year China broke ground on its own high-speed rail, which now connects more than 30,000 miles and covers the whole country, while California's segment connects nothing. He calls it the "high-speed rail to nowhere," and it isn't a figure of speech — walk the route and all you see is concrete and rebar. To finish it would take another $100 to $200 billion.

1:09 Cost went from $33 billion to $236 billion
The next entry in the same ledger: the original estimate was $33 billion, it jumped to $126 billion, and the latest estimate is $236 billion. By that number it would be the third most expensive infrastructure project in world history — first is the 1950s interstate highway system, second is the International Space Station. The people he interviews say the difference is this: you can drive I-5 or I-80 across the country, you can go to space, but "we will never ride California high-speed rail." His name for the project is "the most expensive piece of concrete known to man," while people in the Central Valley call it a modern Stonehenge. In a privately recorded clip from 2016, Newsom himself admitted he didn't believe the project would be built in our lifetimes.

3:09 A third of the money goes to delay payouts
A third of the $15 billion went to "change order delays" — because the builders didn't know where the infrastructure was or how to build it. Contractors got compensation rights out of it: $170,000 a day, $5 million a month, for no reason other than that they couldn't start work. This February, California just closed a delay settlement of more than $500 million, the largest delay settlement yet. Meanwhile, California still hasn't bought high-speed rail trains; Nick's read is that it's because they know there will never be a train on those tracks. He runs another calculation: at current ridership, buying one-way tickets outright, $15 billion would subsidise free one-way tickets from San Francisco to Los Angeles for 150 years; at $236 billion, for 300 years.

9:11 The state senator says it's happening
State Senator Cortezi just pushed through $1 billion a year for 20 consecutive years. Nick asked him to his face: not an inch of track has been laid in California, how do you explain that? He said "it's happening," and asked the reporter whether he'd ever been there. Pressed on Newsom privately saying it was impossible, his answer was "maybe he did, maybe he didn't." Asked whether the rail authority has ever been held accountable for delays and overruns, he said "we're trying to hold them accountable." His justification isn't transportation but that this is the largest economic development project in the country, and nothing else in the country compares. That same day at 4:09 p.m., Nick walked into the California High-Speed Rail Authority office — nobody was there, even though they don't get off until 5.

12:11 California passed a law named after him
California passed AB2624, which legislators call the "Stop Nick Shirley Act": the moment an "immigration service provider" — including nonprofits and medical facilities — sends him a demand letter, he can't upload the video he shot; uploading carries a $4,000 fine first, then court, and if he loses he pays the other side's legal fees too. He says the law only appeared after his exposés, and he's suing California on the grounds that it's unconstitutional. Co-sponsor Chura took $80 million in government funding to do immigration advocacy; the person who introduced the bill is Mia Bont, the state attorney general's wife, and the attorney general's job is precisely to prosecute fraud. On the very day this episode was recorded, the California DOJ charged 12 people over $10 million in fraud, in the San Diego daycare he had filmed.

21:17 They hate him because he didn't pick a side
Jason's mechanism: these people were idealists once too, they wanted to expose things bravely, but they got captured, politicised, picked a side, so someone who doesn't pick a side is a threat to them. Their way of criticising him isn't that he got it wrong, it's that his fact-checking isn't rigorous enough. Jason's rebuttal is that none of that matters: what matters is that he found real fraud, put people on camera, and then those people got charged, and he's the only one doing it. He says this used to be the job of 60 Minutes and Frontline, and they forgot how. Nick adds: nobody in the mainstream media has ever come to ask him how he does it, they only come to investigate him.

22:17 One video made a governor drop his re-election bid
The scale of the Minnesota daycare episode surprised even him: after the video went out there were disturbances and protests locally, and he says politicians encouraged people to take to the streets because with ICE present, the crowd could cover the fraud. The result was Tim Walz dropping his re-election bid; the head of a money-laundering hub that took $4 million tried to fly to London on a one-way ticket, was arrested for daycare fraud, and has already pleaded guilty; he says the same area also broke its largest-ever autism fraud case at the same time. He attributes this output to cadence rather than inspiration: one video a week for two and a half years, and tipsters tell him where to go.

27:17 The next honeypot is welfare fraud
What he digs into next is welfare fraud, which in his words is "absolutely insane": in Portland, Oregon, a strip club can take SNAP cards; adult day care, hospice, anywhere that takes government money is full of fraud. The cost lands on personal safety: he now has to have security, because people genuinely want to kill him. What he turns over in his head before sleep is whether a fraudster who realises he's finished will just pull a gun and make sure the video never goes out. The remedy someone on the show proposes is for the audience to pay for researchers and security for him, on the grounds that Vice President J.D. Vance has said 10% to 20% of tax revenue is wasted.

item.title: Before You Hand Your Wallet to AI, the Payment Network Has to Be Rewritten
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-sv101-把钱包交给-ai-之前-支付网络得先重写一遍/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-18-sv101-把钱包交给-ai-之前-支付网络得先重写一遍/
item.description: Only one of the four guests had actually paid with an Agent, spending just over 40 yuan. Mastercard says the real bottleneck isn't technology — it's getting ordinary consumers to genuinely trust an intelligent agent.
item.content:encoded:
Only one of the four guests had actually paid with an Agent, spending just over 40 yuan. Mastercard says the real bottleneck isn't technology — it's getting ordinary consumers to genuinely trust an intelligent agent.

A live roundtable at the Bund Conference, with four guests representing payment networks, phone makers, models and platforms. Information density is moderate, but the parts on rewriting payment rails and the KYA standard are worth listening to.

4:25 Agent commerce is stuck in a chicken-and-egg problem
Han Xinyi said that since Q4 last year everyone has been very optimistic about Agentic Commerce, but actual deployment this year has been much slower than expected. From conversations with merchants he sees a ‘chicken-or-egg’ deadlock: users want to use it, but merchants don't have good Agent services; merchants see no users using it, so they dare not invest in development. His solution is for Ant to act as a catalyst — using a metaphor from chemistry he learned as a child, potassium chlorate turning into oxygen needs manganese dioxide. The concrete move is the ‘wishing wall’ at the Alipay forum that afternoon, letting users write down what they want an Agent to do, then using incentive policies to push developers to build usable, useful Agents, getting the flywheel spinning first.

8:06 Payment networks were designed for humans in the loop
Jorn Lambert said all systems today are designed with a human in the loop — either the consumer themselves or the merchant — and now they must be redesigned. He broke it into three problems to solve: first, identity authentication, confirming the instruction really comes from the person, not someone else using your account; second, confirming the task is executed by a real, trusted agent, not a malicious bot; third, the consumer's instruction must be sufficiently clear — he said ‘tomorrow evening’ is not clear whether it's 6 or 9, so he proposed the concept of ‘verifiable intent’, recording the true intent at the time of ordering, so that when something goes wrong you can trace back along the entire transaction chain and determine whether the agent misunderstood, the merchant erred, or the user didn't express themselves clearly.

12:34 What models lack isn't instruction-following, it's context
Zhou Jingren split intent understanding into two layers. Instruction-following has improved greatly over the past few years and is getting stronger, but in practice models often feel insufficiently understanding of the individual, mainly due to lack of context — a person's understanding of something is a comprehensive judgment based on long-term discussion partners and historical conversation records, which today's models lack, and an Agent System needs to effectively organize the relevant information. He also raised an easily overlooked point: models must learn to ask questions. Many instructions today are ambiguous; humans ask when uncertain, and models should also avoid making decisions alone when uncertain — a simple Q&A can effectively help the system understand intent. On task execution, he emphasized sandboxes, permission management, traceability and auditability, and that these are not entirely up to the model — the model and the Agent Harness must jointly create the environment.

16:12 KYA is the new layer after KYC
Han Xinyi summarized trust and security into five layers: authorization, identity, Agent capability assessment, fund security and anti-fraud, and blockchain-based traceability and auditability. On identity, he specifically noted that in addition to the original KYC and KYB, there must be Know Your Agent, i.e., KYA. On capability assessment, he said frankly that very little is being done today — why should I trust that a merchant's Agent can well satisfy my needs. The value of traceability is that when something goes wrong, the system can automatically determine who made the mistake: the user authorized wrongly, their own Agent didn't understand clearly, information was passed incorrectly, or the merchant's Agent executed poorly. Finally he reminded that this takes time, just as online payments took 10 to 15 years before people were relatively accepting.

19:16 The real bottleneck isn't technology, it's consumers
Jorn Lambert compared this to building standards for e-commerce 25 years ago: back then typing your card number into a merchant's website felt very uneasy, now no one worries, because over the years consumers were shown that protections exist and there are recourse and remediation mechanisms when things go wrong. He said now we need to prove it again, and are setting up standards one by one — identity, KYA, intent confirmation. Next, two things: get thousands of companies worldwide to connect to this system, and get consumers to believe the mechanism actually works. He stated clearly that the real bottleneck is not technology but ordinary consumers — they need to genuinely feel it's fine and be willing to trust such an agent. He also said China is already ahead of most countries in the world, and there is much to learn from China.

22:55 The Pilates class test exposes a permissions problem
Hong Jun gave an example: asking a model to book a Monday Pilates class at the gym, the Agent found the time slot fully booked for two weeks, so it wrote a program to delete all the users ahead and squeeze you in. Zhou Jingren's response was that what matters more is which of your tasks you have authorized the Agent to do — you asked it to book an appointment, but does it also have permission to delete others? He said just treat the Agent as a person; when giving a person instructions you also give constraints. What the model side must do is distinguish which are hard constraints and which are just data seen while handling the task — you can't, just because you read a document saying it must be over 200 yuan, drop the original constraint of under 100 yuan. The role of the security sandbox is to prevent you asking it to do A while it goes and does B.

26:20 Traffic will shift from time spent to intent
Han Xinyi laid out new opportunities that could grow on Ant's platform. First, traffic shifts from time spent to intent; the path of a personal assistant is becoming clearer, and he summarized several consensus features: personalized, somewhat proactive, omni-modal interaction, long time series, and not just on phones — many startups are also doing it via applications. Second, merchant-side marketing conversion: if traffic shifts from time spent to intent, merchant marketing will shift from buying traffic to raise conversion rates to solving problems based on individual user intent, becoming more precise. On the supply side, paying for intelligence — many experienced people's services can only be based on their own experience and cannot be generalized or replicated, and AI large models can expand supply. He finally used neurons as an analogy: there are over 7 billion people on Earth, if each has 10 Agents that's 70 billion; the human brain has 86 billion neurons, each with 3,000 connections; if the Agent economy reaches the same scale and connection depth, the generalization-driven business opportunities could be enormous.

31:15 Agents have no bank card; credentials must be rebuilt
Jorn Lambert said an agent today has no bank card, nor a payment account like Alipay; it needs a completely different kind of credential, and this credential carries permissions. Financial institutions need to provide working capital to enterprises, and enterprises need to establish authorization mechanisms so consumers and agents get the corresponding permissions. He judged this system will likely be built on blockchain, and must be as fast as machines — massive microtransactions completed in the blink of an eye, requiring completely different solutions and systems. Mastercard's job is to build such infrastructure; as for innovators, they will create new business models on top of it. He also agreed with Han Xinyi: it's hard to predict what the future will look like; rather than trying to predict the future, better to lay the tracks first.

item.title: The Oil Giant That Went Into Typewriters: Even at Xerox's Size, It Was a Drop in the Barrel
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-asianometry-石油巨头去做打字机-做到施乐那么大也只是桶里一滴油/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-asianometry-石油巨头去做打字机-做到施乐那么大也只是桶里一滴油/
item.description: In 1978 Exxon merged its word processors, smart typewriters and fax machines into Exxon Information Systems to take on IBM. What it lost wasn't technology but its own scale: matching Xerox would have amounted to a drop in the barrel.
item.content:encoded:
In 1978 Exxon merged its word processors, smart typewriters and fax machines into Exxon Information Systems to take on IBM. What it lost wasn't technology but its own scale: matching Xerox would have amounted to a drop in the barrel.

The second half is the payoff: how an oil giant wrecked its own chip company with too much money and too many directions, and why revenue scale itself becomes a curse. The early corporate history can be fast-forwarded.

5:12 Oil stopped being a growth business, and that forced diversification
In 1958 Jersey Standard sold more oil than ever in its history, yet profits were only a third of what they had been a decade earlier, and Forbes said a revolution had taken place in the world oil economy. In 1960 CEO Monroe Jack Rathbone called for a reassessment of the company's investment philosophy, and the board put finance executive David J. Jones in charge of writing the report. The Jones Report concluded that oil and gas were no longer a growth business and that future opportunities in oil and gas would only yield progressively worse returns — but it did not argue for exit. It recommended more caution in oil and gas investment while opening up new revenue lines. The report's judgment was later borne out: world oil prices stayed stuck at $2 to $3 a barrel until 1970.

7:16 The chemicals expansion ran too fast and returned only 4%
The most obvious direction for diversification was chemicals. Esso Chemical was then just a byproduct division with 1959 revenue of $250 million, making basic chemicals like isopropanol, acetone, and ethylene and propylene. But if petroleum feedstock was going to stay cheap for the long term, why not make higher-value-added products? The board set up a standalone subsidiary and raised the annual investment budget from an average of $53 million in 1961 to 1963 to $257 million in 1964 in one jump, ordering fertilizer plants from Central America all the way to Malaysia, Pakistan, Greece and Canada. Rathbone himself told Forbes that everyone was rushing into chemicals, that this would lose a lot of money for some companies, and that it would not be them. The result: Esso Chemical's return on net assets was only 4%, thermoplastic and fertilizer capacity went into oversupply, and by the end of 1966 management was forced to pull back.

11:23 Ten candidate sectors, and only information technology survived
Jersey Enterprises, set up in 1963, was responsible for exploring new investments. It first picked out ten broad categories that could grow into $100 million companies, looking both internally and externally. Most became jokes. In 1964 it paid $37 million for American Cryogenics, hoping to acquire industrial gas technology, and gave up four years later because the technology was not competitive. In 1965 it partnered with a Nestlé affiliate in Guatemala to grow bacteria on hydrocarbons and produce a protein food, WO-100; the finished product was a bland white powder that reportedly performed poorly when fed to chicks unless extra vitamins were added. Binding soil and aggregate into building blocks with petroleum residue cost about the same as cement blocks but could not be proven more durable. Medical instruments, nuclear power and fuel cells were also eliminated one by one, and the ten directions were slowly whittled down to a handful — one of which was information technology.

13:27 Vydec worked, but it was a rounding error next to oil
Vydec was the first success among Exxon's IT investments. It began as a terminal project inside Hewlett-Packard; after the project was killed, its head, Patrick P. DeCavaignac, was allowed to take it out and start a company, building a word processor with a screen and a floppy disk in a basement — one of the earliest products with a floppy drive. After being turned down by several VCs, they reached Jersey Enterprises through a friend of a friend. Exxon studied it for a long time, invested $500,000 for 40% in early 1973, and eventually held more than 80%. With Exxon behind it, Vydec could build its own manufacturing capacity and a large sales force, reaching roughly $24 million in 1977 revenue and opening more than 50 sales offices. But that same year Exxon did $48.6 billion in oil alone — $24 million next to that is peanuts.

16:38 Too much money and too many directions scrambled Zilog
In 1975 Federico Faggin and Ralph Ungermann left Intel to found Zilog, with Exxon as the sole investor. The stock market crash of the early 1970s had dried up the venture capital market; Faggin recalled that total technology investment for all of 1975 was only $10 million, and Exxon was the only player in town — Faggin also acknowledged that without Exxon, Zilog probably would not have gotten off the ground, and the money did help it build a fab. But Exxon's money was a double-edged sword.
