Former employee Bernard Pueto said the oil giant gave them too much money and too many directions, making Zilog do things it should not have done, while its young managers lacked the experience to judge when to push back. Faggin later spent more time fending off Exxon in New York than with customers in California, and his relationship with Ungermann broke down over it; Ungermann left.

19:38 Analysts believed the office business could surpass oil
At the end of 1978 Exxon merged Vydec, QWIP and Qyx, along with a dozen other investments, into Exxon Information Systems. Sykes said the operation did $100 million in 1978 and $200 million in 1979, with the goal of becoming a major player in office equipment within three to five years. A Yankee Group analyst said in 1980 that the business could eventually match or even surpass their oil business, and predicted that the entire IT market would be worth $150 billion to $200 billion by the end of the 1980s, with Exxon taking 10%. The arithmetic on the other side was blunt: Exxon's 1979 revenue was $84 billion, so even if the office business grew as big as Xerox, it would add only $7 billion — a drop of oil falling into a barrel. And EIS was born with 6,000 employees and a 40-page organization chart.

21:43 A typewriter caught fire in Exxon's own New York headquarters
Faggin recalled the company's decision speed: every decision had to work its way up from the very bottom, until senior vice president Ben Sykes said yes or no. On the product side it was just as embarrassing. The second-generation Qwip fax machine took six years to develop and died on arrival — the paper feeder jammed. Vydec was shut out of U.S. government orders over security concerns. A Qyx smart typewriter caught fire inside Exxon's New York headquarters. The Houston marketing department preferred Wang, was forced to switch to Exxon equipment, and switched back a year later. Exxon had bought a whole generation of old-style word processors just as the PC revolution hit, and it had neither the structure nor the culture to cope with a fast-changing, talent-centered information technology industry.

22:44 After twenty years of trying, they were still oilmen
Exxon's identity as an IBM competitor ensured that IBM would not choose Zilog's Z80 to drive the IBM PC — Faggin later confirmed this was indeed a factor. In 1981 Exxon cut staff twice, taking EIS from 6,000 people down to 4,000; that same year the IBM PC arrived and rendered EIS's already outdated product line even more obsolete. In 1984 the company finally admitted it did not work and began selling off business lines and shutting down the rest; according to a former manager, the remaining QWIP fax machines were hauled to a junkyard and crushed with bulldozers. Zilog was the last of the portfolio to be sold: a late-1980s management buyout backed by Warburg Pincus at roughly 4 times free cash flow; it went public in 1991 and was acquired in 1997 for $527 million, a 12x return on the $17 million investment. In 1993 Lee Raymond became CEO and reaffirmed that they were oilmen, and nothing else.

item.title: The McCarthy Era's Operative Handed His Playbook to Trump
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-freshair-麦卡锡主义的操盘手-把打法传给了特朗普/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-freshair-麦卡锡主义的操盘手-把打法传给了特朗普/
item.description: Roy Cohn was not an aberration of the McCarthy era but a product of the paranoia that seizes American democracy every few decades — and the playbook did not die with him. It carried through to today via Trump.
item.content:encoded:
Roy Cohn was not an aberration of the McCarthy era but a product of the paranoia that seizes American democracy every few decades — and the playbook did not die with him. It carried through to today via Trump.

High density of oral history, with concrete cases and mechanisms showing how Cohn's rules became Trump's rules one by one — not vague generalities.

2:07 Cohn's three rules became Trump's rules
Bird says Cohn's rules became Trump's rules: never admit error, deny and deny again, and when accused, stall and stall. That is exactly what Cohn did when he was indicted three times in the 1960s — delay the trial as long as possible, deny the charges, and name and attack the judge. He was a habitual rule-breaker his whole life; rules were for little people, not for him. Trump later copied the playbook wholesale: stiffing people on bills, using delay tactics to cut what he owed to ten cents on the dollar, and paying very little tax through various avoidance schemes.

3:09 He beat the charges with more than tactics — he had luck
Bird and his wife and co-author Susan Goldmark argue in the book that Cohn was partly just lucky. In one trial, a juror's father suddenly died and the judge was forced to declare a mistrial; in another, Cohn's own lawyer suffered a heart attack in court, collapsing just as he was about to give the closing argument. Cohn said on the spot, "Judge, I'll do the summation myself," and got two days, seven hours total, to defend himself — because he had chosen not to take the witness stand, he was not cross-examined, and the jury acquitted him 12 to 0. Jurors were said to have been moved to tears by him.

5:22 Don't tell me the law, tell me the judge
Another of Cohn's rules was "don't tell me the law, tell me the judge" — he knew which judge favored him and which judge could be manipulated. His father, Albert Cohn, was a Bronx judge appointed by the Roosevelt administration, and from childhood he was introduced by his father to lawyers and judges; after becoming a lawyer at 20, he cultivated judges as friends, very transactionally: do someone a favor first, then knock on the door for the return. Trump went further on this rule — as president he appointed judges and Supreme Court justices, some of whom later ruled on his own cases. Bird says this is Cohn's most insidious and longest-lasting legacy: he was a lawyer, but he did not care about the law at all. He practiced law by telephone, avoided leaving any notes or records, and taught this to Trump.

8:26 In four phone calls, Trump kept praising Cohn
Bird conducted four phone interviews with Trump, each about 10 minutes, and they were very strange. The first was a cold call; Trump picked up and said "Hello?" with no idea who Bird was. Bird said he was writing a Cohn biography, and Trump said, "Oh, great, great, he was a wonderful man, a good lawyer, we won a lot of cases together," gushing about Cohn, genuinely missing him. Bird believes they really were friends. Trump is utterly unashamed of his association with Cohn, which Bird finds baffling — the book's sordid episodes are backed by 1,300 footnotes, so how could anyone read it and not feel shame.

12:43 Cohn was McCarthy's brain
Bird says McCarthy was politically an empty shell, not a true ideological believer, who stumbled into this anti-communist witch hunt by accident. But Cohn joined with zeal and professional skill and became McCarthy's brain — McCarthy was by then a functional alcoholic, and Cohn was effectively steering him. They successfully launched a political offensive against the newly installed Eisenhower administration: Cohn was hired in early 1953 and began attacking Eisenhower himself, a Republican president, on the grounds that he was not Republican enough, not anti-communist enough. Cohn was brutal and unrelenting in interrogating witnesses, publicly asking male government employees about their sexual orientation and whether they had had relations with men, destroying the lives of hundreds if not thousands of people.

16:49 Trump knew Cohn was gay
Bird says Trump certainly knew Cohn was gay. After Studio 54 opened in '77, Cohn often brought Trump there in the 1970s; in the 1980s Cohn was more open, surrounded at his law firm by a group of young gay men. Once Cohn called Trump to plead for a boyfriend who was dying of AIDS, asking whether he could stay at a Trump hotel; Trump arranged it, the man stayed three or four months, and after he died Trump sent Cohn a bill. Bird sees a connection between Cohn's closeted state and the McCarthy-era persecution of gay people, and Trump's anti-DEI, anti-LGBTQ line today.

17:53 Cohn's politics was the politics of resentment
Bird traces Cohn's politics in the 1960s and '70s: he resented intellectuals, hated the Ivy League despite being a Columbia graduate, and preferred hiring young lawyers who had not gone to Ivies; he was suspicious of immigrants, anti-black, an isolationist who wanted America first. He opposed affirmative action, seeing it as discrimination against white people. Bird says this politics is exactly what we see in the Trump administration today — the same politics of resentment. And Trump likewise went to an Ivy League school and likewise came from a wealthy, high-profile family; there are many parallels between the two.

25:00 The Art of the Deal was arranged by Cohn as he was dying
Bird says Cohn did one overlooked thing for Trump: before he died, he went to his old Horace Mann schoolmate Cy Newhouse, the Condé Nast magazine publisher and Random House owner, and suggested he have a Random House editor sign Trump to write a memoir. That is where The Art of the Deal came from. The book was published after Cohn's death and became a national bestseller, turning a star developer comfortably settled in New York into a national figure and famous businessman, which led to the TV show The Apprentice, which led to Trump running for president. Bird says the starting point of that chain is Cohn's relationship with Cy Newhouse.

item.title: Dark matter detection is outrunning Moore's Law, and all it got was one event
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-intotheimpossi-暗物质探测跑得比摩尔定律还快-却只看到一个事件/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-intotheimpossi-暗物质探测跑得比摩尔定律还快-却只看到一个事件/
item.category: Into the Impossible With Brian Keating
item.description: The one nuclear recoil event LZ bought with seven tonnes of liquid xenon is over 3σ locally, but only 2.6σ once you fold in the look-elsewhere effect — which is why the team has to keep saying it might just be a background fluctuation.
item.content:encoded:
The one nuclear recoil event LZ bought with seven tonnes of liquid xenon is over 3σ locally, but only 2.6σ once you fold in the look-elsewhere effect — which is why the team has to keep saying it might just be a background fluctuation.

The first half is the hard mechanism of dark matter detection; the second half is how a real experiment faces the honesty of "this might be noise." High information density, but it takes a little patience.

5:28 AI cannot conjure an event out of the analysis chain
LZ uses AI heavily in the analysis chain, but the constraints are far stricter than in ordinary settings: any step that uses AI must have a rigorous understanding of why it works the way it does. The reason is straightforward — when you are discussing a single event, they absolutely cannot accept the analysis chain popping the event out because some AI component "magically" did so, and then have the team vouch for that result. This treats interpretability as a precondition for publication, not an explanation bolted on afterwards.

8:54 Students thought their advisor was assigning them problems with no answer
Rick describes a feedback session with his graduate students: one student wrote in feedback that they felt the advisor was deliberately assigning them work that would never produce an answer, because the research kept producing negative results. His conclusion was that the team had failed completely — they had not made clear to the student that this is simply how research works. His figure: more than 95% of the time you get no positive result, and even good research, well motivated and imaginative, Nature will still ignore completely.

16:16 One dark matter particle crossing ten light-years of lead
How weak the interaction between dark matter and ordinary matter is: shoot a hypothetical dark matter particle into lead, and stack the lead all the way past the nearest star beyond the Sun and more than twice over — that is, 10 light-years — and the probability that it interacts while crossing that much lead is still less than half. But the flux is enormous — roughly a hundred million pass through your body every second. So as long as the detector mass is large enough, over weeks to months the probability of a single interaction starts to become finite rather than zero.

26:38 Dark matter detection is outrunning Moore's Law
In 40 years underground experiments have covered nearly eight orders of magnitude in the dark matter–nucleon scattering cross section. Why such a huge span is possible: if the exchanged propagator has mass, in the low-momentum limit the propagator typically carries a 1/mass⁴, so a propagator differing by one order of magnitude can make the cross section differ by four orders of magnitude. Rick says they were forced to demand of themselves in turn that the pace of improvement in detector scale, sensitivity and background rejection keep up. Moore's Law is about one order of magnitude every 10 years; they do about one order of magnitude every six years.

37:58 A ten-gram detector achieved the sensitivity of seven tonnes
The dark matter detector Rick used during his PhD was only about 10 grams, while LZ today is seven tonnes of liquid xenon, yet the sensitivity is basically comparable — in between is a scale change of more than a million times. That leap rests on measuring single electrons and single photons: in liquid xenon, a particle interaction produces scintillation light and ionisation electrons, the electrons are drifted by an electric field to the liquid surface and read out, and these single-photon, single-electron-level measurements are combined to determine that an interaction really did occur at the centre of the detector that ordinary background or radioactivity cannot account for.

1:16:05 In 220 days of data there is only one event
After unblinding 220 effective days of data, only one event remains, and it sits near the nuclear recoil band but high up. The low-energy event is an accidental coincidence; in the high-energy region accidental coincidence is not the dominant background. The main background contribution in the high-energy region is high-energy gamma rays that may scatter multiple times inside the detector. To estimate this kind of background, the team simulated the equivalent of 220,000 days of data — because they had to rule out the extremely rare misidentification of multi-site scattering with single ionisation (MSSI), whose rate is on the order of one in a million.

1:25:18 One event falls from 3.4σ to 2.6σ
The nuclear recoil event LZ saw has a local significance above 3σ, but once the look-elsewhere effect is included — because the signal could appear over a very broad range of recoil energies, and there are many physical models that could produce a dark matter recoil — the global significance drops to about 2.6σ, that is, a probability of one or two percent. Rick says this is why they have to keep saying "this could be a background fluctuation." He also says there is no unique correct way to statistically combine a pile of possible models and background contributions, and that part of the reason they published the result was to hear which combination method their peers find most natural.

1:38:48 The neutrino fog: 20 boron-8 neutrino events
Last December LZ announced it had accumulated about 20 neutrino events, from the 8-boron component of solar neutrinos, at 15 MeV, which can leave an observable nuclear recoil in xenon through coherent scattering. This means that when searching for dark matter at the lowest energies, dark matter events will be mixed together with low-energy boron-8 neutrino events. Going to higher energies, solar neutrinos cut off at 15 MeV, but atmospheric neutrinos have much higher energies. Rick says that if you go from 10 tonnes to 100 tonnes and run for ten years, you will start to see nuclear recoils caused by atmospheric neutrinos and even the diffuse supernova neutrino background — this is "entering the fog": you have to measure the neutrino signal well enough to see whether there is an anomaly above the rate.

item.title: Moving Trees Uphill: The Bet and the Cost of Saving Forests
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-sciencepod-把树往山上挪-救森林的赌注与代价/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-sciencepod-把树往山上挪-救森林的赌注与代价/
item.description: In high-elevation burn scars, seedlings moved up from lower ground survive at 80% to 90%; but seed banks are limited, and staking precious genetic material on unproven large-scale planting is itself a gamble.
item.content:encoded:
In high-elevation burn scars, seedlings moved up from lower ground survive at 80% to 90%; but seed banks are limited, and staking precious genetic material on unproven large-scale planting is itself a gamble.

The first half is solid field reporting, with concrete numbers and scenes from the ground; the second half's discussion of philosophy and animal cognition is more conceptual, and the information density drops off noticeably.

4:06 When the big trees die, the next generation has no seed
In places that burned at high intensity, large areas have no living trees left. Many conifers depend on the seed bank in the cones of living trees to regenerate the next generation; with no living trees, natural regeneration has nothing to work from. Scientists are increasingly seeing natural regeneration fall short of expectations in high-severity burn areas in the interior. Layer climate change on top and the seedlings themselves are sensitive; managers report that planted seedlings are not surviving the way they used to. The low-elevation Ponderosa pine belt is already at its ecological edge, with little natural regeneration and poor replanting survival, and some worry these places will degrade into grassland or shrubland.

6:12 Assisted migration means moving seed somewhere warmer
The core worry is this: replant with local seed sources and the trees may be adapted to the past climate, not today's or the future's. Hence assisted migration — taking seed from somewhere slightly warmer (downslope or from lower latitudes) and planting it at higher elevation. In this burn scar, researchers planted 11,000 seedlings of 7 conifer species, putting high-elevation species down low and low-elevation species up high, with seed sources drawn from multiple elevation bands, to see how each performed.

9:21 Trees live for centuries, so which climate do you aim for
A tree can live for centuries, and the climate when it germinates will not be the climate when it is 50 or 100 years old, so there is no simple answer to ‘which climate to aim for.’ British Columbia is relatively far ahead: in 2023 it implemented a planting regime that roughly plants at the quarter point of the so-called species rotation — that is, discounted to the point in the forestry cycle when the plan is to come back and harvest — essentially a hedge, putting the tree at its optimum adapted state at about a quarter of its life cycle. Others can make different choices, but this really is hard.

12:24 High-elevation sites see 80% to 90% survival
The high-elevation site is about eight kilometres from the ignition point, and seedlings planted in 2022 have already grown to around half a metre, doing very well. The only poor performer was the low-elevation pinyon pine. Camille Stevens-Rumman says every high-elevation site looks like this, with survival across all species planted in 2022 at 80% to 90%. Ponderosa pine, Douglas fir and pinyon pine do not naturally grow at that elevation, but so far a good number of the Ponderosa and Douglas fir have survived there. The conclusion only goes as far as ‘seedlings can survive’; the long term remains unknown.

13:28 Seed is a scarce resource, not something to scatter freely
Maren Chambers says she is on the conservative side here: using precious biological resources for large-scale implementation when you do not yet know whether it works strikes her as irresponsible, so she favours small-scale trials first. Seed collection itself is extremely labour-intensive — sending people out to stands that have seed, hauling it back to nurseries to grow seedlings, then returning the seedlings to the forest; every step of that pipeline faces capacity problems, and the US currently cannot keep up. Enormous effort went into selecting multiple seed sources per species, with workers handling seedlings in near-freezer conditions just so the seedlings can get into the ground as soon as they reach the site, rather than dying before they are planted.

15:33 Short term you watch survival; long term you wait decades
The key metric is first survival: in their first years seedlings have short roots, and a dry spell in the soil or a cold snap can kill them. But long-term performance matters just as much. A study launching in 2028 will plant 40,000 seedlings in Colorado and track them for decades; the study Katie visited will probably be tracked for about 10 years, still not enough for long-lived tree species. Another study will space the trees further apart so their growth can be tracked as they mature and begin to reproduce.

16:36 Snow is a protective layer for seedlings, not just a water source
These Christmas-tree-shaped conifers have long branches that cast shade and delay spring snowmelt, which benefits downstream water users by avoiding an early melt pulse; but the roots also take up water, and snow sitting on the branches sublimates in winter, lost straight out of the system, so it is hard to quantify precisely. What surprised Katie is that snow is good for the seedlings themselves: scientists think high-elevation snowpack provides an insulating layer that helps seedlings ride out winter wind and cold. And as the climate changes, that snow layer may be shrinking, making the whole equation more complicated.

18:40 Whether there should be forest here becomes a human choice
At the low-elevation Ponderosa pine site, scientists look at rows of dead seedlings and discuss almost philosophical questions: should the same genetic material be put back on this land? Is that the best investment? Or would those resources be better spent on another ecosystem? No one has answers. Once you start intervening, you have to decide again at a very basic level: should there be forest here? Can forest survive here? And if so, who should its members be? Choices that nature used to make now fall to people.

item.title: Feeding post-Newtonian terms to a neural network cuts training data by ten thousand times
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-instituteforad-用神经网络补后牛顿项-比纯数据驱动省一万倍训练量/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-instituteforad-用神经网络补后牛顿项-比纯数据驱动省一万倍训练量/
item.description: A pure neural-network waveform model needs 10^8 to 10^10 training waveforms, but writing known physics into the network and letting it learn only the corrections takes just 8 numerical-relativity waveforms.
item.content:encoded:
A pure neural-network waveform model needs 10^8 to 10^10 training waveforms, but writing known physics into the network and letting it learn only the corrections takes just 8 numerical-relativity waveforms.

The first half is the state of the field in gravitational-wave modeling; the second half, on surrogate speedups and the concrete numbers behind the PINN, is the part worth hearing.

2:19 LIGO's error bars may come from theory, not the instrument
The speaker says that for some LIGO events, it cannot be ruled out that the analysis result is limited by understanding of waveform systematic errors, rather than only by cryogenic cooling or mirror defects. GW23123 is an example: run different models and the posterior distributions show non-trivial differences. His position is not to take sides on who is right, but to give the models better error bars so the data-analysis people can keep arguing about who is right.

8:25 Double the simulation length, quadruple the error
The mismatch of numerical-relativity simulations scales roughly as the square of the wavelength. Because simulation accuracy is dominated by phase error, phase error accumulates linearly in time, and mismatch is the square of phase error. So wanting a simulation twice as long does not just mean waiting longer; you also have to make it more accurate, and the cost is penalized multiplicatively. Most simulations today land at about 30 orbits, while the reference line is about 25 orbits.

18:36 On next-generation detectors, pure numerical relativity has no hope
The speaker showed a plot: the horizontal axis is event signal-to-noise ratio, the vertical axis is the number of simulations in the catalog that are accurate and long enough. For LIGO, about 85% to 90% of the catalog is good enough, roughly 3000 simulations; but for heavy systems at 10^4 signal-to-noise ratio, only about 10 simulations in total are good enough. For Cosmic Explorer and Einstein Telescope, the conclusion is that numerical relativity alone is completely insufficient and other models are needed to fill the gap.

21:38 Hybrid waveforms are actually stitching together two different physical systems
When splicing post-Newtonian waveforms to numerical-relativity waveforms, the cost function has many local minima in parameter space, and the global minimum sits in a narrow, shallow valley that optimizers struggle to find. The test is to run a simulation of about 60 orbits and then move the matching window to see what the early waveform looks like. The result is that the early numerical-relativity waveform and the post-Newtonian waveform look completely different, which amounts to smoothly sewing together waveforms from two different physical systems and introducing bias.

33:50 Let the neural network learn only what post-Newtonian cannot compute
Each additional post-Newtonian term is a PhD thesis worth of work, so the speaker's idea is to treat the neural network as encoding all the post-Newtonian terms he does not want to write by hand. The network needs only about 100 parameters, about 120 CPU hours of training, and only 8 numerical-relativity waveforms in mass-ratio space. Besides the waveform difference, the loss function also requires the orbital velocity to be close, the correction term to vanish as orbital velocity goes to zero, and equal-mass symmetry plus weight regularization.

39:54 Physics-informed networks extrapolate better outside the training set
At a point outside the training set, mass ratio 9 to 5, post-Newtonian fails completely near merger, the surrogate model (trained to mass ratio 8) gets worse as extrapolation error grows, while the physics-informed neural network does much better. If you add one data point at mass ratio 15 after already training to mass ratio 8, the error all the way up to mass ratio 15 drops substantially. This promises to reduce the amount of training data needed to build models.

44:58 Pure neural-network approaches need more than ten thousand times the training data
The speaker says that most other attempts he has seen at modeling waveforms with neural networks throw physics away entirely and use only neural networks or autoencoders, and that really does require 10^8 to 10^10 waveforms to train, which means you would have to build a surrogate first in order to generate the training data, because you cannot get that many numerical-relativity waveforms. His conclusion: machine learning is a useful tool, but do not forget that you actually do know something about the thing you are modeling.

55:08 The surrogate's 30x to 40x speedup comes from changing the algorithm
The speaker says all he did was make the code less bad, with no revolutionary insight. The starting point was about 30 milliseconds, and now there is about a 30x to 40x speedup. The biggest speedup came from changing the algorithm: from cubic interpolation to tenth-order Hermite polynomials, with far fewer time nodes. Right now the dynamics part dominates, at about 370 microseconds, while waveform evaluation takes only 50 microseconds. He estimates that in the end it can deliver a frequency-domain waveform in 0.2 milliseconds, comparable to or better than the fastest phenom waveforms.

item.title: The Antidote to Data Center Backlash Is Writing Tax Revenue Into Teacher Paychecks
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-allin-数据中心挨骂的解药-是把税收写进教师工资/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-allin-数据中心挨骂的解药-是把税收写进教师工资/
item.description: In a Louisiana parish, Meta routed the sales-tax surplus from its data center straight into teacher salaries, with one teacher netting about $45,000 more a year — the conclusion being: build real impact first, then talk about how you communicate it.
item.content:encoded:
In a Louisiana parish, Meta routed the sales-tax surplus from its data center straight into teacher salaries, with one teacher netting about $45,000 more a year — the conclusion being: build real impact first, then talk about how you communicate it.

The first 20 minutes are a concrete community ledger, with numbers on teacher checks and water bills; the settlement's structure in the middle is unusual; the back half on AI and glasses is mostly position statements, lower density.

6:22 The teacher paycheck became the data center's permit
Louisiana law sends the sales-tax surplus straight into teacher salaries, so every purchase on the construction site becomes a line on a paycheck. The Richland Parish school district's sales-tax collection growth was originally 5% to 10%; after the site broke ground it rose to 60% to 70%, peaking at 260% during the construction workforce surge. The district's half-cent sales-tax check went from about $4,000 a year to about $8,000, and then one teacher's annual check netted about $45,000 more. The parish's average salary before that was only $36,000 to $38,000. Dina stresses this was not Meta's idea — it is what local law requires.

13:36 Meta pays hurricane bills for a state it doesn't operate in
Jason lists the community's legitimate concerns: pollution, power prices, water, noise, building appearance. Susan's answer is that these were settled in the original agreement: the site was farmland, Meta chose a more expensive but more water-efficient system, and its water use is less than when the land was farmed; on power, Louisiana has about 32,000 miles of natural gas pipelines, and Meta through Entergy has paid from day one for generation, grid resilience and grid upgrades, and also absorbs hurricane damage — in a state it does not operate in, effectively taking the burden off local ratepayers. She argues that because these were solved in advance, they never became public issues.

16:47 Dina says blocking America is the adversary's playbook
Dina first concedes the concerns are legitimate and that the industry has not communicated well; but her core claim is about sequencing — real impact first, then narrative. She says Senate Intelligence Committee chairman Cotton and vice chairman Mark Warner believe there is evidence adversaries are artificially amplifying the backlash, which she declines to comment on, and instead reframes the question: if you wanted to stop America right now, the thing you would most want to do is exactly to make America stop building data centers and stop pursuing AI dominance. Her conclusion is that communities that want the jobs and teacher bonuses should get them, those that don't want them can opt out, but American companies should not be forced to build data centers overseas.

21:59 Can't hire fiber techs? Start your own school
What blocks data centers is people, not money. Meta couldn't find enough fiber technicians, so it built a five-week crash course that guarantees a job on its own sites upon graduation. Dina cites David Sachs: there will be a gap of 500,000 such jobs in the coming years, and the gap isn't in the jobs but in waiters, rideshare drivers and home health aides who can't afford unpaid training time. So America's Workforce Academy pays people at the on-the-job wage during training: 40,000 applied over four months, 250 graduated, 90% retention. The program deliberately does not carry Meta's name, and Google's Ruth Porat and BlackRock's Larry Fink are both adding people to the same coalition. Dina's line: we will compete on models and products, but we don't want to compete on people.

29:15 The settlement's killer clause is making rivals join
Meta reached a settlement with 52 bipartisan state attorneys general, and Dina says the terms themselves set an industry standard: users under 18 in signatory states get only two hours a day, with automatic shutoff at the limit, a full overnight shutdown, no notifications during school hours, and parents with extensive controls that can override defaults. More unusual is the structure: Meta agreed to put up another $500 million on the condition that YouTube, TikTok and Snap join too, at which point the limit drops to one hour a day. The reasoning is that users switch from one app to another, so one company alone can't shut it off. Some in the room argued this is really a parent's job, not the government's, and sensed a bit of a tech-company hunt in it.

34:35 Set the reward function to time spent and even Word traps you
This segment connects teen addiction and AI safety: RSI, recursive self-improvement — define a reward function for an AI and let it improve itself, and it will keep getting stronger. Set the reward function to time spent, and any app — from World of Warcraft to Angry Birds, even Word — will grow without limit. The mechanism is used to explain why platforms must set a threshold themselves and shut off at the limit, rather than relying on competition or users' self-discipline. The room's judgment is that this term will come up again and again over the next 18 months.

39:43 AI makes glasses useful as a form factor for the first time
Dina is repeatedly asked about the reuse cases for glasses, and her answer is that engineers worked on it for ten years, and success or failure comes down to weight and appearance — if it isn't fashionable, nobody wears it. Functionally it cuts both ways: conversation focus can leave only the voice of the person across from you amid restaurant noise, and translation can read street signs and conversations directly. The most unexpected use case came from blind veterans: they designed features together with Meta engineers, and one veteran put on the glasses, dialed his son, and cried, because it was the first time he had called his son on his own. Someone in the room added: in the Google Glass era battery, bulk and looks all fell short, and now those obstacles are gone.

42:44 Zuck thinks the more widespread AI is, the more stable society is
Asked about Dario's article calling for regulation, Dina says safety is a precondition, that Mark talks about it every day, and that the team led by Alex Wang and Nat Friedman works on safety too. The disagreement is over path: Mark's judgment is built on 20 years of the business of connecting people — 3.6 billion people use Meta's platforms daily, and 200 million small business owners do business on them — so he believes the more widely this technology is distributed, the more ordinary people can get education, health care and potential they never imagined, and the better it is for society as a whole. His position in the piece titled The Future is for Everyone is that democratizing AI leads to a more stable society. Meta released its first American open-source model just a few weeks ago.

item.title: Multi-agent isn't smarter, it's buying time with parallelism
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-dwarkesh-多智能体不是更聪明-是用并行买时间/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-dwarkesh-多智能体不是更聪明-是用并行买时间/
item.description: Serial thinking hits a latency ceiling for reasoning models, so parallelizing thought is the only way out; but Navier-Stokes shouldn't be credited to multi-agent, and solving alignment would actually favor the incumbents.
item.content:encoded:
Serial thinking hits a latency ceiling for reasoning models, so parallelizing thought is the only way out; but Navier-Stokes shouldn't be credited to multi-agent, and solving alignment would actually favor the incumbents.

Noam Brown rarely breaks down the engineering details of multi-agent and the disagreements over alignment; the second half, on the degradation of chain-of-thought monitorability and models seeing through eval environments, has the highest information density.

0:00 Multi-agent buys time with parallelism, it isn't smarter
The mechanism Noam Brown gives is plain: reasoning models get better the longer they spend on test-time compute, but serial thinking hits a latency ceiling, so you parallelize thought the way humans team up. The cost is a drop in efficiency — a single agent no longer owns the whole context. He says explicitly that this is ‘scaling test-time compute in parallel instead of serially’, and done well it's very effective. Parallelizability depends heavily on the domain: math is quite parallelizable, a Deep Research-style report that flips through a pile of sources is extremely parallelizable, while writing a novel probably has about as little payoff as having ten thousand people co-write a novel.

0:00 Navier-Stokes shouldn't be credited to multi-agent
The outside world treated 10,000 agents, 130 billion tokens and 88 hours to crack a Millennium Prize problem as a multi-agent victory, and Noam Brown pours cold water on it directly: he wouldn't give even 10% of the credit to multi-agent. The core reason is that OpenAI trained a very strong general model that can operate over long time horizons and think in parallel; multi-agent is just ‘flashy and new’, and so it got disproportionate credit. He also admits it doesn't hold up scientifically: there was no control experiment of a single agent solving Navier-Stokes, there's only one data point, and the ablations at 64, 128 and 256 agents haven't been done.

0:00 They deliberately stripped the scaffolding down to the minimum
Most LLM multi-agent setups use scaffolding where a coordinator hands work to sub-agents, and Noam Brown says that structure has a hard flaw: two sub-agents doing similar tasks usually can't talk to each other, and when a sub-agent has a question it can only choose between ‘return the question’ and ‘assume something and finish it yourself’. Their approach goes to the other extreme — almost no built-in structure, just one primitive tool given to the agent: send a message to another agent, and the message is inserted into the other's context. The agent figures out the rest of the coordination itself. The result is behavior resembling humans collaborating on Slack: one agent says ‘I have the answer’, another says ‘I got something different’, they go back and forth interrogating each other's reasoning, and finally one publicly changes its mind.

0:00 Early multi-agent got stuck in a local optimum
A counterintuitive engineering detail: getting multiple agents to collaborate is very hard, because reasoning models are trained to think deeply on their own, and constantly sending and receiving messages with other agents interrupts their chain of thought. Worse, there's a local optimum — all the agents just solve the problem independently. Noam Brown says early versions struggled even to get agents to talk to each other, and only later, when models became more general and more capable, did this collaborative ability emerge naturally. He also cautions that human text and the initial priors are baked into the model, so the hierarchies and ‘middle management’ that emerge don't come from nowhere.

0:00 Solving alignment would actually favor the incumbent
Noam Brown starts from the classic explanation of startups disrupting giants: inside big companies individual and company interests are misaligned, people become territorial, fight for headcount, build their own fiefdoms, and that's a real drag. AI benefits both sides — it amplifies an individual to the point of building a multi-million-dollar company alone; but if the alignment problem is solved, 10,000 agents can all be aligned to the company's interest and work like a co-founder holding 20% equity. Still, he's explicitly conservative about ‘10,000 agents collaborate better than 10,000 people’: there's no measurement data, and he thinks 10,000 people right now very likely collaborate better.

0:00 Math progressed faster than his own prediction
Noam Brown uses ‘how long would a human take on this problem’ as his yardstick: GSM8K about 5 seconds, MATH about 1 minute, AIME about 10 minutes, IMO gold about 100 minutes, roughly 10x per year. Extrapolating that trend line, after IMO gold comes 15 hours, nowhere near enough to solve a Millennium Prize problem, so he judged it wouldn't happen in 2026, probably not in 2027 either, maybe 2028. It came much faster. But he rejects the narrative that ‘AI is already broadly superhuman at math’: models are clearly weaker than humans at posing new problems and judging which branches of math are worth developing — it's jagged.

40:22 The Hugging Face incident isn't a multi-agent problem
Noam Brown splits the Hugging Face incident into two layers: one, the model itself was misaligned; two, the sandbox was insecure and monitoring was insufficient. He stresses this has nothing to do with multi-agent — ‘That's true if it's a single agent or if it's 1,000 agents. It's a misaligned model.’ The genuinely new problem is that when the reward is misspecified, the model optimizes for that reward. He acknowledges OpenAI had alignment metrics at the time and most looked fine, but ‘I think we underestimated how serious a problem the ones that were concerning could be’ — because the model had acquired new capabilities, and misalignment evals targeting those capabilities simply didn't exist.

46:00 Is training agents to cooperate safer, or more dangerous
Inside OpenAI there's a real disagreement over whether agents should be trained to be highly cooperative. Noam Brown says the majority view is ‘training these agents to be highly cooperative is actually a bad idea’, but he doesn't buy it: ‘I'm not convinced that that's the case.’ His reasoning is that the alternative is worse — training them to be adversarial and deceptive toward each other means you have to verify that each of 1,000 agents is individually aligned; train them to be fully cooperative and you only need to ensure one entity is aligned. The cost is that the kind of ‘cooperative ability’ seen in the Hugging Face incident spills over into places where cooperation is not wanted.

item.title: The Most At Home Person in the Odyssey Is a Slave Who Was Sold
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-verybad-奥德赛里最有归属感的人-是个被卖掉的奴隶/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-verybad-奥德赛里最有归属感的人-是个被卖掉的奴隶/
item.description: Odysseus wanders twenty years without getting home, Telemachus grows up among the suitors; the only person who treats Ithaca as solid ground is Eumaeus, the swineherd sold into slavery as a child — because it is the only place he has ever known.
item.content:encoded:
Odysseus wanders twenty years without getting home, Telemachus grows up among the suitors; the only person who treats Ithaca as solid ground is Eumaeus, the swineherd sold into slavery as a child — because it is the only place he has ever known.

A pure literary close reading, with no tech or business content. But the discussion of home, hospitality and suspicion spiraling out of control is more grounded than most philosophy podcasts.

3:30 The person who feels most at home is the slave sold as a child
This episode's theme is what home is. Eumaeus — the swineherd sold into slavery — is the one who feels most at home of anyone: he was sold as a child, this is all he has ever known, so he is like a foundation stone; everyone else is drifting. The speaker splits homelessness into two layers: the literal having-nowhere-to-go, and a deeper one — you lack some connection to roots. This is exactly what Odysseus has been struggling with since Calypso's island: he is rebuilding his connection to home bit by bit, but still can't stop lying and disguising himself, maybe more than he should.

6:31 The swineherd taught him how to be a host
Odysseus has been absent twenty years, Telemachus grew up in a house full of suitors — how would he know how to be a host? The speaker realises here: Eumaeus modelled it for him. Eumaeus has very low status, but his domain is caring for people — the scrap of land with his pigs; as a low-power figure he plays the most generous host. And Telemachus is already considerate to Athena disguised as a stranger at the start of this book, so it isn't something he learned on this trip: more likely the swineherd gave him the heart to want to do it.

25:40 Only with company can a person begin to enjoy his grief
Eumaeus invites Odysseus to sit and drink, says such nights are wondrous, then delivers the heaviest line of the episode: after long years of pain and being far from home, a man can begin to enjoy his own sorrow. The speaker presses: why did Laertes get eaten away by grief while Eumaeus can grow old with his? The answer lies in sharing — unloading the pain and having someone witness it is not just relief but a real, positive pleasure; the same logic behind mourning rituals where everyone tells stories together. It is fighting grief itself that makes you suffer.

29:42 The Phoenician nurse's end is like a seagull
Eumaeus tells how he got here: Phoenician traders spent a whole year earning trust, and the nurse agreed to steal her master's son and sell him for money in exchange for being sent home. Seven days of fair wind, and on the eighth Artemis shot her dead with an arrow — she pitched headfirst into the cargo hold like a seagull, then was thrown into the sea to feed the fish. The speaker says the ending is as cursory as a declaration that fate is both cruel and arbitrary; we know little about the Phoenicians, also because their records were written on papyrus and didn't survive, and most of what remains comes from Greeks and Romans who looked down on them. After hearing it Odysseus still says, you were lucky, you met good people, ruining all the tenderness that came before.

33:47 The first to embrace him is the swineherd
The moment Telemachus enters the yard, Eumaeus jumps up, the cup in his hand falls and the wine spills; he runs and kisses his master's face and shining eyes, weeping like a father seeing his only son return from a foreign land after ten years. The speaker stresses: this simile gives the position of father to the man who raised the child — in the years Odysseus was gone, Eumaeus was more of a father than Odysseus. And in this moment the only one who can jump up is the swineherd; Odysseus is still trapped in a beggar's body and getup. This is also the first time in the whole poem anyone is called godlike Telemachus, a title that until now belonged to Odysseus.

38:50 He never got any joy from me — that line reads two ways
Explaining why the suitors can behave this way, Telemachus says the house is down to a single heir, and his last line is: he never got any joy from me. The speaker offers two opposite readings: one, he is grieving for his father, who never enjoyed the pleasure of raising a son — which resonates with a speaker who has just had a nearly two-year-old son; the other, the father simply had no interest in raising a baby and went off to fight a war nobody forced on him. Support for the second reading is Odysseus's own account that after returning from Crete he felt family life didn't suit him, back when he was still in a warrior's mindset. Neither of them can tell from the English translation, so they agree to check other translations next episode.

49:53 Testing everyone isn't caution, it's adaptation gone past its stop
Odysseus makes his son keep the secret from everyone, even Penelope — he wants to test her attitude first — and then all the male slaves. The two disagree here: one holds that this is extreme suspicion, an overfiring adaptation — something that kept you alive in war now running out of control; the same speaker adds it could also be procrastination, self-preparation before the question of whether I can really kill them all, and admits he isn't sure. The skill he knows best is testing people, lying and impersonating others. Telemachus pushes straight back: testing everyone one by one takes too long, and the suitors will keep eating your estate.

57:00 However hard she curses him, she never says I won't marry you
Penelope publicly tears into Antinous: you are a beast, a thief, a criminal; people say you are the cleverest of your peers, that isn't true, you are mad. She also reminds him that when his father was hunted by the men of Ithaca, Odysseus saved him — and now he eats his benefactor's estate, courts his wife and wants to kill his son. But she never says the most direct thing: I will never marry you, get out. The speaker's explanation is that she too is stalling: if Odysseus really is dead, she still needs someone to support her, and the web woven and unravelled is I don't want to decide right now. In the same scene Eurymachus is worse — he says he loves Telemachus most of all, and that no one can harm him as long as he lives.

item.title: AI Safety Doesn't Lack Money, It Lacks Founders Willing to Get in the Mud
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-eightythousand-ai-安全缺的不是钱-是愿意下泥潭的创始人/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-eightythousand-ai-安全缺的不是钱-是愿意下泥潭的创始人/
item.description: Coefficient Giving's cap on AI safety grants is not $200 million, and a larger single grant will appear in the next year or two; the real bottleneck is talent, especially founders willing to bet before the problem has happened.
item.content:encoded:
Coefficient Giving's cap on AI safety grants is not $200 million, and a larger single grant will appear in the next year or two; the real bottleneck is talent, especially founders willing to bet before the problem has happened.

This episode has medium information density, but it lays out concrete funding tiers, six categories of gaps, and founder screening criteria for AI safety nonprofit entrepreneurship — suited to people who want to get money and do things.

0:00 The only bottleneck is talent, not money
Max says it plainly: the most important bottleneck, perhaps the only bottleneck, is talent. AI safety organizations all have long lists of projects they want to do but lack the people to execute, including partnerships with AGI companies and governments. Coefficient Giving's cap on a single grant to a technical AI safety organization is not $200 million, and a larger single grant will appear in the next year or two. So the problem is not a lack of money, it is that no one is raising their hand.

3:26 Three funding tiers, decisions in as little as two weeks
Project Tailwind splits funding into three tiers: preseed, for founders who have not yet assembled a team and have only a preliminary idea, at $200,000 to $2 million; seed, which requires a founding team, multiple people covering key functions, and preliminary results, at $2 million to $20 million; and for organizations that have already built a track record, they are willing to give up to $200 million in a single grant, and this can even be the first grant. They also borrowed VC pitch day: founders present for 15 minutes and get a decision within a few weeks.

6:07 Hits-based giving: most grants are destined to have no impact
Coefficient Giving has long used hits-based giving, borrowed from VC's hits-based investing: make a bunch of grants, most have no impact, and a few are good enough to make the whole portfolio worth it. They are now leaning harder into this logic, deliberately avoiding the common failure mode of grantmaking institutions — over-scrutinizing budgets and making sure every penny is spent correctly — and instead making sure the best projects get all the funding they need.

8:00 The $160 million grant was for ‘using AI to accelerate safety research’
Resolution received $160 million. CEO Geoffrey Irving is a leader in technical AI safety, formerly chief scientist at the UK AI Security Institute, and before that led AI safety teams at Google DeepMind and OpenAI. What moved Coefficient was not just his résumé but his plan: build a large research center directly studying the alignment of superintelligence, and spend a lot of time using AI to accelerate safety research — because on the capabilities side there is a ‘five years of progress compressed into one’ opportunity happening, and they want grantees to seize it.

16:00 AI safety founders must be willing to think about problems that have not happened yet
Max says AI safety nonprofit entrepreneurship shares grit, energy, and management ability with ordinary entrepreneurship, but has one unique requirement: being extremely picky about impact theory, willing to pivot substantially; and being willing to think about speculative questions with no clear answers, and to bet on where AI is heading. Many people's instinct is to work only on problems that are more solid and verifiable today, but most AI safety problems have not yet appeared. METR is an example: coming up with evaluation methods before AI capabilities took off has held up better over time than the benchmarks of the same period.

22:05 Nonprofits most easily forget ‘who is supposed to change their behavior because of this’
Max points out a common failure mode of nonprofits: because they do not need to actually make customers pay, they do not think hard enough about ‘who in the world is supposed to change what they do because of your work’. You either want others to read your report and change their views, or you want them to adopt a practice you developed, or you want them to pursue a line of research you cannot do. As a nonprofit entrepreneur, you have to think through every step of the entire impact supply chain; having a good idea and getting a good idea into someone else's head rely on different abilities.

23:31 Redwood cut to two people, then rebuilt a year later
Redwood Research's Buck Shlegeris and Ryan Greenblatt judged that mechanistic interpretability was not producing enough, and made a hard decision: shrink the organization to just two people, spend a year thinking about the biggest holes in the AI safety landscape and the most undervalued approaches, then re-expand with ideas like AI control. At the time they took a lot of criticism, and it was unpleasant for everyone. But Max says that in hindsight, they and almost everyone they know think this had far more impact than continuing down the original path. No market force pushed them, and funders did not pressure them; the pressure came from acquaintances.

29:08 Safety teams inside AI companies are squeezed by a race to the bottom
Max thinks safety teams inside AI companies are in a brutal race to the bottom: they are pushed to develop safety techniques that are not costly to implement, to do pre-deployment evaluations quickly so models can be deployed internally to accelerate research or externally to make money, and to put out the fires burning right now. The conclusion is that these companies do not have enough willingness to pay, and lack top-down organizational priority and resource allocation. The best opportunity to increase willingness to pay and release the pressure of the race to the bottom is outside the AI companies.

item.title: Zapier CEO: 80% of agent tasks should be deterministic code
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-cogrev-zapier-ceo-80-的智能体任务本该用确定性代码/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-cogrev-zapier-ceo-80-的智能体任务本该用确定性代码/
item.description: Wade Foster says 80% of what customers do with agents should really be old-fashioned deterministic code; no code is over, and the new no code is code.
item.content:encoded:
Wade Foster says 80% of what customers do with agents should really be old-fashioned deterministic code; no code is over, and the new no code is code.

A first-hand post-mortem on Zapier betting on MCP, agents, SDKs and guardrails at once, including Automation Bench and how AI transformation is done internally.

5:21 Knowledge work is moving into people's everyday tools
Foster walks through his biggest shift in thinking over the past 18 months: most people have already picked a daily AI tool — maybe Cursor, Claude Code or ChatGPT — and that is where the work happens. So getting context and data into that daily tool (an MCP server like Zapier MCP, for instance) is where knowledge work is heading. He splits the market in two: one camp wants to keep people on its own platform building agents, the other, like Salesforce, goes headless and lets you take it wherever you want. He is explicit that the latter is the winning strategy, because that is what tool consumers want and where the growth is.

10:20 The strongest model gets only four in ten automation tasks right
Zapier's Automation Bench tests models on roughly 600 real knowledge-work tasks, for example ‘just signed the Meridian Core platform contract, mark it as won per the routing policy and hand it to the right team, confirm the account from the account hierarchy table, convert currency if needed, check whether there is an open support escalation’. Foster says the newest strongest model lands at about 40% accuracy, the current high, but costs far more than Gemini 3.7, which produces a curve of ‘how much are you willing to pay for incremental performance’. He stresses the benchmark is nowhere near saturated, and what Zapier wants to prove is that putting Zapier next to an agent produces better output than the model alone.

23:02 80% of agent tasks should be deterministic code
Foster's core judgment: the vast majority of what customers do with agentic products — his number is 80% — should really be old-fashioned deterministic code. The approach is to have the agent first decide which steps to write as code (cheaper, more reliable) and only call AI or build agents where reasoning is genuinely needed. He concedes models will keep getting better, but finds it hard to imagine a world where deterministic code is no longer more reliable and cheaper. At the same time he keeps the visual layer: people still need to see what the workflow looks like, to verify ‘is this what I want it to do’, and to use it as documentation.

30:34 Your real rival is the product director who leaves in two years
Asked what kind of competitor he worries about most, Foster brings up what PG said during YC: the question back then was not ‘what if Anthropic or OpenAI does this’ but ‘what if Google does this’, and what PG wanted to instil was — you rarely fight Google directly, you face a mid-level product director who wants a promotion and will be gone in two years. He says OpenAI and Anthropic are now big companies and will be strongest on models, but they cannot do everything. On the other side, ordinary AI users have actually done nothing, maybe only used ChatGPT or Gemini, so most companies are not competing with each other but with ‘do people even know what to do with these tools’.

39:30 Let AI watch you work and find automation opportunities for you
Foster thinks the hardest part has always been recommendation: what should you do with this thing. This year he started running a workflow where AI looks at his own daily activity in Gmail, Slack, the browser and chat, then tells him ‘you should do this differently’. Most Zapier employees plug their tools into Zapier MCP and run an automation once a week, collecting a week of work signals and producing ‘you did this and this, here is a tool I suggest you build’. He says half the battle is just getting you to react to a suggestion — the idea does not need to be perfect, 50% good is enough to start brainstorming. He confirms this will very likely be productised.

46:09 The bottleneck in AI transformation moved from tech to people
Foster says phase one was AI fluency for everyone; within a year nearly 100% of employees used AI daily, and technical adoption was not the bottleneck. After that the question became: how do you turn individual success into company-level production-grade workflows, and so the challenge looks more and more like a people problem — rewriting job descriptions, rethinking compensation, reorganising teams, retraining people from teams you do not need into teams you do. Brandon, the people officer at the time, was good at this and the team was at the frontier, so he was asked to help the whole company. Foster stresses this is not a claim that ‘the people officer must own AI’: a CMO or CPO could do it too, the point is to see where your bottleneck is and then find the right person.

55:46 Some people burn $30,000 of tokens a month
Foster says a few individual engineers spend $30,000 a month on tokens, which is an outlier. Zapier currently sets no per-person budget, but has built tools so people can see their own spend and see the cost difference between a strong model and a cheap one across different workflows. When he sees someone spending especially much, his first reaction is to talk: ‘what are you doing, I'm curious’. It turns out some are doing extremely high-output work, while others are using Fable or Astro where they are not needed. He expects token budgets will eventually become a real thing, and that part of AI fluency is some people getting a higher budget because they use it better.

55:46 Using AI is not the problem, low quality is
Foster says he is not against employees using AI to write communications; the real problem is low-quality communication: people with poor judgment can produce enormous amounts of low-quality content extremely fast and drown the reader. He offers a few rules: you are responsible for what you send, and the author should spend more time than the reader; you have to understand what you sent and not be unable to answer when questioned; write requests clearly, whether you want a decision, feedback, or are marking it as a draft; verify details, because AI hallucinates and may also pull up an old project from three months ago as relevant material, and summaries of summaries passed down the chain turn into misinformation. He also calls out the AI voice — ‘it's not this, it's that’, em dashes, honest truth, load-bearing point.

item.title: A Civilization Doesn't Forget Its Technology Exists, Only How to Build It
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-isaacarthur-文明不会忘记技术存在-只会忘记怎么造它/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-isaacarthur-文明不会忘记技术存在-只会忘记怎么造它/
item.description: Technology is rarely lost because the knowledge was burned; it's lost because no one pays anyone to remember it — the underlying tools, suppliers and apprenticeship pipelines disappear layer by layer, and the civilization still knows the thing exists but can no longer reach it.
item.content:encoded:
Technology is rarely lost because the knowledge was burned; it's lost because no one pays anyone to remember it — the underlying tools, suppliers and apprenticeship pipelines disappear layer by layer, and the civilization still knows the thing exists but can no longer reach it.

Medium information density, but two mechanisms are worth hearing — "economic forgetting" and "colonies inheriting a tech stack that runs too deep" — the rest is standard sci-fi extrapolation.

2:02 A machine that works too long becomes scenery
The question this episode asks is not a civilization destroyed by technology, nor one that deliberately abandons it, but one hollowed out in its understanding by technology that is "too usable." The core metaphor: a machine that runs perfectly long enough stops being a machine in its users' minds and becomes scenery — and scenery is maintained by no one, until it falls on someone. So the starting point of loss is not ignorance, it's "out of reach": you still know the thing exists, but the underlying ladder to build it is gone.

3:02 Knowledge is not capability, a recipe is not a craft
A library can preserve facts: how a turbine spins, how aluminum is smelted, how orbital transfers are calculated. But knowing antibiotics exist is not the same as being able to mass-produce them safely; knowing the periodic table is not the same as being able to run a wafer fab. Technology has a recipe, and it also has a craft — tolerances, gauges, calibration procedures, institutional memory, and all those little habits that "everyone in the shop knows so nobody writes them down." So loss is both less realistic than people think (as long as records and physical objects survive, the concept almost never disappears) and more realistic (the ability to make things cheaply, safely and reliably evaporates along with the experts, the tooling, the supply chain and the apprenticeship pipeline).

5:05 Hand Newton a RAM stick and he'll just think the letters are small
The author uses this image to show that "the concept of stored knowledge can survive, the interface cannot": hand a memory chip to Newton or Einstein, tell them it holds an entire library, and their most reasonable guess is that the letters are written very, very small. And among people alive today, how many have seen what RAM or an SSD looks like, let alone read one without the corresponding interface, controller, files and software. A modern factory is not a building full of machines either, but a living ecosystem: spare parts, lubricants, sensors, trained technicians, quality control, software updates, raw materials of a specific purity, and other factories that build the machines that build the machines. Cut a few of those links and the knowledge is still there in theory, but the civilization cannot act on it.

8:07 A maintenance guild can turn from public service into monopoly
Automation moves skill off people and into machines; that in itself is not decline, it's specialization. The danger appears when the system is still needed but people are no longer trained to understand what it's doing. The author extrapolates: in a hundred years few will understand, in five hundred it may become a hereditary guild, in five thousand it may become a temple — and temple-style maintenance is not necessarily nonfunctional, ritual can preserve procedure, just as "the red light must not be ignored" sounds mystical but is actually good engineering advice. The genuinely subtle risk is that the ritual survives and the understanding dies: when the red light is replaced by an orange light, no one knows whether orange is "junior red" or the wrath of another machine god. Worse is when the guild turns from public service into monopoly, taking the manuals, the keys and the apprenticeship slots hostage.

14:12 Loss is not getting dumber, it's a chain of locally reasonable decisions
The first generation knows what was lost, the second knows the story, the third knows the taboo, the fourth only knows that "whoever opens panel 12 angered the sky." It sounds absurd, but everyone who opened panel 12 did die — because a high-voltage busbar sits underneath it. The conclusion is wrong, yet not entirely irrational. Technological amnesia usually accumulates like this: don't open the dangerous panel, don't modify the reactor software, don't question the irrigation algorithm during planting season, don't let everyone learn the old technology, because some technologies can build weapons, plagues and runaway machines, or bring political trouble — and political trouble can be as petty as some self-important meritocratic applicant taking the apprenticeship slot your nephew would have had. Every rule has a reason, the reason becomes a story, the story becomes a tradition, the tradition becomes a legend, the legend fades into myth, and the warning finally becomes scripture.

17:14 If no one pays anyone to remember, the technology disappears
Beyond deliberate prohibition there is a quieter path: economic forgetting. Once a technology is automated, cheap and reliable, the labor market stops rewarding the old skills, companies stop training, schools drop it from the curriculum, suppliers close, documentation gets locked into obsolete formats, corporate archives, legal disputes or subscription systems, the last expert retires, and everyone says you can always call him when you need him — which is a rather optimistic view of mortality. The ready-made example the author gives is rocketry and nuclear engineering: when NASA revisited the Saturn V's F-1 engine, it could only test-fire surviving hardware and rebuild components with modern CAD, to recover a technology whose original production ecosystem had long since vanished. Scaled up to the future: design templates are proprietary, factories are autonomous, most citizens use their devices as "invisible services." The machines are still there, but the right to repair, the unlock keys, the model files to print parts, the diagnostic AI that can read error codes — all gone. The civilization didn't forget nature, it misplaced the password.

19:15 The tech stack a colony inherits may run too deep
An interstellar colony ship would probably carry a giant library, automated factories, medical systems, agricultural templates, genetic archives and robots — that really is good insurance. But if the colony leans too hard on automation, it may arrive able to build a city without fully understanding how the city was built. The first hundred years look like a miracle, the second hundred turn into maintenance, cannibalization, rationing, and the slow discovery that the colony starter pack contains no "backup factory to build the backup factory." The author's own phrasing: the machine that builds standard template constructs needs to include a standard template for building a factory, and that factory has to be able to build backups of those standard template constructs. The key to survival redundancy is not preserving information, it's preserving capability.

25:19 A stagnant civilization is the quietest in the Fermi paradox
The author gives four futures: the optimistic version, where automation gives people more time to learn; the controlled but risky version, where most people don't understand the deep systems but there are enough experts — which is basically our world, and the default state of an advanced society; a darker version, where the civilization becomes a passenger on its own infrastructure, maintained by automation and explained by tradition no one dares question, able to coast for centuries or millennia — but coasting is not driving. The darkest version: the civilization spreads to the stars yet grows ever more dependent on tech stacks it cannot reproduce locally, colonies lose contact, lose experts and parts, some worlds worship the weather-control towers and go to war over the patch of land the mirrors focus on, some worlds live under the guardianship of an AI they cannot understand — and by the translation of its last readable state, that AI is benevolent. From the outside these worlds need not look like failed civilizations; they may be stable, happy, prosperous — but they no longer move forward, they just live inside an inheritance. And an inheritance runs out. This also gives the Fermi paradox a new explanation: civilizations maintaining old infrastructure may be far quieter than expansionist ones, and may even regard building Dyson swarms and launching starships as the immature behavior their ancestors warned against.

item.title: Philippine Immigration Detention: If You Don't Pay, Your Deportation Never Moves
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-cn907a40-菲律宾移民局拘留所-不交钱-你的遣返程序永远走不通/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-cn907a40-菲律宾移民局拘留所-不交钱-你的遣返程序永远走不通/
item.description: A Chinese surfer was held in the Philippines for 41 days. What he saw wasn't a prison — it was a business with prices posted on the wall: beds, boxed meals, phones, lawyer fees, every one of them bought with cash. Those who don't pay stay locked up for years, even decades.
item.content:encoded:
A Chinese surfer was held in the Philippines for 41 days. What he saw wasn't a prison — it was a business with prices posted on the wall: beds, boxed meals, phones, lawyer fees, every one of them bought with cash. Those who don't pay stay locked up for years, even decades.

StoryFM's Behind Bars series. Medium information density but solid detail. The first half is one man's ordeal; the second half — the gang economy inside the detention center, the ransom quotes from scam companies, the lawyers who jack up prices on the spot — is the part actually worth your time.

10:05 The Immigration Bureau quoted 1.5 million pesos to walk free on the spot
The night Feili was arrested, an Immigration Bureau officer pulled him aside and said quietly, "I can help you." After talking to a lawyer, the word came back: hand over 1.5 million pesos, roughly 160,000-170,000 RMB, and you can be released immediately, no problem at all. Of the 12 to 13 people arrested in the same batch, nobody agreed to pay. Everyone thought it was impossible that such a thing could still exist in 2026, and wanted to resolve it through normal legal procedure. But the price of refusing was this: they were transferred from the holding cells of the General Santos police station to the Immigration Bureau detention center in Manila, where Feili ultimately spent 41 days.

18:21 When his phone was confiscated, the money in Gcash was transferred out
When Feili was detained his phone was taken, and they asked for his unlock code. He assumed it was standard procedure and gave it. His phone unlock code was the same as his Gcash payment password — the Philippine equivalent of Alipay. For the next four or five days he applied repeatedly and could not get the phone back, until he kept pressing the Chinese consulate and his lawyer, at which point it was returned. When he turned it on, the interface had all switched to English, and the Gcash transfer records showed money had been sent out — but then sent back the night before he got the phone. There was only about 1,000 RMB in there. Feili says it isn't about the amount; it's that someone touched it while it wasn't in his hands. His read: many Chinese in Manila doing gray-industry scams who get arrested go through this same layer of skimming, but they don't dare approach the Chinese consulate, because their phones are full of criminal evidence.

24:26 The air conditioning and takeout the Immigration Bureau promised exist — in another form
For those unwilling to buy their own plane ticket to transfer, the Immigration Bureau works on them in shifts, saying conditions at the Manila bureau are excellent: air conditioning, plenty of freedom, you can work out, play basketball, order takeout, use your phone. Feili says they weren't lying — there really is air conditioning, you really can order takeout. It's just another form. A completely different form. They arrived at the main detention center past three in the morning. What he saw after getting out of the vehicle was a square area wrapped in a layer of iron grating, a sheet-metal roof overhead, and all around it iron cages like dog kennels, with long communal platforms inside, hundreds of people. Past three in the morning, many weren't sleeping — bare-chested, in nothing but underwear, clinging to the cage bars to stare at the newcomers. Feili says he and the other foreigners didn't say a word for several minutes after getting out, and then it hit them: the Immigration Bureau had lied to them.

32:38 The detention center is a business invested in by a Chinese boss
The story Feili heard inside was that this Immigration Bureau detention center was invested in by a Chinese boss, in cooperation with the Immigration Bureau, and that the beds, toilets and other facilities were all newly built by that Chinese boss. Foreigners just stay there, but Chinese who come in have to pay. The cheapest tier, a spot on the communal platform, is 10,000 pesos a month, about 1,100-1,200 RMB. The wealthy panzong and gambling bosses can pay 50,000 pesos a month, over 6,000 RMB, for a so-called "air-conditioned room" — in reality the bed is the same, just wrapped in tin foil and wooden boards, with a styrofoam box of ice beside it, a hole cut in the box, and an exhaust fan pulling the cold air into the bed. That is where the Immigration Bureau's promise of "air conditioning inside" came from.

34:38 Chinese gangs collect protection money: you want out without paying?
On Feili's first day inside, the head of the Chinese gang came to collect a "rumor fee," saying the facilities were all their investment and there was no way he'd stay for free. Feili said he had no money, that he was here to serve time — how could he be expected to pay on top of that? The gang boss, in a threatening tone, said: you're already in here and you don't want to spend money, and you still think you're getting out? Feili learned that the place is run through gangs, and the Chinese gang monopolizes everything for Chinese inmates — food, clothing, daily life — running a Chinese restaurant and a Chinese supermarket. The whole detention center holds about 200 people; when Feili arrived it was the off season, and there were still over 100 Chinese, more than half of them gambling and gray industry. The Chinese gang's staff draw wages: the head chef gets 10,000 pesos a month, the kitchen hands 5,000 pesos. The pay is very low, but many people can't get out precisely because they have no money for a lawyer, so they can only work to earn.

43:48 A young man from Yunnan held over a year; his family thought he died in Southeast Asia
A young man from Yunnan asked Feili for help. Before the pandemic he'd been lured to the Philippines by a high-salary recruitment ad; the moment he landed his phone and passport were taken and he was dragged into a compound to run telecom fraud. With poor numbers he was shocked with an electric baton by his supervisor every day. After the company was busted he served a few months, then was transferred to the Immigration Bureau detention center. The normal deportation procedure is simple — a few departments sign off, you buy your own plane ticket, and you're gone. But the Immigration Bureau, in order to extract money, keeps you locked up a long time; without paying, the procedure doesn't move. He'd already been held over a year, with not a cent, no phone, eating only prison food every day, unable to reach his family, who thought he had died in Southeast Asia. Feili helped him write a letter in Chinese, translated it into English, and through an introduction from a Japanese man got to see the warden. The warden had a guard bring Feili's phone, and let the young man add his father on WeChat and send a selfie and a voice message. Afterwards the Immigration Bureau bought a basic phone specifically to solve this problem.

51:29 Scam company ransom: 3 million pesos per person
The only Chinese Feili talked with at any length came from a scam company. The company's 70 or 80 people had been surrounded by the Immigration Bureau together with the police and the NBI — three agencies. The first wave of skimming was the NBI and police locking each person in a toilet, because there are no cameras in the toilets, and stripping them of everything valuable. The second wave was the Immigration Bureau negotiating with the company boss for the release of people, with different quotes per person — 1 million, 2 million, 3 million pesos — depending on the mood of whoever was in charge.
