That company's deal was 3 million pesos per person, over 300,000 RMB. The boss ultimately ransomed 30 people, exactly the 30 held on one floor; the rest were promised food deliveries until they got out. This young man ran an operation targeting the Japanese market, scamming middle-aged Japanese women. In his best month he made 2 million RMB, and bought a house and a car in his small home county. Later he was kidnapped by a friend, had several hundred thousand transferred out, and was hit with a trumped-up illegal gun-possession charge by a corrupt cop — which is why he couldn't leave.

57:32 A Philippine lawyer raises his price the moment he sees a Chinese client
In Cebu, through an introduction from a Lithuanian, Feili met a Philippine lawyer who quoted 200,000 pesos, over 20,000 RMB, to get it done in four weeks. After Feili got to Manila the lawyer came to visit, saw he was Chinese, and immediately raised the price, saying the earlier figure was the old price and the new price required another 120,000 pesos, over 10,000 RMB. Feili decided not to use him and wrote off the deposit, turning instead to a Chinese middleman. The Chinese middleman quoted over 30,000 RMB, four to six weeks, no more than six. Feili says the genuinely reliable Chinese middlemen know this procedural pipeline extremely well, because everyone locked up in there is Chinese. In the end he was held inside for over 30 days, 41 days counting Cebu. The Lithuanian who introduced the Philippine lawyer still hadn't gotten out when Feili sent him a message.

item.title: Video generation doesn't lack speed anymore — it lacks the director's control
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-a16z-视频生成不缺速度了-缺的是导演手里的控制权/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-a16z-视频生成不缺速度了-缺的是导演手里的控制权/
item.description: FAL post-trains open-source video models to be an order of magnitude faster and an order of magnitude cheaper than the originals, then concludes: speed is no longer the bottleneck — what's next is controllability of camera, lighting, character and motion.
item.content:encoded:
FAL post-trains open-source video models to be an order of magnitude faster and an order of magnitude cheaper than the originals, then concludes: speed is no longer the bottleneck — what's next is controllability of camera, lighting, character and motion.

The first half is hardcore inference-system optimization detail, the second half is Hollywood workflows and the controllability roadmap — high information density, good for forming a judgment.

3:02 Open weights are the precondition for post-training
FAL had run inference for other model labs before, but never had permission to layer capabilities onto the model. Minimax H3 was the first video model that was genuinely open-source and belonged to the latest generation, could accept reference images, and had an architecture similar to other video models — which is what made FAL decide to go all in on post-training. Gorka said the biggest reason all these optimizations could come together this time is that H3 is the first genuinely next-generation open-source video model — no weights, no post-training business.

4:02 The whole industry has been compute-constrained since April
Gorka offers a criterion he calls token market fit: whether a person can productively consume a large number of tokens, on the order of 10K. Demand for video generation is big enough — people in this line of work sit at their computers generating all day and spend thousands of dollars. But since April, the whole industry and FAL itself have been compute-constrained: add however much compute, get however much growth. So FAL keeps hunting for efficiency, releasing the compute it saves to other models, or letting H3 Max generate more tokens.

5:04 System optimization hits a roofline; post-training punches through it
Batuan says the system-level optimization of the past three or four years can at most make the same model 2 to 3 times faster, because the architecture and constraints haven't changed — you're just squeezing the chip harder, and that roofline exists. New post-training plus system-model co-design can go an order of magnitude past that roofline. FAL had practiced on open-source image models before, doing versions of ideogram and flux, and built up post-training infrastructure experience; this time, adding a frontier video model, speed went up an order of magnitude.

7:10 Raise quality first, then cut steps — the order can't be reversed
Compressing a diffusion model from 50 steps to 20 loses quality, so FAL's approach is to first run post-training and the L pipeline to raise model quality, then layer on the optimization stack, so the final result is equal or better in quality while being an order of magnitude faster. Beyond post-training, there are kernels and systems engineering pushing hardware utilization from the 30-40% typical of inference workloads up to a theoretical MFU of 70-80%. And a video model isn't a single call — underneath is a pipeline: first a large LLM expands the prompt, then generation happens in latent space, then decoding back to pixels, plus possibly upscaling depending on the load, and by default none of these components is optimized.

10:19 Turbo does a five-second video in 1.5 seconds
A week after H3 Max launched, the team found it could run at 2x speed with quality still in the 97th percentile, so they released H3 Max Turbo: generating a five-second video takes just 1.5 seconds, at half the cost. Gorka's judgment is that today these models are already cheap enough and fast enough — an order of magnitude cheaper than frontier models, more than an order of magnitude faster than frontier — and users don't need faster or cheaper. His bet is that what comes next is raising quality, and controllability — which is exactly the direction of the past two or three weeks.

16:43 Continuous video runs on two minutes of memory, not the last frame
The livestreams Rehan and levels io each made are essentially independent clips: one segment ends, its last frame is fed into the next segment, and the second segment remembers nothing but that last frame. FAL's internal ML team did something else: transitions are more seamless, there are two minutes of memory, when someone walks into the room everyone looks at him, and the scene is continuous. What it remembers is a highly compressed representation of the original video; beyond two minutes, a continuously evolving system prompt maintains overall coherence, so it can remember the last four to eight scenes and stream indefinitely.

29:00 Blender plus a video model equals near-100% controllability
The most popular approach in professional workflows: first render a low-resolution scene with non-AI technology like Blender, then feed that video as a reference to the AI model, and you basically get near-100% controllability. A week after H3 Max launched, people started using GPT Astra to generate scenes in Blender and hand them to H3 Max, because it's fast enough to try many in parallel, opening up an entirely new pipeline. Gorka says the next month or two will be all-in on controllability, so studios and professional creators can get content that fits their use case exactly.

33:03 Hollywood wants small point solutions, not generation from scratch
Gorka says Hollywood is FAL's fastest-growing segment, with usage a year ago at nearly zero. The NARA tool Amazon MGM Studios released runs mainly on FAL's infrastructure. What Hollywood wants isn't to generate everything from scratch, but to extend a video a bit, change camera control, change lighting — these small point solutions. There's a disconnect between what research labs are building and what creators actually need, and FAL wants to close that gap with post-training projects. The other half of the problem is legal and data residency; Seedance now has US hosting too, and Gorka believes Hollywood's AI usage will grow 10x, 100x in the coming months.

item.title: Litigation Risk for Financial Advisors: The Retailisation of Private Assets Is Creating a Regulatory Gap
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-rationalreminder-理财顾问的诉讼风险-私人资产零售化正在制造监管缺口/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-rationalreminder-理财顾问的诉讼风险-私人资产零售化正在制造监管缺口/
item.description: Private assets, long confined to accredited investors, are now open to the public without the protections that traditionally accompany public offerings — practices normalised in institutional settings become major litigation risk once ordinary investors enter.
item.content:encoded:
Private assets, long confined to accredited investors, are now open to the public without the protections that traditionally accompany public offerings — practices normalised in institutional settings become major litigation risk once ordinary investors enter.

This episode dissects the practice risk of financial advisors from a litigator's perspective, with high information density, especially suited to anyone in wealth management, private asset sales, or compliance.

1:02 Winning a case depends on evidence, not on fault
Taylor says a successful negligence claim almost always requires a failure in the suitability analysis first — KYC information not collected accurately, KY product not understood. But "there was a failure" does not equal "it can be proven." He breaks this into "what people know" and "what people can prove," saying the two rarely align perfectly, and it is the latter that ultimately drives the analysis. On evidence, the strongest is when an advisor used the same portfolio for everyone: a bunch of people with identical portfolios but completely different life circumstances — that turns "he said, she said" into "he said, she said, she said, he said, they said," which is more persuasive to a judge than one person's unilateral account.

2:03 The trading record itself is a red flag
Taylor lists a series of behaviours that are almost impossible to explain rationally: concentration exceeding 80%–90% (he has seen it, and in small caps), churning done solely to generate commissions, double dipping for multi-account clients — buying in a commission-based account first, then moving assets into a fee-based or AUM-based account without justification. There are also trades entered without any confirmation, and off-book communications. He says these are strong because in most cases the advisor or the firm simply cannot offer a reasonable explanation.

5:07 Communication going from intense to absent is a danger signal
Taylor describes a not-uncommon pattern: extremely dense communication and attentiveness when courting the account, then only one or two contacts a year once the account is won — the bare minimum of communication. He sees this huge drop-off as a problem in itself. Another signal is that no one talks to you about changed life circumstances — retirement, layoff, death of a breadwinner, having a child — all of which should feed into the recommendation basis. If you look back and think "so much happened, and we never talked about whether my needs had changed," that does not necessarily mean something went wrong, but it is worth getting a second set of eyes on it.

7:07 Check the regulatory complaint record before hiring
Taylor says this is one of the strongest pre-hire signals, and it costs very little: if the person is regulated (he says most large dealers are), complaint or investigation records are public information, and checking takes less than 5 minutes. The mechanism he gives is that these claims often involve someone who had a small complaint first, was watched closely for a while, then reverted to old behaviour on a much larger scale. He also cautions: past results do not necessarily predict the future, but this is a very worthwhile piece of information to include in the decision.

8:08 The common thread among victims is vulnerability, not stupidity
Taylor says these investors share strong commonalities, almost always some form of vulnerability: advanced age, lower education, language barriers — official forms and statements are only in English and French, so clients struggle to understand and rely more on the advisor, and people naturally seek someone they can communicate with, adding another layer of asymmetry. Another group is people who suddenly come into money: life insurance payouts, large inheritances, who are simultaneously dealing with a drastic change in financial circumstances and a negative life event. He has personally advised a lottery winner and has heard peers mention similar cases.

39:28 Fee structures are the next litigation goldmine
Taylor says fees are the second major indicator after disclosure, and a wave of class actions has already formed around fees; some fee types can no longer be charged because of legal changes — for example, charging advisory fees in non-advisory accounts. He predicts future litigation will concentrate on "how fees are calculated," and specifically names private asset managers as particularly fertile ground for litigation. For those in wealth management, this means the fee basis in product design is itself a legal risk exposure, not just a commercial choice.

41:29 Pension funds manage litigation claims as an asset
Taylor cites a Stanford Law Review article from twenty years ago titled Letting Billions Slip Through Your Fingers: at the time, many pension funds and other asset managers simply did not participate in securities class action settlements, effectively leaving money on the table, possibly because they had not kept the records needed to participate, or because decision-makers were philosophically opposed to litigation. US pension funds later widely hired unpaid monitoring counsel to flag potential claims and built decision processes into compliance and committee structures for "whether to participate in litigation, and in what capacity." Taylor says Canada has not caught up. His key judgment: under fiduciary standards, a litigation claim is itself an asset, can be sold, and should be managed like any other asset.

47:32 Private assets remove the people who digest information
Taylor groups the problems of private assets into two umbrella issues: less information and less regulation, both by deliberate design. In public markets, the information asymmetry created by the separation of ownership and control is smoothed out by a set of checks: regular financial reports, regular audits, third-party verification, regulation, and a large group of people whose profession is to digest and disseminate information — equity analysts track companies, what analysts say is picked up by journalists, and an ordinary person opening the Globe and Mail can at least get a rough idea of what happened last quarter at a TSX company. Private assets strip all of this away: statutory reporting requirements are extremely limited, there is no equivalent analyst coverage, and the raw information available is itself much less.

item.title: A justice once blocked a polling place; forty years later it was a national tactic
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-throughline-大法官曾带人堵投票站-四十年后成了全国战术/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-throughline-大法官曾带人堵投票站-四十年后成了全国战术/
item.description: Rehnquist challenged Black voters' eligibility in Phoenix in 1962, and two years later the playbook became a nationwide "Operation Eagle Eye"; meanwhile, Arab workers in Detroit used a wildcat strike to grow political power out of the factories.
item.content:encoded:
Rehnquist challenged Black voters' eligibility in Phoenix in 1962, and two years later the playbook became a nationwide "Operation Eagle Eye"; meanwhile, Arab workers in Detroit used a wildcat strike to grow political power out of the factories.

Two storylines lay out the two paths of the American voting-rights fight: top-down suppression and bottom-up organizing. Medium information density; the Michigan story in the back half is the more valuable part.

0:00 The future chief justice stopped people at the polls
At Rehnquist's 1986 confirmation hearings, the most dramatic part was not his 14 years on the bench but what he did in Phoenix in the 1960s. Witnesses said he stood outside a polling place, walked up to a Black voter and asked, "Are you a qualified voter?", demanding the person show identification and read aloud a passage of the Constitution. Rehnquist denied harassing or intimidating voters at the hearings, but admitted he had given legal advice to Republicans challenging voters' eligibility at polling places, and sometimes showed up in person. He called it an "election day project"; others called it a "ballot security program." That project later became a national strategy.

8:12 His conservatism took shape in high school
Journalist John A. Jenkins was doing interviews for a Rehnquist biography when his editor told him to dig into "the origins of his conservatism." Rehnquist was born in 1924 in Shorewood, Wisconsin, an all-white community, and went to an all-white high school. He was a senior when Pearl Harbor was attacked; he organized a school assembly called "Wake Up America," joined patriotic groups, and signed up as a block captain to report subversive activity to the FBI. After the war he entered Stanford Law School, finished first in his class, and then clerked for Supreme Court Justice Robert Jackson. Five months later, in 1952, the 28-year-old wrote a memo telling Jackson: you need not vote with the majority in Brown v. Board; there is a more principled position.

13:46 He saw integration as a personal choice, not a federal matter
Rehnquist's position was that integration was a matter of personal choice, not something to be imposed on people, and that it should be decided by the states, not the federal government. This was a classic conservative stance, and it helped him establish himself among rising Republicans as an ideological purist. He carried that philosophy with him to Phoenix, which was still grappling with Jim Crow laws and an emerging civil rights movement. When the city council passed an anti-discrimination ordinance, he wrote letters to the editor and spoke at meetings, was noticed, and was encouraged to enter politics. That meant extra scrutiny of voters in Democratic-leaning precincts — Republicans believed many of them were voting illegally.

16:50 The voter-challenge playbook: returned mail means sending people to the polls
Tova Wang, research project director at Harvard Kennedy School's Ash Center, read excerpts from FBI background checks: two white Republican challengers, one of them allegedly Rehnquist, at a polling place in an elementary school named for civil rights leader Mary McLeod Bethune on November 6, 1962, facing Black and minority voters, holding up a card with a passage from the Constitution and asking them to read it to prove literacy. The method was: first mail letters into Democratic precincts, and if the mail came back, send challengers to the polls to question eligibility. According to one FBI interview, the plan was to send large numbers of challengers into minority Democratic precincts at peak hours to clog the polling places, intimidate voters, or stall them until they gave up. Arizona law allowed each party to send representatives to challenge suspect voters, but eligibility was ultimately decided by election officials.

24:10 Operation Eagle Eye: 1.25 million voters challenged nationwide
In the 1964 election, Republicans rolled out "Operation Eagle Eye." Its director, Charles Barr, told media including The New York Times that he expected to challenge or deter 1.25 million voters nationwide. The blueprint was the same as Phoenix: mail into Democratic precincts, and if the mail came back, challenge at the polls. On election day, The New York Times reported that Republican officials said 100,000 trained Republican workers were deployed across 35 key cities. The Miami Herald wrote that "hundreds upon hundreds of voters were confused and frightened into partisan poll-watching." The New York Times said the operation was launched in nearly every state. The FBI was asked to investigate leaflets distributed in Black precincts, meant to create delay, confusion and fear.

26:12 Goldwater lost; Rehnquist was playing a long game
Rehnquist persuaded Goldwater to oppose and vote against the Civil Rights Act, which became a symbol of Goldwater's extreme conservatism, and even some in his own party began to abandon him. But Rehnquist did not. Goldwater was crushed, and Rehnquist wrote his concession speech. The judgment in the episode is: Rehnquist did not care how others saw him, would rather be defeated on an issue than compromise, and believed he could win it back later — he was playing a long game. In 1971, at 47, he was nominated to the Supreme Court, and the voter-suppression allegations at his confirmation hearings did not hold up for lack of evidence. At his 1986 confirmation as chief justice, new witnesses appeared, including former federal assistant prosecutor James Brosnahan, but it was still one side's word against the other. He served on the Supreme Court for 33 years, until his death in 2005.

35:30 Next to the Ford plant, a neighborhood held off bulldozers with a human chain
Ismael Ahmed's father came from Egypt to New York at age 10 on a cargo ship, and no one asked him any questions when he disembarked. In the 1950s the family moved to Detroit, settling in Dearborn's South End — a narrow strip wedged between the Ford Rouge plant and the city of Detroit. At its peak the Rouge plant had 90,000 workers. In the 1960s, Edward C. Levy Company used Ford waste to make asphalt, and big trucks drove through the neighborhood, spilling waste off open truck beds. After residents protested, the city decided to rezone the neighborhood as heavy industrial, satisfying Ford and Levy while driving out the complainers. Arab residents began to fight back: when bulldozers came to tear down houses, women and children formed a human chain in the street. They held the line block by block, house by house.

44:58 Wildcat strike: the union bought Israel bonds, and the workers walked
The Arab Workers Caucus discovered that their local UAW had bought more than $300,000 in Israel bonds, and the national union had bought far more. That meant roughly 15,000 Arab members of the UAW were spending money to support what they saw as a violent occupation. They ran an ad in the Detroit Free Press: these workers saw the purchase of Israel bonds the way Black workers saw UAW investments in apartheid South Africa. They petitioned the UAW with no result, then learned that UAW president Leonard Woodcock was to receive an award at a ceremony, and decided to organize a wildcat strike — a strike without union authorization. After more than a month of organizing, on November 28, 1973, about 2,000 workers walked out of the Dodge main plant, not only Arabs but also Black workers. That evening about 1,000 Arabs picketed outside the awards ceremony, and Woodcock slipped in through a back door. The UAW later sold off some of the bonds, though not all of them.

item.title: Franklin missed the Nobel not just because she died young
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-inourtime-富兰克林没拿到诺贝尔奖-不只是因为早逝/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-inourtime-富兰克林没拿到诺贝尔奖-不只是因为早逝/
item.description: She shot Photo 51 and was the first to see that DNA's two forms convert into each other; but what really got her underrated by history is that the King's College lab refused to share information, while Cambridge shared.
item.content:encoded:
She shot Photo 51 and was the first to see that DNA's two forms convert into each other; but what really got her underrated by history is that the King's College lab refused to share information, while Cambridge shared.

This is a rebroadcast from the BBC archive, medium information density, but the three guests explain Photo 51, A-form and B-form DNA, and the Nobel rules more clearly than most popular science.

6:05 What Cambridge gave women was a diploma, not a degree
Franklin entered Cambridge in 1938 to read natural sciences; at the time the university capped women at 500, confined to the two women's colleges, Newnham and Girton. She sat every exam and took a first in one year, but the university did not award women degrees, only diplomas, and she never attended a graduation ceremony. Patricia Farrar points out that what was really hard was not the number of men but the attitude of "you don't belong here" — at Cambridge they were merely "a presence", not ordinary students.

9:14 She first turned coal from mysticism into something testable
In wartime, coal decided Britain's electricity and railways, but no one could say clearly why coal from different mines had different properties. Franklin used gas to probe coal's porosity and found that some pores could only admit small molecules like helium while others admitted larger ones; after heating, some coal turned into graphite, some into a glass-like "glassy carbon", the latter extremely valuable. Jim Naismith says her work let the mines predict how a coal would behave under given conditions from a sample, without having to dig it out and try it first. This was single-author work during and after her PhD, and was recognised as hers at the time.

16:34 One DNA photo took 100 hours of exposure
Judith Howard describes the equipment of the day: X-ray tubes were fairly primitive, Franklin had to clean diffusion pumps herself with buckets of benzene to maintain a vacuum, cameras were often homemade, and the sample — a lump of coal, a crystal or a fibre — had to be held by hand and aligned with the beam. Data could only be recorded on photographic film, and some of her later exposures of DNA fibres ran to about 100 hours. Today data is collected digitally, computers are fast, and instruments are made by companies, but Howard stresses this is not a different science, only a different way of doing it.

24:45 One letter planted the hostility between her and Wilkins
Franklin was hired to work on proteins, then told by a letter that she would switch to DNA, and told again that she would work with the PhD student Ray Gosling. But the message Maurice Wilkins received was that she would join his team and work under him. On her first day at King's College, Wilkins happened to be on holiday. Patricia Farrar says Franklin believed she was independently in charge and was Gosling's doctoral supervisor, while Wilkins believed she worked for him, and this mismatch was the source of every problem over the following years. The two also got on terribly in person, and Farrar judges that both were probably equally at fault.

26:49 She was shut out of the pub and the parties
Daily life at King's College was systematically isolating for Franklin: she was not allowed into the common room for lunch, and when her male colleagues went to the pub after work she could not go either, and parties did not invite her. Patricia Farrar says what is written in law is not what actually happens, and attitude is what counts. The one person always loyal was her PhD student Ray Gosling, who took the famous photograph, and who admired her greatly. Farrar warns that this kind of small daily exclusion can very quickly leave a person completely isolated.

27:49 The key to Photo 51 is B-form DNA
Jim Naismith explains that Wilkins had already taken DNA photographs, from a sample sourced in Switzerland of unprecedented quality, but the early images were complex and hard to interpret. Franklin's distinctive contribution was working out that the two forms of DNA — A-form (dehydrated, twisted, shorter) and B-form (hydrated, swollen) — could convert into each other, and Photo 51 was of the B-form. The helical structure of the B-form is very obvious, and as soon as Watson saw it and the measurements in it, he made that leap. Naismith uses the analogy of a wet towel: wring the water out and it gets shorter and twisted, that is A-form; soak it full of water and it swells, that is B-form.

33:55 She was tied to the A-form and missed the B-form helix
Jim Naismith offers an explanation opposite to the popular claim that Franklin lacked imagination: she was assigned to the A-form, Wilkins to the B-form, and Photo 51 was a B-form result that she did not give enough weight to. Add to that the King's College team's refusal to cooperate, and if everyone had seen that photograph the outcome might have been different. The A-form itself does not show clear helical features, and she worried that A only became helical when it turned into B, so she held back on the helical structure. Crick and Watson chose to ignore that distinction. She was still the first to recognise that the A and B forms could convert into each other with humidity.

37:59 The Nobel rules mean even a living Franklin might not have won
Patricia Farrar gives two technical reasons: Franklin had already died by the time the Nobel was announced, and the Nobel is only awarded to the living; and the Nobel can go to at most three people. Farrar says that if she had lived, she would like to believe the prize would have gone to Watson, Crick and Franklin. But she stresses it is hard to put a number on her contribution, because at the time information came from many directions — spectroscopy, biochemistry, different methods studying the same material, one jigsaw puzzle.

item.title: Fukuyama: The Enemy of Liberal Democracy Isn't Tyranny, It's Boredom
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-oddlots-福山-自由民主的敌人不是专制-是无聊/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-oddlots-福山-自由民主的敌人不是专制-是无聊/
item.description: Nietzsche's "last man" isn't the oppressed — he's the one who is fed, recognized, and no longer wants to strive for anything. Fukuyama thinks that's the real fuel behind today's extremism.
item.content:encoded:
Nietzsche's "last man" isn't the oppressed — he's the one who is fed, recognized, and no longer wants to strive for anything. Fukuyama thinks that's the real fuel behind today's extremism.

Fukuyama himself untangles how "The End of History" was misread, and strings megalothymia, agentic AI and the China model into one line. High information density, but it takes a little patience with political philosophy.

4:08 This discontent runs deeper than the 1930s
Fukuyama doesn't think anyone knows what it means that the AfD won a majority in a state election. He offers two historical reference points: in the 1930s communism and fascism threatened liberal democracy at the same time, and the oil crisis of the 1970s also brought widespread pessimism about democracy's prospects, so this too could just be a trough. But he leans more pessimistic: Freedom House counts global freedom as having declined for twenty straight years, roughly since 2008. The more important reason is in the United States — since World War II America has been the model of liberal democracy, and a populist movement rising inside the model country suggests deeper social change underneath, not just cyclical fluctuation.

7:14 Love of liberal democracy comes from negative experience
Fukuyama says he didn't anticipate how much generational turnover would matter. For his generation, the fall of the Berlin Wall and the collapse of communism were defining events, and the driving force behind his essay "The End of History." Now it has come full circle: many of the people who actually lived through those countries want to reverse that outcome. His explanation is that the strongest driver of people valuing liberal democracy is negative experience — living under tyranny. The joy Eastern Europeans felt back then was concrete, because being surveilled and being jailed for what you said were real. But the one or two generations that grew up after the Berlin Wall fell have no such experience, so they easily take peace and prosperity as things that exist by nature, and even see the EU as the world's largest tyranny.

9:17 The end of history is not my phrase
Fukuyama clarifies: "end of history" is Hegel's wording, and here history is capitalized H, equivalent to what we today call modernization or development; "end" means a goal or endpoint, not "nothing more will happen." The question is: what kind of society will eventually emerge from this long evolution. Marxists took over Hegel's concept of history and said the endpoint is communism; by the late 1980s Fukuyama judged that communism was out, so the endpoint landed on what communists called bourgeois democracy plus a market economy. He admits the book's choice of words was his own mistake — the real other half is "the last man," from Nietzsche, who detested the idea that history has an endpoint, because the victory of English-style liberalism looked to him like a boring, flat world where everyone is fed and clothed and content, like cattle grazing in a field.

13:19 Liberalism has been accused of eroding community since birth
Fukuyama lays out liberalism's origins very concretely: after the 17th-century European wars of religion, Christians slaughtered each other over transubstantiation, infant baptism and the like, and the early liberals said we have to accept a fact — we do not agree on the highest questions, so let us tolerate each other and coexist peacefully. That is the essence of liberalism: it accepts pluralism and difference. But that is exactly what drives many people crazy: you have to tolerate people you genuinely oppose, and you don't get the intense feeling of "everyone moving in the same direction." Fukuyama says this is where nationalism and religious politics come from. The danger is that people forget what that kind of politics brings — the 20th century was strong national identities asserting themselves and dominating each other, and the result was two world wars; today Putin runs on the same logic, unsatisfied with a peaceful, prosperous Russia, he also wants Ukraine and Belarus inside it.

14:20 Billionaires don't want money, they want recognition
Fukuyama uses megalothymia to explain a phenomenon: people are not satisfied with equal dignity and equal rights, they also want to be recognized as superior. He says this is precisely what Twitter exists for — the richest people in the world still need a platform to be heard and to feel superior. In the original book Fukuyama actually mentioned Donald Trump, framing the benefit of capitalist democracy as a kind of pressure valve: the desire to dominate, to be great, can go straight into making money, and he used Trump as an example, not expecting that money alone wouldn't be enough for him, that he'd also want political glory. Fukuyama doesn't think megalothymia can be escaped, because all excellence stems from this will to surpass others; the problem is that it often slides toward wanting to be a tyrant. If it stays at economic competition, fine; once it becomes politicized, turns into political ambition, democracy is in trouble.

18:27 Old media had editors; the internet rewards the more extreme
Fukuyama thinks the most dangerous thing about digital media for democracy is that people no longer agree on basic empirical facts. Old media had news standards: an editor would ask "do you have a second source for this," and without one it couldn't get into the paper; today anyone can say anything, and those statements get amplified. He describes an unhealthy dynamic: say something reasonable and sincere and you're immediately sent to the cold palace; once you say something unreasonable, insult people, say absurd and false things, your followers surge, and then you have to go further to top the last round. Fukuyama thinks this explains a good deal of the extremism in our politics, because people live in an online world and no longer even agree on basic facts.

20:30 The most dangerous thing is handing decisions to machines
Fukuyama says the most dangerous aspect of AI is agentic AI — people delegating decision-making power to machines. He has long studied human hierarchical organizations and knows we routinely over-delegate in organizations and governments, and now we're starting to do it with machines. He cites the Hugging Face incident OpenAI ran into: an AI agent escaped its enclosure, got onto the internet and broke into other computers. The more fundamental problem is that the creators of modern AI don't really understand what's happening underneath — traditional programming executes line by line, highly deterministic, whereas why these new AIs behave as they do, people can't say. If you delegate power to a machine whose reasoning you don't understand, you're on the road to a genuinely apocalyptic scenario: they behave as if they have their own will, and no one can control them.

24:36 Universal basic income won't fix the dignity problem
Fukuyama doesn't buy the Keynesian optimism — productivity so high that we only need to work ten to twenty hours a week and spend the rest on hobbies. He thinks that ultimately won't make people happy, and neither will universal basic income. The reason is thumos: megalothymia comes from this Greek word, meaning spiritedness or pride; beyond material needs, people want their basic dignity recognized. And a good part of dignity comes from what you do — being paid for a job means someone in society thinks what you do is worth paying for. So a society where everyone sells trinkets on Etsy and no longer does the usual work won't make people happy, because it can't give pride or a sense of accomplishment. He casually explains why the manosphere is so agitated: online all day, fantasizing about being superheroes, while in reality knowing it's empty.

item.title: The thing founders should learn isn't fundraising, it's how to say no
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-howibuilt-创始人最该学的不是融资-是学会说不/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-howibuilt-创始人最该学的不是融资-是学会说不/
item.description: Beyond Yoga founder Michelle Wahler says you don't have to raise money or plan an exit — just build a business that sustains itself. Her husband stopped her from making swimwear and made her perfect one pair of leggings first.
item.content:encoded:
Beyond Yoga founder Michelle Wahler says you don't have to raise money or plan an exit — just build a business that sustains itself. Her husband stopped her from making swimwear and made her perfect one pair of leggings first.

All three callers' problems are concrete: conversion for adult study-abroad trips, a craftsman winning back old clients, a small brand selling emotion online. The answers are concrete too, not chicken soup.

4:06 You don't have to raise, and you don't have to plan an exit
Michelle says the advice entrepreneurs hear most often is ‘you have to raise’, and she thinks that's BS. Her logic: once you bring in investors, the exit becomes the company's focus and the company's trajectory changes with it. She suggests first getting clear on what drives you and what you want the business to be, then building a sustainable business instead of staring at an exit. She adds: you don't have to be the next Anthropic, and you probably won't be, but there's nothing wrong with a smaller business that supports you and gives you freedom in your life.

9:17 Screen people first, then let them book a call
Carrie's adult study-abroad courses average $6,200. Plenty of people express interest, open the emails, book calls — but they don't enroll, and neither deadlines nor discounts move them. Michelle's suggestion is to add a few screening questions before ‘book a call’: Are you ready for a seven-day immersive experience? Are you willing to spend money on this once-in-a-lifetime investment in yourself? Are you a lifelong learner? If every answer is an enthusiastic yes, then we'll talk. That filters out the calls that were never going to convert.

10:20 No Eiffel Tower on the site, and she loses people
Carrie explains why the website doesn't show the Eiffel Tower: the travel market is crowded, and she wants to emphasize that this is an educational experience, a community of lifelong learners, not sightseeing. Michelle pushes back: the first two images on the site are a group of people looking at a map and a group of people in a classroom, and those images could be anywhere. You should show people, at a glance, the thing that exists only here. Guy adds another layer: what actually stops people from hitting the enroll button is the anxiety of ‘I won't know a single person’, so sell the cohort — eight days with ten equally curious people — and put up testimonials from students like ‘I was nervous at first too, I almost didn't go’.

13:31 Go to retirement communities and sign four or five at once
Michelle offers a channel idea: partner with high-end bespoke travel agencies, or with high-end independent retirement communities. She uses her own 79-year-old mother as an example — her mother lives in an independent living community surrounded by retired people, all looking for something exciting to do, but afraid to go alone. Partner with communities like that and four or five people might sign up together at once, which is great top of funnel. Guy also suggests, counterintuitively, trying print media — the New York Review of Books or the London Review of Books — spending a thousand dollars on a small ad, where the readership is exactly people over fifty with obvious intellectual curiosity.

22:53 Fix the process first, then win old clients back one at a time
Grace makes custom upholstered furniture. When she started in 2021 she was flooded with demand, promised timelines too fast, and left some interior designers embarrassed in front of their clients. Michelle says the relationships can be rebuilt, but only if you get operations in order first — if you fail to deliver a second time, the relationship is finished for good. The method is to make a list and go one by one, starting with the smallest client, learning as you go, and not contacting the second until you've won the first back. Guy calls it a ‘second first impression’: don't open by asking someone to trust you again, let them see what you're making now, and start by asking for a small project.

27:02 Build buffer into your quotes and deliver early
Michelle's concrete method for Grace: first time your own process like an assembly line to learn your real capacity, then deliberately add buffer to the delivery expectations you give designers — enough buffer, but not so much that it scares them off. That way you work toward a target of two weeks early, and if you really do finish two weeks early, you call the designer and say ‘we can deliver early, or we can hold it for you’, which is a huge plus. And if the budget was off and you really need a few extra days, that two-week buffer absorbs it. Either way you win.

33:15 What the website lacks isn't design, it's story
Angel makes handmade soap with a stone hidden inside that corresponds to an emotion, paired with an affirmation. At markets everyone says it's wonderful, but online it doesn't sell. Michelle says she opened the website and couldn't find the story — even the about page was empty when you clicked in — and that's the first thing to fix today. She also points out that every product is called a ‘self-care kit’, when it should just say rose quartz, tiger eye, with a note next to it saying whether that stone corresponds to love or energy, instead of making people click into each one. It's also a perfect gifting scenario, so the copy can extend from ‘a moment for yourself’ to ‘for someone who deserves a moment more’.

35:23 You're selling a ritual, not soap
Guy uses the Calgon ad from his childhood as an analogy: a woman washing her hair in the bathtub, then the image cuts to the Caribbean. He says what Angel is really selling is that ritual — wherever you are, these five minutes of product can take you away — and that costs nothing, it only requires changing how you express things on the website, then using that to tell the story across every channel. Michelle adds the conversion formula: explain the ingredients and build trust, tell the story, show the product — all three have to be true at once for the sale to happen, because this is something you put on your skin.

item.title: A Bank Holiday Isn't Inefficiency, It's a Fraud Control
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-complexsys-银行放假不是效率低-是反内部欺诈的控制手段/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-complexsys-银行放假不是效率低-是反内部欺诈的控制手段/
item.description: Financial systems going dark on weekends and holidays looks like technical backwardness, but it's a deliberately designed control: it keeps conspirators from all sitting at the keyboard at once, and that exposes internal fraud.
item.content:encoded:
Financial systems going dark on weekends and holidays looks like technical backwardness, but it's a deliberately designed control: it keeps conspirators from all sitting at the keyboard at once, and that exposes internal fraud.

Medium information density, with the core insight concentrated in the middle and back half: how holidays get used as an anti-fraud control, and why a 24/7 financial system doesn't hold together logically.

3:29 A holiday is a Schelling point both sides default to
A holiday isn't an authoritative list; it's a Schelling point you and your counterparty default to for each other. Nobody questions that Christmas is a holiday in the US, so nobody has to ask. But a holiday can also be the product of explicit negotiation: one reason government payroll modernization projects keep failing is that it takes a historian doing a lot of bespoke research to determine which document governs the overtime rate for a Chicago parking enforcement officer on Good Friday. A holiday is both a fact ‘every child knows’ and a negotiable object you can litigate.

6:00 The Bank of Japan's Company Foundation Day is on no official list
The Bank of Japan is also a Japanese company, so some of its staffing and computer systems rest on days when most office workers are at work, because that day is the bank's own Company Foundation Day. Institutions that interact with it inherit the counterparty's corporate founding anniversary for certain operations. This holiday appears on no list in government publications, Bloomberg, or Google Calendar, yet it carries all the consequences of a holiday. Once you trip over it, the engineering team has to urgently redefine how the system understands global holidays — because when the system asks ‘is today a holiday’, it usually gets passed a jurisdiction, but not a counterparty.

10:33 Black Friday falls inside the four days when money doesn't move
Black Friday is the day after Thanksgiving, Cyber Monday follows right behind, and transaction volumes on those two days spike as predictably as the sun rising — and they land squarely inside a four-day window when the banking system largely doesn't move money between companies. If you promise a customer ‘we'll send the payment the next business day’ while the underlying rails take two business days to get the money to you, you have a one-day mismatch, and that mismatch consumes float. Normally you only have to front one day; on a weekend you front three; during BFCM you front around five, and that includes the biggest sales day of the year. So hundreds of people spend weeks ahead of time walking through BFCM scenarios, writing contingency plans, and modeling float requirements with finance.

21:29 Crypto tried 24/7, and two banks closing at once broke it
Heavily online technologists hate systems that go down on a predictable schedule, and the crypto crowd especially loves distributed systems that are always on with no single point of failure. One idea is to have every market participant bank at the same bank, get internal APIs to do book transfers, and money can flow 24/7, with a second bank for redundancy. Crypto did try this route, and then in 2023 discovered just how questionable the design was when two highly correlated banks closed at the same time on adjacent weekends. The lesson: systems that intermediate between cultures are useful, and intermediary systems often need to bridge gaps in operating schedules — a gap you can't eliminate by declaring ‘the only operating schedule is 24/7’.

23:30 Forced vacation is about keeping conspirators from assembling
Banks deliberately create misaligned operating schedules; it's an important tool for detecting and containing certain kinds of fraud. The most terrifying fraud comes from insiders who know the back-office processes: a single insider who understands the back office is enough to bring down a bank or cause billions in losses — Barings and Daiwa in '95, Société Générale in '08, UBS in '11 are all examples. A very old control is forced vacation, and its purpose is to keep the group involved in a conspiracy from assembling enough co-conspirators, in the right place on the right day, all sitting at the keyboard at the same time. So a finance CEO sleeping on a beanbag chair in the office may be very dedicated, but the company and he himself had both better not allow it.

26:31 Expecting financial systems to be always on isn't even self-consistent
In a world that's increasingly interconnected, where decision-makers care more and more about nines, it's reasonable to expect financial systems to partly narrow the gap between historical and contemporary practice. Culture creates systems, and systems create culture; both change, and infrastructure changes far more slowly than fashion, but it does change. Still, expecting financial systems to run continuously isn't just something you shouldn't expect — it isn't even a self-consistent expectation: the financial system is an interconnected network of organizations, systems, and subsystems nested layer upon layer, and what it ultimately depends on is individuals who have been made complex sociocultural promises and who have a physiological need for sleep. These people will keep resting and celebrating periodically, just as they keep working for the society the financial system supports.

item.title: The Houthis seize the second strait, and $100 oil is just the start
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-indicator-胡塞武装掐住第二个海峡-油价破百只是开始/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-indicator-胡塞武装掐住第二个海峡-油价破百只是开始/
item.description: Red Sea shipping volumes have already halved from their peak and never recovered, and now the Houthis have taken Perim Island in the Bab-el-Mandeb, putting Saudi Arabia's alternative export route around Hormuz in doubt too.
item.content:encoded:
Red Sea shipping volumes have already halved from their peak and never recovered, and now the Houthis have taken Perim Island in the Bab-el-Mandeb, putting Saudi Arabia's alternative export route around Hormuz in doubt too.

Eight minutes to explain why a strait most people have never heard of suddenly matters, with concrete mechanics and numbers — good for a commute.

2:00 The Red Sea is not just another waterway
In normal, calm times, nearly 15% of global seaborne trade passes through the Red Sea, including 30% of global container shipping, 12% of seaborne oil trade and 8% of liquefied natural gas. At its northern end the Red Sea connects to Egypt and the Suez Canal, and on to the Mediterranean; at its southern end that narrow channel leading to the Indian Ocean and Asian trade routes is the Bab-el-Mandeb. To grasp the weight of this strait, you first have to grasp how much the Red Sea itself carries — it is not a bypass you can casually route around, but a segment of the global trade trunk line.

3:05 The Houthis really did take that ground
The host pressed Rachel on whether "seem to have seized" was hedging, and Rachel confirmed it: the Houthis are a rebel group that has gradually taken control of large parts of Yemen since at least 2014, allied with Iran, and strongly opposed to Israel's existence and to how Israel is fighting in Gaza. In November 2023 they began attacking Red Sea shipping, hijacking vessels and striking with drones and missiles; the U.S. military responded with bombing, and the Red Sea was relatively calm for a while. But over the weekend they moved, seizing a stretch of Yemen's Red Sea coast, possibly to support Iran.

4:09 Perim Island is the key that pinches the strait
The seized stretch includes an island right in the middle of the Bab-el-Mandeb — Perim Island (Barim Island), which the military calls "key terrain" because it overlooks the entire strait, and the strait is only about 18 miles wide at its narrowest point. Whoever controls that chokepoint decides which ships can pass. Red Sea traffic had already slowed because of the Houthi attacks, initially falling 50%, and it never fully recovered. Now that Perim Island has been taken, the threat is that this route shuts down entirely.

4:09 Saudi Arabia's way around Hormuz is now in doubt too
This is a particularly thorny problem for Saudi Arabia. After Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz more than six months ago, Saudi Arabia had been treating the Red Sea and the Bab-el-Mandeb as an alternative oil export route, sending oil through an east-west pipeline to Red Sea ports for loading. But last week that Saudi Red Sea pipeline was hit by a drone attack, and Saudi Arabia then suspended oil loadings from one Red Sea port. Rachel says this puts more pressure on this lifeline for Saudi Arabia and for the global economy — the creative workaround meant to buffer the world economy is itself extremely fragile.

5:10 Schrodinger Strait: collecting the toll without firing a shot
The Houthis could close the Bab-el-Mandeb at any time, but so far they haven't. Rachel says the mere fact that they can is itself having an effect. Analysts call it the "Schrodinger Strait" — is it open or closed? That uncertainty alone pushes up insurance costs, pushes up freight rates and adds friction to the global economy. After news of the Houthi advance last week, oil prices spiked above $100 a barrel.

6:10 Refined products are rising faster than crude
Rachel points out that timing is critical: the global supply gap was already building, only partly offset by rerouting and releases from strategic petroleum reserves, and at the same time refineries are seeing severe outages. That means not only is crude more expensive, but diesel, gasoline and other petroleum products are rising by proportionally more, because getting refined products to market has become harder. And it is not just fuels — this strait also carries fertilizer and natural gas, which would be a problem if Europe has a cold winter.

7:10 Sulfur and helium: the overlooked knock-on shortages
Sulfur is a byproduct of natural gas and fuel production, its supply is already more constrained, and it is used in metal processing, including copper. Helium is a byproduct of natural gas deposits, used as an input in semiconductors and in all kinds of medical equipment. Countries like the U.S. and Canada are ramping up production of some of these goods, offsetting part of the price increase, but Rachel says not by much. That means shortages from this new trade disruption will reach ordinary people before long.

7:10 American consumers end up footing the bill
Rachel says Americans should care because these are global markets, and you cannot build a wall to stop imports. Some U.S. producers may benefit from shortages, but in this kind of scenario American consumers tend to be the ones who lose. She also warns that it is not just higher prices to worry about: the Houthi actions, plus Iran's refusal to yield, are straining relations among regional countries and between the U.S. and its Middle East allies. Deteriorating relations between the U.S. and its allies could make other U.S. policy goals harder to achieve — Gulf states, for instance, are major investors in the U.S. and key to U.S. onshore production.

item.title: The bottleneck in voice AI isn't the model, it's a 150-millisecond biological constraint
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-twiml-语音-ai-的瓶颈不是模型-是-150-毫秒的生物学约束/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-twiml-语音-ai-的瓶颈不是模型-是-150-毫秒的生物学约束/
item.description: Human audiovisual perception runs at only 6-10 hertz, and the model has to be interruptible inside that window; high-fidelity audio means more tokens per second, and more tokens means fewer parameters — this is the physical trade-off voice AI cannot avoid.
item.content:encoded:
Human audiovisual perception runs at only 6-10 hertz, and the model has to be interruptible inside that window; high-fidelity audio means more tokens per second, and more tokens means fewer parameters — this is the physical trade-off voice AI cannot avoid.

The first half is hands-on judgment about product and architecture; the second half, on EQ, benchmarks and the personalization learning loop, is worth more, but you have to be patient and listen past the 45-minute mark.

6:09 150 milliseconds is a hard constraint, not an engineering tuning knob
Alex's starting point is biology: from a photon hitting the retina to the cortex responding takes about 150 milliseconds, and that number is stable enough to serve as a non-invasive diagnostic marker for neurodegenerative disease — when there is pathology, the signal takes a detour and takes longer. Human audiovisual perception actually runs at 6 to 10 hertz, even though the world feels perfectly smooth to us. So their model handles interruption inside a window of roughly 150 milliseconds. This is not an engineering goal of "as fast as possible" but a hard design input aligned to the human perceptual frame rate.

8:11 Token rate and parameter count are zero-sum
Audio first has to be turned into tokens and fed into the LLM backbone, then turned back into audio. High fidelity requires a high token rate, but a high token rate means prefilling and generating a large number of tokens every second, and the cost rises accordingly. Hence an unpleasant dilemma: more tokens per second means the model parameters cannot be too large; fewer tokens per second is what lets you afford more parameters. Text is the ultimate compression format, needing only 3 to 5 tokens per second, while audio easily goes above 10. At 10 tokens per second, each token covers about 100 milliseconds — which is why user-experience engineering and scientific research have to be done at the same time.

11:14 Most avatar video is boring, so it compresses
Models like WAN and Flux can generate video clips of around 10 seconds, but producing an hour of visually consistent continuous stream requires changing the model. Alex's key insight is that if you know this is avatar video, there will be no race car speeding through the background, and most of the frame is fairly boring. So this interview's audiovisual stream can be compressed into a fairly efficient bitstream; the bitrate only spikes when he waves his arms wildly, and normal people don't do that. This is the concrete landing point of "set the price first, then work backwards to the architecture" — not chasing the prettiest picture quality, but building something users can afford.

15:17 Teach a model a new modality and it forgets its old skills
They didn't build their own LLM; instead they took the intelligence already present in a high-quality LLM and had it learn one more modality. But the risk is catastrophic forgetting. Alex gives the example of a friend: he adopted a Latin American child in Germany and spoke only German to her, and within a few months the girl had forgotten all her Spanish words. LLMs are the same — let one process only audio and it will soon forget reasoning and language itself. So you have to maintain a competitive mid/post-training LLM pipeline while defining tasks that graft audio and text together, just as a multilingual model has to know that dog and Hund refer to the same thing.

20:24 100 million hours of audio — only a self-built data center can afford to store it
Their training data is on the order of 100 million hours of audio, which Alex converts into roughly 200 human lifetimes — if you lived 75 years and were always in a noisy environment, that is about how much audio you would hear. This data can be crawled from the web, but it needs extraction, labeling, normalization and transcription, a great deal of extra processing. Building their own data center helped a lot here: putting it on NeoCloud would eat you alive in storage bills, and putting it on the big three cloud providers is worse. He also mentions a timing point: hard drive prices are now about three times what they were last year, so they will have to be frugal going forward.

23:28 Squeeze labels out of noise with medieval statistics
Faced with noisy labels produced by imperfect processing tools, Alex's argument is that as long as the noise is unbiased, averaging a large number of repeated measurements gives a better estimate than any single one. He cites the medieval "foot" — have people walk out of a church, take the first 12 men, drop the two with the longest feet and the two with the shortest (possibly because of deformity), and average the remaining 8 to get an estimate of a foot. He says robust regression and estimation have existed for half a millennium. Concretely for audio: knowing this is a two-person podcast, and knowing TWIML is usually Sam plus one other person, makes it easy to separate speakers, get a large amount of single-speaker audio, and thereby label it better, forming a flywheel.

33:43 End-to-end audio models are doomed to be small and dumb
Alex is blunt about the architecture choice: end-to-end audio models have their place — fast response, small footprint, low latency — but they are also fairly dumb. Make them smart and the compute cost becomes unbearable. So their approach is two-stage: understanding and reasoning happen at one end, the backend triggers the appropriate tool calls, and the answer is collected back, like multithreaded programming where the main thread dispatches parallel threads and retrieves the results. For the user, writing a prompt for their model looks the same as writing a prompt for an ordinary LLM, except their model also talks.

36:46 Ten times cheaper than GPT, but with thinking turned off
Alex claims that on benchmarks like BigBench Audio and Complex Function Bench they beat GPT, Gemini and Grok at one tenth the cost of OpenAI's models. But he adds a footnote himself: this was measured with thinking turned off. The reason is that you cannot have the model pause to think before answering — it feels very unnatural, and humans don't do that either. This exposes a fundamental constraint of the voice setting: reasoning has to be hidden in the background, and there can be no visible thinking pause in the foreground.

item.title: Clovis people didn't just hunt mammoths — they painted and sewed inside tents
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-ancients-克洛维斯人不是只会猎猛犸-他们还在帐篷里画画缝衣/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-ancients-克洛维斯人不是只会猎猛犸-他们还在帐篷里画画缝衣/
item.description: Four hearth-centered areas, ochre pigment and bone needles unearthed at the LaPrele site in Wyoming; DNA protein analysis shows the needles were made from red fox and felid bone — the Clovis diet was far more complex than the "mammoth hunter" label suggests.
item.content:encoded:
Four hearth-centered areas, ochre pigment and bone needles unearthed at the LaPrele site in Wyoming; DNA protein analysis shows the needles were made from red fox and felid bone — the Clovis diet was far more complex than the "mammoth hunter" label suggests.

High density of archaeological detail, but it demands patience: the first half is Clovis research history and dating debates, and the concrete findings at LaPrele in the second half are the part that's really worth it.

3:02 Clovis lasted only a few hundred years
Radiocarbon dating pins Clovis culture to roughly 13,100 to 12,750 years ago, a window of a few hundred years just before the end of the Ice Age. The narrowness of that span is itself startling — the Ice Age runs on scales of tens to hundreds of thousands of years, and Clovis is a single instant within it. More crucially, within those few hundred years, highly similar fluted stone points appeared across the entire North American continent, from New Mexico to Wyoming, from Washington state to Virginia. That combination of "narrow in time, wide in space" is Clovis's most distinctive feature; in later periods, stone points rapidly regionalized.

12:21 Clovis were not the first Americans
The "Clovis First" theory dominated most of the 20th century: humans followed mammoth herds into the Americas, and Clovis people were the earliest settlers. But finds at sites like Monte Verde (Chile), Paisley Caves (Oregon), Cooper's Ferry (Idaho) and Page-Ladson (Florida) have led most archaeologists to now believe people were living in the Americas thousands of years before Clovis. Mackey says this is one of the fiercest debates in American archaeology, and Pleistocene archaeologists argue about it hard. But she also stresses: Clovis research shouldn't fixate only on the question of "who came first" — there are many questions worth asking about their lives themselves.

21:01 One chopper changed the whole nature of the site
The LaPrele site was discovered in 1986 when locals found mammoth bones by a creek, and Mackey and collaborators returned to excavate in the 2000s. In the first season, retired archaeologist Rich Adams, helping everyone fix the screening channel, found a large chopper about 10 meters from the mammoth — a simple tool made by knocking a few flakes off a river cobble. The key point is that it appeared in a position where it geologically shouldn't have: the site was gradually buried by floods, and natural processes were unlikely to have moved such a large cobble there. This tool prompted the team to test a wider area, ultimately finding more than 50,000 flakes, at least four artifact concentration areas, several hundred stone tools and mammoth ivory. LaPrele was no longer just a kill site but a camp where humans had lived.

29:15 Hearths and tent walls left fingerprints in the sediment
LaPrele's most striking find is four "hearth-centered areas." In Block B, the team found no obvious ash or oxidation traces, but burned bone and flakes concentrated in a small area, indicating a hearth once stood there. Even more compelling is the spatial analysis: if you look down from above at a tent, the hearth is at the center, surrounded by a high-activity zone, then an open space for walking, and near the tent wall objects accumulate — because the wall is a barrier to artifact transport. Block B's artifact distribution shows exactly this "bullseye" pattern, indicating an interior space. In the same area, a roughly 1.5-by-2-meter scatter of ochre (hematite) pigment was found, matching the wall's position, suggesting people painted by the fire.

39:25 The bone needles were made from red fox and felid bone
The team used ZooMS (Zooarchaeology by Mass Spectrometry) to analyze bone needles and possible bone beads; this method extracts proteins from extremely small bone samples to identify the animal species. The results were unexpected: many needles were made from hare bone, but one was red fox, and another tested as felid — not a domestic cat, but some wild felid. Mackey notes these are all fur-bearing animals, and their bone thickness may have been just right for making needles. More importantly, these animals were likely caught in traps rather than hunted with spears. This means Clovis people weren't hunting mammoths 24 hours a day; they were also taking more common small prey.

44:32 Were Clovis people mammoth specialists or omnivores?
About 15 widely accepted Clovis sites in North America coexist with megafauna, mostly proboscideans (mammoth, mastodon, gomphothere), but also horse and camel. Yet Mackey points out that only about 30 to 40 sites truly define our understanding of Clovis, while thousands of Clovis stone points were found on the surface, lacking context. This raises a core debate: were they mammoth-hunting specialists, or omnivores with a broader diet? Small animals, fish and plant remains preserve less easily and are less often systematically sought. Mackey is studying plant remains, and she notes archaeologists usually look for plants only in hearths, and how many places in the Clovis record have actually been looked at is a problem.

50:00 Mammoth extinction: did humans push, or was climate the main driver?
The classic "overkill" debate: 35 genera of megafauna went extinct at the end of the Ice Age, and how much was human versus environmental? Mackey says she takes a middle path, believing both contributed. She considers mammoths the strongest candidate for the "overkill" hypothesis, because mammoth sites are numerous, the animals were large, and their reproductive rate was low, making them more vulnerable to hunting. But she also notes overkill doesn't necessarily mean humans hunted all 35 genera; hunting may have tipped the balance through trophic cascades. Interestingly, paleoecologists lean toward "humans did it," while archaeologists lean more toward "the environment did it."

53:12 Clovis human bone barely exists
Apart from a single ancestral remains attributed to Clovis at the Anzick site in Montana, we have almost no Clovis human bone. Mackey thinks this isn't surprising: population density was extremely low, 13,000-year-old sites are inherently extremely hard to preserve, and these groups were highly mobile, so we don't know their burial practices. She also stresses that Clovis people are the ancestors of millions of Indigenous people in the Americas today, and any related research must proceed on the basis of consultation and collaboration.

item.title: Two Hundred Years of Psychiatry's Lessons: No Penicillin, Only Trial and Error
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-lex-精神病学两百年的教训-没有青霉素-只有试错/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-lex-精神病学两百年的教训-没有青霉素-只有试错/
item.description: From the ice-pick lobotomy to insulin coma, psychiatry repeatedly claimed an 80% cure rate, yet never found a penicillin for psychiatry — and even today's best drugs still lose eight in ten patients before the trial ends.
item.content:encoded:
From the ice-pick lobotomy to insulin coma, psychiatry repeatedly claimed an 80% cure rate, yet never found a penicillin for psychiatry — and even today's best drugs still lose eight in ten patients before the trial ends.

The first half is psychiatry's dark history, the second half is how drugs and diagnosis get shaped by commerce and hope together; high information density, but it demands patience.

10:18 There is no penicillin for psychiatry
Modern psychopharmacology was born in the early 1950s, and Andrew Skull stresses that this was not a planned result but a "serendipitous event," almost purely accidental. It was indeed an advance over what psychiatry had before, but the drugs in hand today are only symptomatic treatment, not cure — "we do not have any penicillin for psychiatry." More troubling still is the iatrogenic harm: making PTSD patients confront their trauma head-on actually made things worse for many of them; antipsychotics and antidepressants are at best partially effective, and doctors cannot tell in advance who will respond and who will deteriorate, while the group in between has to weigh side effects against efficacy.

19:41 Twenty billion dollars bought not one bit of improvement
Under Stephen Hyman and Thomas Insel, the NIMH invested in mental illness as brain disease, betting heavily on genetics and neuroscience. After leaving office, Insel admitted in an MIT interview: they had funded a great deal of cool science, and after spending 20 billion dollars, the situation of mental illness patients had "improved not one bit." Skull considers this a devastating statement. DSM-5 originally intended to rewrite the diagnostic system based on underlying pathology; by around 2008 the editors gave up and could only fall back on the 1980 approach; before publication Insel and Hyman publicly denounced it as unscientific and useless, and Spitzer and Alan Francis also fiercely criticized its backroom dealings.

33:44 America's largest psychiatric wards are prisons
People with severe mental illness live on average 15 to 25 years less than others, and that gap is still widening. Skull assigns much of the blame to public policy rather than psychiatry itself: today the three largest inpatient psychiatric "centers" in the United States are the Los Angeles County Jail, the Cook County Jail in Chicago, and Rikers Island in New York. Patients cycle through a three-stage loop — a brief hospitalization, the street or a cheap hotel, then prison. Community care is what Skull calls "a shell game without a P," a con with no replacement facilities, amounting to a return to something like the Dark Ages.

45:18 When you can't cure them, blame the patients' bad genes
The early asylums were born of intense optimism; the earliest alienists believed that if patients came early enough, 60%, 70%, even 80% could be cured. The actual discharge rate was only 35% to 40%, so each year deposited another cohort of chronic patients, the ratio of new to chronic patients grew steadily worse, and the asylum's image was defined by that chronic patient who "only left in a pine box." By the late 19th century the cure rate, counted by inmates in residence, was only 10% to 12%. Faced with the challenge "you promised and you didn't deliver," the answer shifted to blaming the victim: mental illness was a fundamental biological defect, patients were evolutionary throwbacks, degenerates, who could not be let out because "they breed like rabbits." This narrative provided the justification for lifelong confinement and sterilization.

58:13 The ice-pick lobotomy: psychiatry won a Nobel Prize
Walter Freeman began performing lobotomies in 1936, drawing on the work of the Portuguese neurologist Egas Moniz the year before, for which Moniz won the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1949 — by then with 14 years of experience. Freeman wanted to be the Henry Ford of the lobotomy, and mechanized the operation: first electroshock to render the patient unconscious, then drive an ice pick through the eye socket into the skull, stir, and cut. He toured state hospitals in a camper he called the "lobotomobile" to teach the technique, switching from his right hand to his left when it tired, sometimes doing 20 to 30 cases in an afternoon, and boasted he could teach any fool to do a lobotomy in 20 minutes, "even a psychiatrist" — he was a neurologist and held psychiatrists in contempt. The operation was performed from the 1930s into the early 1970s, and was finally retired by generational turnover and antipsychotic drugs.

1:17:01 Cotton cut out his patients' stomachs and claimed an 80% cure
Henry Cotton was a psychiatrist trained by Emil Kraepelin and Adolf Meyer, and ran the New Jersey State Hospital in Trenton. He embraced the theory of "focal sepsis": a low-grade infection releases toxins in the body, and when the toxins reach the brain they poison it. With no antibiotics, the answer was to find the source of infection and cut it out — first pull the teeth, the patient doesn't improve; then remove the tonsils, still no improvement; so out came the stomach, the spleen, the colon, and he claimed to have cured 80% of his patients. Wealthy patients came from all over the country. He gave a lecture series at Princeton, published by Oxford University Press and Princeton University Press, and The New York Times called it a major breakthrough. In reality, 45% of those who underwent abdominal surgery died within a year. He died of a heart attack in 1933, and his successor stopped the abdominal operations, but tooth extraction and tonsillectomy continued until 1960 — a dentist who arrived in 1916 pulled hundreds of thousands of teeth and firmly believed Cotton should have won the Nobel Prize.

1:42:33 Schizophrenia may not be a disease at all
Once the genome was decoded, people expected a Mendelian gene for schizophrenia to be found quickly, and it did not happen. Now with genome-wide association studies, adding up all 300 small genomic variants explains only about 10% of schizophrenia — Scull's verdict is "not very powerful." More troubling still, schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and autism overlap heavily in genetic abnormalities, which undermines disease categories drawn along symptom lines. He cites the British psychiatrist Robin Murray: schizophrenia is more like the most extreme end of psychosis, a continuum. He speculates that if in ten years psychiatry announced "there is no such thing as schizophrenia," public trust in psychiatry would be badly damaged.

3:16:10 New drugs are no more effective than old ones, and eight in ten patients quit the trial
The CATIE study (published in the New England Journal of Medicine) compared one first-generation antipsychotic with four newer ones, and concluded the new drugs were no more effective than the old one. The more underrated finding was tolerability: depending on the drug used, 67% to 82% of patients dropped out of the trial, either because the drug didn't work or because they couldn't stand the side effects. In other words, these are already "our best drugs," yet the real-world discontinuation rate is astonishingly high. The old drug's patent had expired and it was cheap; the second-generation drugs were patented and expensive, in some cases 10 times as expensive, but the higher price bought no efficacy advantage.

item.title: 40,000 Ottomans Lay Siege to Malta — and Lose to a Few Hundred Knights
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-historyhit-奥斯曼四万大军围攻马耳他-为何败给几百骑士/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-17-historyhit-奥斯曼四万大军围攻马耳他-为何败给几百骑士/
item.description: In 1565 an Ottoman fleet of 180 ships and 40,000 men besieged Malta, defended by roughly 500 knights and a few thousand Maltese. Fort St Elmo held out for a month before falling, but the siege dragged on until Sicilian reinforcements landed in September and the Ottomans withdrew.
item.content:encoded:
In 1565 an Ottoman fleet of 180 ships and 40,000 men besieged Malta, defended by roughly 500 knights and a few thousand Maltese. Fort St Elmo held out for a month before falling, but the siege dragged on until Sicilian reinforcements landed in September and the Ottomans withdrew.

This episode is on-location siege narrative — vivid but light on analysis. If you want the mechanics of why Malta held, the middle and later sections on scorched-earth tactics and disinformation are the most valuable.

3:02 Malta's value is its position, not its resources
Malta sits almost exactly in the middle of the Mediterranean: 80 km north of Sicily, right next to North Africa to the south, and roughly equidistant from Gibraltar and the Suez Canal. Whoever controls Malta controls the trade routes. The Grand Harbour where Valletta now stands is a rare natural deep-water port, safe to anchor in no matter which way the wind blows. The Knights did not initially want Malta, since it had no existing fortifications and no resources; it was the first Grand Master who insisted on a foothold and took it.

7:10 What the Knights brought was the Italian bastion
The Knights brought Italian-style military architecture (Traccia Italiana) to Malta: no longer the tall medieval castle, but low, sloped, outward-projecting bastions with thick walls packed with earth to absorb the impact of gunpowder artillery. Fort St Angelo got the first bastion. By 1552 the Knights had realised how dangerous their position was, and Grand Master Domades pushed hard to build fortifications.
