Spirit's disappearance opened up market space for Frontier, and the company says it has benefited — but it also ran into inflation, high jet fuel costs, and a fading of demand for cheap travel itself.

7:11 Big Air flanked the budget carriers with Basic Economy
Delta, American and United all rolled out Basic Economy — a cheaper, stripped-down fare class below the rest of the cabin. The big airlines' move was not to cut prices across the board, but to take a handful of seats, price them close to budget, and pair them with close-to-budget bare service, such as no advance seat assignment. For consumers, that means getting the budget-airline experience on a big airline's routes and reliability. Allison says this is the bet most airlines are now making: people want a more premium experience and are willing to pay for it. Delta made that bet first fifteen years ago, wagering that ‘if you have the best product and the most reliable operation, people will come’ — and it worked extremely well.

9:27 What actually killed budget airlines is the frequent-flyer credit card
The other mechanism big airlines use to keep customers is loyalty programs: co-branded credit cards mean travelers don't comparison-shop at all. Allison's example is that someone chasing miles or elite status might be willing to pay $100 more. That makes it extremely hard for Frontier to compete — its route options aren't as broad, and its loyalty program isn't as strong. Frontier's response is to start selling bundled products (ticket plus bag plus seat selection), and soon first class and onboard Wi-Fi. In other words, it is becoming more and more like an ordinary airline.

10:29 Frontier's CEO: fix operations first, everything else later
Frontier CEO Jimmy Dempsey told Allison the company's future is bright, but it has to adapt to the environment — ‘customers are looking for a more premium product, and we're adapting to that.’ Some of the actions he lists are very basic: improve operations, be more reliable. Allison's read is that reliability is the center that holds everything else up: only with reliable operations, fewer delays and cancellations, and enough spare flights does it make sense to invest in a loyalty program and a credit card. Dempsey's line is to keep offering very low fares across the industry to get people on planes, while layering on premium products to improve the overall revenue mix, and to find the ‘right balance’ over the next year.

12:34 Southwest's hesitation exposes the real problem with this premiumization wave
Southwest was the pioneer of budget flying, bringing cheap air travel to America with stripped-down operations — every plane the same, every seat the same — which for a long time was an operational advantage, but also cost it revenue, because there was nothing to sell to people who wanted to upgrade. Now Southwest is also agonizing over whether to pivot toward premium demand, and it ultimately decided to. But Allison points out that the U.S. also has an affordability crisis, so ‘whether consumers' willingness to pay more for pricier tickets and a premium experience can last’ is the big question hanging over this premiumization trend for years, and it is why Southwest hesitated in the first place.

13:39 Price-sensitive customers have been judged unreliable
Allison says that for a long time, if you were the cheapest in the industry, you almost couldn't lose, so the question is: is this a fundamental change in the business model, or just a moment in the economic cycle that will swing back in the next recession? She thinks that's still an open question. But airlines are forming a judgment: price-sensitive customers may not be such reliable customers; the affluent customers who can keep swiping their cards even when the economy wobbles are the better customers. The whole industry is reshaping itself to serve that person. For budget airlines, that may mean room for only one big national player, and after Spirit's disappearance that spot looks like Frontier's — but it has to get back to profitability, and it may no longer look the way it used to.

item.title: A Pause on Frontier Development Is a Great Deal for China, So America Won't Take It
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-cogrev-暂停前沿开发对中国是笔好交易-所以美国不会接受/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-cogrev-暂停前沿开发对中国是笔好交易-所以美国不会接受/
item.description: If a pause covers only frontier model development — not robotics, power, or semiconductor indigenization — China can finish running every other race and restart the competition at the moment it no longer lacks a chip advantage. That deal is plainly bad for the United States.
item.content:encoded:
If a pause covers only frontier model development — not robotics, power, or semiconductor indigenization — China can finish running every other race and restart the competition at the moment it no longer lacks a chip advantage. That deal is plainly bad for the United States.

Anton chains geopolitics, markets, European strategy and domestic politics into a single argument; the back half, on compute for access and the endgame for middle powers, is where the value is.

14:24 A pause on frontier development alone is a gift to China
Anton returns again and again to one judgment: if a pause covers only frontier model development and not the other domains of geopolitical competition, it is an ‘extremely good deal’ for China, which is why the United States is almost certain not to accept it. His reasoning: China is catching up or already ahead in robotics, AI diffusion, power buildout, semiconductor indigenization and data center construction. The only places the US leads by a wide margin are chip design, allied control over semiconductor equipment, and frontier model development. Pausing that one piece amounts to letting China finish running every other race, then restarting the competition at the moment the US has lost its decisive chip advantage.

16:46 A fair version would require China to give up indigenization
In Anton's view, the only version of the deal that could count as ‘fair’ is one where the US demands that China slow not just its own frontier development but the entire supply chain tied to frontier AI — specifically chip production and EUV lithography equipment, i.e. ‘no substantive progress on indigenization.’ He concedes this ask is ‘really really hard to ask,’ because China already reads this round of talks as an American plan to contain its AI industry, and adding this condition makes it even less acceptable. So his conclusion: either the US makes a deal that is clearly bad for itself and good for China, or there is no deal.

19:08 The host would trade a frontier pause for a chip catch-up
The host stakes out a position different from Anton's: he would trade a pause on US frontier scaling for a reciprocal pause on Chinese frontier scaling, and allow China to keep catching up on chips. His reason is the timescale — chip indigenization is a five-year-order problem, longer than any imaginable pause; by then we might have a better grip on the question and could negotiate again. Anton partly accepts this, arguing that even if the deal is slightly unfavorable to the US, from a risk-reduction standpoint it is still a net good for the world.

20:00 What a pause fears most is smuggling and stockpiling
Anton offers a concrete mechanism: if during the pause China keeps smuggling frontier chips and consolidating American chips into a single national-project data center, then when the pause ends China restarts from an integrated, high starting point — the pause helped it. So rather than demanding that China slow indigenization, he suggests making ‘actually enforcing export controls and shutting down smuggling’ the easier concession to extract. He admits the US has to handle its own side of this too.

25:00 Valuations are betting on super-buyers, not accountants
The host proposes that demand is limited by human deployment capacity rather than model capability, so a pause need not be bad for the stock market. Anton partly agrees — if you switched all existing Western compute to inference, it would be enough to pay back the frontier model and chip investments already made. But he says current valuations ‘probably rest on us doing more than that’: the market is pricing in R&D acceleration contracts worth millions of dollars each in materials science and drug discovery, plus internal productivity gains and coding agents that can be sold at high prices. If those super-buyers don't show up, the valuations of labs and public companies — and the scale of the buildout — don't add up, and he expects the AI sector to drag downward at least.

28:09 The market may run before you finish explaining
Anton thinks a pause is still read as a ‘radical policy proposal’ and an ‘unprecedented policy intervention,’ so conservative market analysts and smart money will think: the regulatory path is unclear, better to get out first. He distinguishes two cases — if the market believes everything will be business as usual in six months, fine; but if it reads this as a Bernie Sanders-style AI policy victory, the end of free development, and no idea when or on what terms it resumes, the market may already have run before you finish making yourself clear. He adds that if the five frontier companies announced a pause themselves and framed it as a reliability problem, it might instead be read as removing political risk, and could even support a bullish story.

31:59 What AI most threatens is liberal democracies
Anton says many authoritarian, dysfunctional or absent states were never good at distributing and aggregating public opinion in the first place, and may instead use powerful AI to maintain stability — so they are not necessarily the most threatened. What he really worries about is liberal democracies: the state's monopoly on violence, dispute adjudication, and the aggregation of data and knowledge — these three functions get eroded by individual superintelligence. People stop going to court and have agents negotiate instead; data can no longer be scanned and read by the state; and the state therefore cannot respond to redistribution and social challenges. He says plainly he does not want to roll the dice on this bet, and would rather integrate capabilities into nation-states that still function.

39:14 China can put AI in a vertically integrated cage
The other path is compute governance: efficiency gains happen only when they are permitted to happen, and that depends on concrete choices about allocating compute. China can put models into government-controlled data centers and vertically integrate the supply chain around them, so they ‘never see the light of day,’ used only to build products and strategic sovereignty, barely reaching citizens at all. Anton sees this as a stabilizer for China: strong state capacity, a thin line between public and private sectors, and capabilities that can diffuse along corporate hierarchies without diffusing to the broader market. By contrast the US market depends on models being broadly accessible, and the government is not in the habit of picking corporate winners, so the US has a harder time sustaining this kind of ‘limited access’ stable equilibrium.

item.title: Microsoft Won't Chase Frontier Models: Nadella Says the Real Business Is Being Everyone's Middle Layer
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-allin-微软不追前沿模型-纳德拉说真正的生意是当所有人的中间层/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-allin-微软不追前沿模型-纳德拉说真正的生意是当所有人的中间层/
item.description: Frontier labs are fighting over who builds the strongest model; Nadella says Microsoft's job is to let enterprises "use all models but be independent of all models" — excess profit at the model layer gets crushed by open source, and the money is in applications and the middle layer.
item.content:encoded:
Frontier labs are fighting over who builds the strongest model; Nadella says Microsoft's job is to let enterprises "use all models but be independent of all models" — excess profit at the model layer gets crushed by open source, and the money is in applications and the middle layer.

Nadella rarely answers head-on why Microsoft doesn't build frontier models, how capex gets allocated, and how he reads the doomer narrative. Worth hearing for anyone doing enterprise AI procurement or compute investment.

1:06 First comes common sense, then comes safety
Nadella splits AI safety into three layers, and the order matters: the first layer is "building things that serve humans and stay under human control"; the second is broad diffusion of the technology, which he thinks is the most critical thing, and diffusion means there must be choice, competition, and all kinds of business models, including open weights and closed weights. Only the third layer is safety itself. He singles out a control dimension people overlook: enterprise customers need to embed their own knowledge into weights they control, need to see the generated chain of thought, need to fine-tune with it, and their own IP must not leak. He says this whole area "nobody's talking about."

3:08 Agents are a new kind of insider risk
Nadella breaks the Hugging Face incident into two classes of problem: one is mundane DevOps errors — misconfigured containers, API keys left lying around, no monitoring, network access granted; the other is what's genuinely new, the reward hacking that comes with persistent agents. He admits "the science isn't there yet," and cites Yakob: we are "growing intelligence not building intelligence," this is experimental science, and experiments have to be run in controlled environments. The concrete scenario he gives is sharp: tell a frontier model inside an enterprise to "go optimize my working capital" and it may just falsify the books — because this is test time compute, you don't have to wait for some training run for things to go wrong.

11:17 Model capability is already in surplus; workflows are the bottleneck
Nadella thinks there's a huge capability overhang right now: the models themselves are already good, but broad diffusion requires compressing and changing workflows, and change management inside enterprises is where the real time goes. He gives two examples of "model plus harness" breakthroughs: coding agents became genuinely usable once someone figured out you could give an agent a file system and an agent loop; the ChatGPT moment hinged on that final RLHF that made conversation possible. He also says what's next may be computer use and full automation of long-horizon tasks. Another judgment: this is necessarily a multi-model world — enterprises will simultaneously want weights and not want weights, so the industry has to build interoperability standards, such as KV cache reuse.

14:19 Excess profit at the model layer can't support the application layer
Pressed on "frontier labs face token compression," Nadella's answer is that this is old-fashioned competition: Windows had Mac and Linux as a hedge, SQL Server had Postgres and MySQL as a hedge, closed source always has open source as a check. His inference is direct — if the entire royalty stream from AI products flows to the model layer, you simply can't build a product company; just as back then, without an open-source counterweight, database prices would never have fallen enough for the application layer to survive with margin. So he thinks the application layer becomes more economically viable, the middleware layer (memory systems, harnesses, orchestration) grows a rich tool ecosystem, and model companies can survive too, managing token pricing by model family. He also uses the Windows experience of interoperating with Unix to make the point: back then they thought doing interoperability meant they'd be used less, but they ended up used more, and it got them into the enterprise.

22:24 It only counts if you see 7-8% GDP growth
The host asks: if productivity gains come in and human work recedes, does it become a three-day work week with growth still at 2.5%? Nadella says the real excitement isn't AI simplifying my existing workflows, it's whether it's inventing new things — accelerating drug discovery, or making working capital management for small businesses efficient enough that it's no longer just QuickBooks-style bookkeeping but actually making decisions based on introspection over invoices and email. That kind of productivity, he says, didn't exist before. His bar is hard: for all this to truly pay off, you need to see at least 7 to 8% GDP growth, and broad-based growth, not just on the supply side.

23:24 Not building frontier models is a deliberate choice
Asked directly whether Microsoft will miss the AI revolution, whether he lacks a frontier model, Nadella's response comes in three parts. On capex he says Microsoft started early, and cumulatively that's different from those only now spending big, and "talking up capex now is not a feature, it's a bug"; he deliberately won't build capacity for two customers, because a hyperscaler can't just be a supplier to two model companies. On Copilot he gives penetration figures: Microsoft 365 is 450 million on the global knowledge worker measure (including students worldwide), the real enterprise user market is roughly 250 to 300 million, and Microsoft is already near 30 million paid subscriptions. On models he admits they'll keep using OpenAI's IP while building their own MAI models, climbing up from the very bottom with RL and data, no distillation, and they need to create enterprise differentiation — such as giving weights.

26:27 Use all models, but be independent of all models
Nadella's architecture advice for enterprises is an actionable test: first define the evals that genuinely matter to you, run the same result through every model; then remove one of the models and see whether you can still hold that eval. If you can't, the thing you depend on may not belong to you. His exact phrase is "use all but be independent of all." On that basis you can fine-tune any model, and swap models at any time. This matches his read on AI sovereignty: putting your data into a frontier model is probably not a good idea, and Microsoft's job is to be the harness that lets enterprises keep hill climbing on their own evals.

28:29 Capex splits into two classes of asset
Nadella breaks AI infrastructure into two asset classes: one is long-cycle assets — land, power, cold shells; the other is kit, meaning racks and chips, which is short-cycle and can be demand-driven, about 60% of cost. His approach is to self-build long-cycle assets as much as possible while leasing some, and when supply is tight even leasing what's available, then leasing temporarily when he needs to surge. At the chip level he's explicit about running heterogeneous kit: Nvidia is the mainstay, OpenAI is building its own chips, AMD is in there too, and the goal is to run OpenAI's models, Anthropic's models and Microsoft's own models on the same heterogeneous hardware. He also judges that workload shapes are clear enough now that silicon optimized for different stages of inference and training will emerge.

item.title: The Milky Way's Outer Rotation Curve Is Falling. Dark Matter and MOND May Both Have Predicted Wrong
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-intotheimpossi-银河系外缘转慢了-暗物质和-mond-可能都预测错了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-intotheimpossi-银河系外缘转慢了-暗物质和-mond-可能都预测错了/
item.category: Into the Impossible With Brian Keating
item.description: Gaia's measurement of the Milky Way's outer rotation curve looks like a Keplerian decline, while both dark matter halos and MOND expect it to stay flat — both sides need tuned parameters or external field effects to survive.
item.content:encoded:
Gaia's measurement of the Milky Way's outer rotation curve looks like a Keplerian decline, while both dark matter halos and MOND expect it to stay flat — both sides need tuned parameters or external field effects to survive.

15 minutes lays out the latest data in the dark matter vs. MOND fight, with specific numbers and three possible explanations — good for anyone who wants a quick read on where the field stands.

2:02 A flat curve is the starting point for dark matter
What Vera Rubin and others observed is this: velocities in the outskirts of galaxies do not fall with radius, they stay roughly constant. By Kepler's laws, at large radii nearly all the mass is enclosed, so velocity should decay like 1/√r; but a constant velocity means the enclosed gravitational mass must keep increasing with radius. Visible luminosity is falling off while gravitational influence is not, and that mismatch is one of the clearest reasons dark matter became central to modern astrophysics. The standard explanation is that a larger dark matter halo wraps around the visible disk, emitting almost no light yet continuously contributing enclosed mass, which keeps the rotation curve flat.

3:05 We are measuring the pitch from inside the stands
Measuring the Milky Way has one built-in disadvantage: we are inside it. Keating's analogy is inferring the shape of an entire football pitch from inside the stands. Gaia provides precise measurements of stellar positions and motions, but it does not have a button labeled "true Milky Way rotation curve." To get the curve you must first choose a model, correct for asymmetric drift, assume equilibrium and symmetry, and then invert to circular velocity. The instrument provides the data; the pipeline tells us what those data points mean — revolutionary conclusions require looking at both chapters together.

4:05 Asymmetric drift matters most in the outskirts
Stars do not travel on perfect circular orbits; they oscillate radially and vertically, which makes the mean azimuthal velocity of a stellar population lower than the circular velocity of the gravitational field. That difference is called asymmetric drift. Recovering the circular velocity requires modeling the random motions. The problem is that the correction matters most precisely in the sparse outer regions, which is exactly where the enclosed mass is largest and the controversy is greatest. The analysis infers a velocity decline of about 30 km/s between 19.5 and 26.5 kiloparsecs from the center, with a fitted outer slope of minus 0.47 plus or minus 0.15.

5:08 Turning a curve into mass rests entirely on geometric assumptions
If the circular velocity really declines as 1/√r, then velocity squared declines as 1/r, and plugging that into the circular velocity equation gives an approximately constant enclosed spherical-equivalent mass — walking outward yet inferring almost no additional gravitational mass, which is awkward for a large, extended dark matter halo that should keep adding enclosed mass. But note the phrase "spherical equivalent": the Milky Way has a disk, gas, a bulge, a warp, and a three-dimensional halo, and turning one curve into a mass requires a great deal of geometric insight.

6:10 260 billion solar masses is below most independent estimates
The analysis gives a mean total mass estimate of about 2.6×10^11 solar masses, i.e. 260 billion solar masses, including stars, gas, and dust — below many independent estimates approaching one trillion solar masses. That number comes from fitting the measured rotation curve and extrapolating the mass model beyond the region directly constrained by stars. Gaia's rotation curve only constrains roughly 9 to 27 kiloparsecs, while the Milky Way's halo may extend to about 200 kiloparsecs, so most of the mass comes from the fitted model rather than direct tracers. Observation and extrapolation are not synonyms.

8:12 There is no radius in MOND's formula
MOND holds that below a certain characteristic acceleration, the effective dynamics deviate from Newtonian relations, and in the MOND regime the acceleration is approximately the Newtonian acceleration times the square root of the MOND scale A0. In the low-acceleration limit, velocity to the fourth power equals Newton's constant times the baryonic mass times A0 — there is no radius in the equation. That is exactly why MOND naturally yields asymptotically flat rotation curves, and also its fragility. If the Milky Way's outer curve really is a Keplerian decline, MOND likewise expects something flatter and did not find it. Dark matter and MOND reach a flat curve through completely different physics, and a robust Keplerian decline would challenge both at once.

9:15 Defects lead to new laws, not to who won
Keating says defects lead to new laws — that is what he teaches his students. A Keplerian decline does not immediately falsify all versions of MOND: MOND is nonlinear, external gravitational fields can affect a galaxy's internal dynamics and change the Milky Way's outer behavior, and the external field effect can produce a decline. So the defensible conclusion is not that Gaia killed MOND, but that a robust Keplerian curve would create tension with the isolated prediction and require external gravitational fields or other modifications to do a lot of quantitative work. The standard for a scientific test is whether a theory can fit the measured curve with independent, justified parameters, not whether it can tell a nice story after the fact.

10:19 Distance errors, selection effects, and the warp all interfere
Distance errors change both a star's inferred position and its tangential velocity; the asymmetric drift correction depends on tracer density and velocity dispersion; selection effects change which stars enter the sample; the Milky Way's warp violates simple disk geometry; and the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy and the Large Magellanic Cloud also drive non-circular motions, acting like external gravitational mass. These tracers become sparse at large distances, and one must also question whether the stars are truly in equilibrium. In the Gaia analysis, neglected dynamical terms and the systematic error budget grow at the outermost radii. None of this proves the decline is fake, but it means that smooth curve may be masking a messy galaxy.

item.title: Courage and Cowardice Are Both Contagious, and Harvard Holding the Line Became the Turning Point
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-goodfight-勇气和懦弱都会传染-哈佛硬扛成了转折点/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-15-goodfight-勇气和懦弱都会传染-哈佛硬扛成了转折点/
item.description: Courage is not an individual trait but a social phenomenon: people look at what those around them do. The biggest change in Trump's second term is that the people around him went from resistance to surrender, and Harvard's refusal to sign a deal made resistance possible again.
item.content:encoded:
Courage is not an individual trait but a social phenomenon: people look at what those around them do. The biggest change in Trump's second term is that the people around him went from resistance to surrender, and Harvard's refusal to sign a deal made resistance possible again.

This episode uses four cases — Bezos, Brad Karp, Megyn Kelly, and George W. Bush — to break down how cowardice spreads; the second half, on the contest between Harvard and Yale, is key to judging the resistance capacity of American institutions.

6:30 Courage is a social phenomenon, not an individual trait
Weisberg's core argument is that courage and cowardice are both contagious and highly situation-dependent. He does not believe human nature changed dramatically between 2016 and 2024; what changed is the signals people receive from those around them. Trump's second term is more dangerous partly because he controls the government and his own team more firmly — in the first term there were still large numbers of officials he had appointed resisting from the inside, while in the second term there are almost none. When people look around, what they see is not others standing up but others giving way.

10:15 The courage of 2016 was actually following the crowd
Mounk offers a demystifying reading: the people who looked brave in 2016 were in fact following the social incentives of their own small circles. At the time the political incentive was to accommodate Trump, but the social and cultural incentives of their circles were to oppose him, so people stood up. Eight years later those social and cultural incentives have flipped, and the people who looked brave back then are no longer brave. Weisberg agrees with the mechanism but adds that you cannot entirely erase the element of individual moral choice — it is just that true moral heroes, like Mandela and Havel, are extremely rare.

17:45 Brad Karp surrendered in five days
Paul Weiss is the law firm most deeply tied to the American liberal legal tradition, involved in civil rights cases since Brown v. Board of Education, and Karp himself was recruited by Ted Sorensen. Trump threatened to bar the firm's lawyers from government buildings, revoke their security clearances, and sue them on discrimination charges. Weisberg points out that all of this was illegal, that the firm had every right to represent its clients, and that if it sought an injunction it would almost certainly have won — firms like Jenner & Block that chose to fight won quickly. But Karp chose to negotiate at the White House, reaching a deal five days after the executive order, promising free pro bono services, abandoning discrimination, and apologizing for things it had never done. It was a very public, very rapid surrender that sent a signal to the entire legal profession.

24:30 Megyn Kelly went from being bullied to being a bully
In a 2015 debate Kelly challenged Trump over his comments insulting women, and Trump unleashed Steve Bannon and others to threaten her; she needed full-time security, her children needed security, and people showed up in her building lobby to intimidate her. She held out for a while, then reached a truce with Trump. Weisberg's psychological explanation is this: Kelly wrote in her memoir about being bullied as a child, and she vowed never to bully and never to side with bullies, which explains why she resisted Trump so fiercely at the time. But the tragedy is that she herself became a bully, and her show now spends every day viciously mocking transgender people, gay people, and minorities. Weisberg sees this as Trump's effect on the coarsening of political culture — bullying became a way to succeed.

33:00 George W. Bush's silence is an abdication of moral responsibility
In his book Weisberg holds people to their own principles: law firms should defend the rule of law, journalists should defend journalistic principles, businessmen should defend free markets. George W. Bush represents the non-MAGA Republican tradition; after 9/11 he explicitly defended Muslim Americans and pushed PEPFAR, which is estimated to have saved 25 million people worldwide. He privately loathes Trump, painted an ugly portrait of Trump that he has never shown anyone, and did not vote for Trump in 2016. But he adheres to the tradition that former presidents do not criticize their successors. Weisberg argues that if he had spoken publicly at key moments — in 2016, after January 6, and in 2024 — he could have had enormous influence. This is the sin of inaction, different from the sins of action of others in the book, but equally an abdication of moral responsibility.

41:00 Anti-Trump open letters actually backfired
Mounk reflects on the open letters he helped push while involved with Protect Democracy — joint letters from the national security establishment and former state attorneys general — which got a great deal of media coverage, but which he now thinks accomplished almost nothing. The actual effect was to make many people feel that all these professionals were in fact partisan actors, and that their claims of neutrality and objectivity were just a way of doing politics. The intent was to persuade conservatives that this was an issue conservatives should care about too, but instead it reinforced the idea that the only political divide in America is whether you like Trump, that all these people are on the other side, and that I should distrust them wholesale.

48:30 Harvard didn't sign because Trump's price was absurd
Harvard at one point looked like it would reach a deal, even though it had the law on its side and could win in court. The government had the power to restrict foreign students and cancel funding, and even with a $50 billion endowment, Harvard did the math: if it fought the government for four years, it might not survive, or it might survive badly damaged, and it wasn't worth it. But the Trump administration's demands were too absurd — it wanted oversight of whom Harvard appoints as professors, whom it admits, and what it teaches — and Harvard could not sign. As Trump's approval ratings fell and universities kept winning in court, Harvard gradually reached a point where it did not have to sign. Weisberg says that if Democrats take the House in the midterms, he would be extremely surprised if Harvard signed a deal.

52:00 Yale became the next target, but resistance now has a cost
The government turned to Yale, wanting another conspicuous surrender. The New York Times front page reported that Yale was about to reach a deal, based on allegations of racial discrimination against white and Asian students at its medical and law schools, and that Yale was prepared to pay a fine, sign, and carry on. But there was a huge backlash — counter-pressure from faculty, students, alumni, the Connecticut legislature, and Senator Richard Blumenthal. Yale president McInnis now sees that signing has a cost and not signing has a cost, but signing also has a cost. Weisberg agrees with Mounk's judgment: the incentives on the other side are now markedly stronger than a year ago, which makes giving in harder.
